Fish and invertebrate communities differed significantly among habitat types, and with respect to trawling exposure.  Habitat characteristics were quantified with video transects sampled with a remotely operated vehicle, and included percentage coverage of tubeworms, bryozoans, anemones, corals, and algae, significantly affecting fish community structure. Diversity indices differed among habitats, with the highest Shannon diversity (H�) and Pielou�s evenness (J�) over shell-rubble, specifically non-trawled shell-rubble. In addition, higher values of H� and J� were found over trawled sand relative to non-trawled sand habitats.  Length frequency distributions of several abundant fish species showed truncated size distributions over trawled and non-trawled habitats and were both habitat- and species-specific. Median lengths of juvenile (age-1) red snapper were significantly lower over trawled sand (97.4 mm TL) in comparison to non- trawled sand (123.8 mm TL), and significantly lower over trawled shell (125.2 mm TL) in comparison to non-trawled shell (143.8 mm TL) habitat.  Numerically, red snapper displayed an affinity for reef habitats both outside and within non-trawled habitats, providing further support for the view that red snapper have an affinity for structured habitats over the sizes found in this study (mean TL 155 mm � 2mm SE).
Juvenile snapper display a strong thigmotaxis, seeking structured environments (Workman et al. 1994, Szedlemayer and Howe 1997, Bailey et al. 2001, Franks et al. 2004). Szedlemayer and Howe (1997) reported juvenile red snapper selected oyster shell versus sand habitat in tank trials, while Patterson et al. (2005) reported highest juvenile densities in trawl samples off Alabama and Mississippi came from high-relief (2-3 m) shell rubble ridge habitats. Seemingly contrary results were presented by Rooker et al. (2004) and Geary et al. (2007) that demonstrated that juvenile red snapper were in high densities in relatively unstructured mud habitats, and Patterson et al. (2005) reported moderately high juvenile densities occurred in sand habitats off Alabama and Mississippi. It is not clear whether these were young-of-year (age-0) red snapper or juvenile (age-1 and age-2) red snapper.
Adult-Adult red snapper are common in submarine gullies and depressions where food may accumulate and over coral reefs, rock outcrops, and gravel bottoms in the Gulf of Mexico (Stearns 1885, Klima 1976). Usually fewer fish are supported by smooth bottom without high relief than by bottom with three-dimensional structures, such as offshore oil and gas rigs, artificial reefs, and wrecks (Johnston et al. 1976, Sonnier et al. 1976).
Wells and Cowan (2007) found that sub-adult and adult red snapper were found over higher relief habitats such as the shell-rubble and natural hard bottom reef habitats.  They showed both significantly higher abundance and larger size over the reef habitat.   No seasonal effects were observed. Red snapper accounted for 59% of the overall similarity within reef fish assemblages and 20% of the total dissimilarity between shell and reef fish assemblages. It has been suggested that red snapper recruit to these high-relief habitats at about 18 months of age or 20 cm TL (Gallaway et al. 1999).

nodes.title: Artificial Reefs
nodes.body:
Ontogenetic habitat shifts in red snapper habitat utilization is complicated due to the proliferation of artificial reefs deployed in the north-central GOM and the vast number of oil and gas platforms, which function as artificial reefs, erected in the northwestern GOM (Wilson and Nieland 2004, Westmeyer et al. 2007, Patterson et al. 2007).
Gallaway et al. (1981) characterized the food habits of red snapper at the Buccaneer Gas and Oil Field located offshore from Galveston, Texas, at depths of about 10 fathoms (20 m).  They suggested that red snapper moved away from the platforms during the late night to early morning period to feed over soft bottoms.  Hastings et al. (1976) obtained similar results for lutjanids at research platforms in the northeastern Gulf.  Peabody (2004), Peabody and Wilson (2006), and McDonough (2009) also suggested that nocturnal movements of red snapper away from Louisiana platforms was related to feeding behavior.
Dufrene (2005) characterized the inner-shelf area offshore eastern Louisiana to panhandle Florida and suggested that this benthic habitat was about 15% shell (submerged oyster shell banks) and 85% soft sand, mud substrate. The vast majority of the inner shelf in this area is composed of sand, mud, and silt, with little or no vertical relief (Gallaway et al. 2009).
On a larger spatial scale, Parker et al. (1983) estimated that 2,571 square kilometers of natural reef habitat (3.3% of the bottom) is present at depths between 18 and 91 m in the region between Pensacola, Florida and Pass Cavala, Texas.  Of this, only 1.6% (1,285 square kilometers) was comprised of reefs having relief >1m (Parker et al. 1983, Gallaway et al. 2009). If one adds natural reefs further offshore not assessed by Parker et al. (1983) the total area with high-relief natural reefs becomes 1, 578 square kilometers (Gallaway et al. 2009).  Thus, high-relief natural reefs constitute about 2% of the shelf area.
Some 4,000 offshore oil and gas platforms are located across the shelf of the western GOM and provide on the order of 12 square kilometers of artificial reef habitat (Gallaway et al. 2009). Platforms differ from natural reefs in many ways but a unique feature is that that they span the entire water column. Offshore petroleum platforms extend from the beach to the abyss, from Alabama to southern Texas. The highest platform densities occur in shallow and mid-shelf areas.
The construction of oil and gas platforms in the GOM as well as other artificial reefs has corresponded to changes in habitat distribution patterns for red snapper (Gallaway et al. 2009).  In 1960, there were about 351 offshore oil and gas platforms in the northern GOM, but these increased to 1,520 by 1970, and reached 2,540 by 1980. From 1990 to the present, the number of platforms has averaged about 4,000, considering both new installations as well as removals. They proposed that the increased construction of oil and gas platforms as well as other artificial reef habitats has provided protective habitat for age 2 fish that would otherwise have suffered high mortality over open habitats. Although fishing mortality can be high at these new habitats (Nieland and Wilson 2003), Gallaway et al. (2009) suggested that prior to their construction mortality was even higher for age 2 fish over open habitat. This being the case, they suggested that the removal of production platforms and other artificial reefs will likely result in a large reduction in red snapper available to the directed fisheries. They concluded that the existing literature is consistent with the premise of density-dependent natural mortality in red snapper for at least age 0 and age 1 fish, and likely for older fish as well. If this aspect is incorporated in the assessment models, management advice may be substantially altered.
An area of 3,108 square kilometers offshore Alabama has been designated for artificial reef placement and it is estimated that on the order of 10,000 small reefs occur in this area (Gallaway et al. 2009). Collectively, these reefs equate to a total area of 0.1 square kilometers. This is the largest of the artificial reef areas. The area of artificial reef habitat in the western GOM is small compared to the area of natural reefs.  However, artificial reef habitats (especially oil and gas platforms) located in near-shore and mid-shelf zones appear to be used by age-2 red snapper much more than their proportional area would suggest.
Age-2 Population Size at Platforms -1992
Stanley (1994) showed that an average of 5,304 (95% CI = 2,756) red snapper occupied each major platform during the winter 1992.  Gallaway and Cole (1997) used the Stanley (1994) estimate along with platform distribution, size and count data along with red snapper age composition data to estimate 3 million (95% CI = 1.7 to 4.2 million) age-2 red snapper were present around oil platforms throughout the entire GOM at the beginning of 1992.
Goodyear�s (1995) red snapper stock assessment estimated the total age-2 red snapper population in the GOM at the beginning of 1992 was 3.7 million fish. Collectively, these data suggest 70-80% of the total age-2 red snapper population were living around offshore platforms in 1992 (Gallaway and Cole 1997, Gallaway et al. 2009).
Age-2 Population Size at Platforms -1995
Gitshchlag et al. (2003) provided data from explosive platform removal studies in 1995 that suggested, on average that 775 (95% CI =482-1,062) red snapper were present at each offshore platform, large and small combined. These data when multiplied times the number of platforms present in the GOM in 1995 (4,000) times the fraction of fish that were age-2 suggested that 1.1 million age-2 red snapper were present at offshore platforms in 1995. The SEDAR7 (2005) red snapper stock assessment suggested that the total age-2 red snapper population in the western GOM in 1995 was 1.6 million fish. These data suggest that approximately 70% of all age-2 red snapper were living around offshore platforms in 1995 (Gallaway et al. 2009).
Thus, results from at least two independent studies (Stanley 1994, Gitschlag et al. 2003) suggest that a high proportion of the age-2 red snapper population in the western GOM reside at offshore oil and gas platforms (Gallaway et al. 2009).
The main finding summarized by Gallaway et al. (2009) was that submerged oyster shell present in the northern GOM acts as essential habitat protecting age-0 and age-1 red snapper from predation. Without this benthic habitat, most of these �recruits� would not survive.  Likewise, artificial reefs created off Alabama, and oil and gas platforms created off Mississippi, Louisiana and Texas provide high-relief benthic habitat that enhances the survival of age-2 red snapper. Prior to the creation of artificial reefs and oil and gas platforms, they suggested there was a high mortality on age-2 fish due to predation.  The general absence of high-relief natural reefs inshore and on the mid-continental shelf tended to limit the survival of these early life-stages of red snapper.
Shipp (1999) and Shipp and Bortone (2009) have proposed that the creation of artificial reefs and oil and gas platforms have tended to enhance the production of red snapper. It was the transformation of the substratum from a predominantly sandy mud habitat to one having increased areas of hard bottom with high-relief that relieved the �bottleneck� that had previously prevented red snapper from increasing in abundance.  Artificial reefs may attract fish but, in addition they also provide increased habitat that relieves a �bottleneck� in the life history that previously restricted population abundance.  Shipp and Bortone (2009) called this concept the habitat limitation hypothesis.
Some studies have indicated attraction because red snapper were mostly feeding on prey from pelagic environments and open sand-mud habitats (McCawley et al. 2006, Wells et al. 2008b), while others have indicated significant feeding on reef species and artificial reefs were enhancing prey resources (Ouzts and Szedlmayer 2003; Szedlmayer and Lee 2004; Redman and Szedlmayer 2009).

Further evidence of the habitat limitation hypothesis rather than purely attraction was provided by Stedlemayer and Shipp (1994). They demonstrated a marked increase in abundance of early-juvenile (age-0) red snapper within the Alabama artificial reef area following large-scale artificial reef placement. Thus, the increased population of this area was likely attributable to a habitat-related recruitment increase and not a result of migration from other areas.
Stedlmayer (2007) concluded that based on fisheries-independent studies on artificial reefs off Alabama that his group had conducted over the previous decade (Szedlmayer 2000, Szedlemayer and Furman 2000, Stedlmayer et al. 2004) that red snapper populations may be in better condition compared to past assessments.  Using SCUBA surveys on shell/block artificial reef habitats, mean total mortality (Z) was estimated as Z=2.3 for age-0 to age-1 red snapper, similar to previous estimates of Z=1.98 (Nichols et al. 2005) and Z=2.12 (Nance 1998) derived from SEAMAP shrimp trawl data.  Natural mortality (M) was estimated by Stedlmayer (2007) based on the difference between total mortality (Z) and fishing mortality (F), with the present estimate M=1.9 for age-0, M=0.6 for age-1, and M=0.35 for ages 2 to 54.  Combining ages, growth rates, mortalities, and length-weight relation, the estimated transitional spawning potential ratio (SPR) was estimated = 0.21 at F=0.19, and maximum yield was attained when F was increased to 0.3. The main difference is that the Stedlmayer (2007) stock assessment used age-specific estimates for M obtained from benthic habitat surveys rather than stock assessment models not tied to habitat-related information.
Shipp and Bortone (2009) concluded that if the habitat limitation hypothesis is correct, it will be necessary to maintain or even increase the amount of artificial reef habitat to keep pace with fishing pressure. Programs such as �rigs to reefs� efforts off Louisiana and Texas would have to be continued, as would reef construction off Alabama.
All previous GOM stock assessments have concluded that red snapper in the GOM are overfished and undergoing overfishing. However, recent published studies (Stedlmayer 2007, Gazey et al. 2008, Gallaway et al. 2009, Shipp and Bortone 2009) have shown that red snapper are density-dependent and that age 0 and age 1 fish have a much higher natural mortality rate than was used in previous stock assessments. By using a density-dependent model and a higher natural mortality for age 0 and age 1 fish, it appears  that red snapper stock are neither overfished nor undergoing overfishing (Griffin and Woodward 2010). Also, because the natural mortality for age 0 and age 1 fish are much higher than originally assumed, shrimp trawls have less effect on red snapper reaching age 2+ than previously thought. Future stock assessments need to consider density-dependent models and higher natural mortality rates for age 0 and age 1 red snapper.
Cowan et al. (2011a) disagreed with the habitat limitation hypothesis proposed by Shipp and Borton (2009) and with what they called �faith-based fisheries management� of red snapper.  While there were a number of concerns outlined in the paper, Cowen et al. (2011a) took exception to the idea that available habitat for age-1+ fish and older red snapper can limit population size.  They claimed that the premise that year class success in red snapper is not determined until the fish are between 1.5 and 2 years old (the time that they begin to inhabit reefs as sub-adults) was inconsistent with a periodic (bet-hedging) life history strategy.
Some believe that the availability of interstices (i.e., small hiding spots) for newly settled post-larvae and juveniles can be limiting; those individuals not finding refuge suffer high predation rates (Cowan et al. 2011a).  In this case, mortality is thought to be density-dependent (Forrester 1990; Holbrook et el. 2000; Forester and Steele 2000, 2004). But, Cowan et al. (2011a) asserted that age-0 red snapper rarely recruit directly to high-relief natural or artificial reefs; that they settle on sand/mud substrates and transition to more structured habitat with size and age. It is this transition that makes them susceptible to shrimp trawling.
Others believe that the supply of ref fish larvae is limiting, with good year classes being determined by density independent factors that occur while larvae are planktonic prior to settlement on the reefs (citations in Cowan et al. 2011a).
In neither of the above scenarios is habitat for adults limiting; many studies have shown that adult fish usually do not saturate reefs (citations in Cowan et al. 2011a).  In nature, however, it is unlikely to be a simple dichotomy, as more than one factor can be limiting at different life stages (multiple causalities).
Cowan et al. (2011a) argued that the amount of habitat for adult red snapper, especially artificial habitats that account for <5% (Stanley and Wilson 2003) of total useable habitat as compared to suitable natural habitats, probably does not limit recruitment or population size.  They argued that artificial reefs may increase carrying capacity, but this may be negated because they attract predatory fish and fishermen. They inferred that red snapper life history was inconsistent with the notion that habitat limitation (Gallaway et al. 2009, Shipp and Bortone 2009) is a strong actor in regulating population size in this species.
A number of arguments against the habitat limitation hypothesis and against the concept that artificial reefs enhance production of red snapper were presented by Cowan et al. (2011a). Perhaps all that can be concluded is that many changes have occurred concurrently, making it difficult to differentiate which factors (fishing pressure, shrimp trawling, impact of hurricanes, management measures, artificial reefs) have been most important in allowing red snapper populations to increase in the GOM.  Given that offshore shrimp fishing effort (early 2010) was down by as much as 75-85% (SEDAR15 Update  2009) owing to recent coastal storm damage, economic woes, high fuel prices and cheap imported shrimp, bycatch has been declining for the last several years, especially since 2002, and the directed fishery (that also has been impacted by high fuel prices) has recently been constrained by the 2006 Magnuson-Stevens Reauthorization Act (MSRA) to lower total allowable catches (TACs).  Simply put, the recovery formula long prescribed in the agency assessment has finally been realized, although recent estimates of natural mortality (M) for age-0 and age-1 red snapper may diminish the role that bycatch reduction can play in recovery of the stock. Even so, recent sampling off Louisiana and the Florida panhandle (Dance 2008, SEDAR7 Update, 2009) indicates that the increase in numbers is mostly comprised of 3-7 year old fish, but numbers are indeed increasing. Given that artificial reefs and especially oil and gas platforms have been in place for many years (Shipp and Bortone 2009), it seems counterintuitive to award credit to artificial structures for the beginning stages of a stock recovery that is just now becoming apparent.
Results of both the Gazey et al. (2008) study and the work presented by Brooks (SEDAR7 Update, 2009) indicate there is a strong likelihood that natural mortality (M) for juvenile red snapper in the GOM is density-dependent and perhaps quite a bit higher than was assumed during SEDAR7 (2005).  Density-dependent mortality was not incorporated into the assessment (SEDAR7 Update, 2009) for two principal reasons. First, doing so would be a radical departure from an update versus a benchmark assessment. And secondly, there was no time to explore coding the CATCHEM model to incorporate density-dependent mortality into the assessment.

A review of several published studies, along with the above investigations indicates that natural mortality (M) may have been underestimated in SEDAR7 (2005) for age 0 and 1 red snapper in the GOM (SEDAR7 Update, 2009). The estimates of M from these studies ranged from 0.98 to 3.7 for age 0 and from 0.6 to 1.4 for age 1 red snapper. The lower ranges are the values used in SEDAR 7 (2005). However, none of the studies were able to distinguish natural mortality from emigration; therefore, it is possible that some of the M values reviewed were too high. Accordingly, the continuity run maintained the SEDAR7 values, whereas two alternative models utilized a value twice that of SEDAR7 (2005).

Syc (2011) compared the age of red snapper to known age of artificial reefs off Alabama. The size and age of red snapper were sampled from April through November 2010 and compared with the age of the artificial reefs at the site of capture.  Artificial reefs were deployed in 2006 (N=20, 4 year old reefs), 2009 (N=10, 1 year old reefs) and 2010 (N=10, 0.5 year old reefs). Red snapper were sampled with hook-and-line and a fish trap. After sampling was completed, SCUBA divers estimated the remaining red snapper densities at sample reefs using visual surveys, photographs, and video recordings. Syc found significantly older fish on older reefs.  This finding supports previous telemetry studies that showed long-term residency of red snapper on artificial reefs (Topping and Stedlmayer 2011). This relation between reef age and fish age supports previous studies that indicated red snapper production from artificial reefs (Szedlmayer and Shipp 1994; Szedlmayer 2007; Gallaway et al. 2009).  The increased production is likely due to an increase in available reef habitat, which was previously found to be a controlling factor affecting the density and growth of red snapper (Szedlmayer and Shipp 1994; Szedlmayer and Conti 1999; Gazey et al 2008).

Red snapper are recruited to the newly deployed reefs rapidly as juveniles (approximately age-1) and then reside on these reefs for several years (Syc 2011).  If these reefs were only attracting red snapper, there would be no correlation between fish age and reef age, since red snapper would simply be migrating to and from reefs.  In the present case (Syc 2011), the age distribution would have been random, with no clear dominate age classes. However, dominate age classes for each reef year were found and correlated with reef age, providing evidence that artificial reefs were producing rather than simply attracting red snapper.  If artificial reefs are enhancing the population and experiencing no fishing pressure, Powers et al. (2003) estimated that these reefs could increase production by 6.45 kg wet weight per 10 square meters in the first year.  Since the reefs used by Syc (2011) were not known to fishermen, fishing mortality was limited and following the rational of Powers et al. (2003), had the potential to increase production.

Several studies have suggested that red snapper populations are overfished and that habitat   limitation is not a controlling factor (Schrippa and Legault 1999, Patterson et al. 2001a, Cowan et al. 2011a). Clearly, there is significant fishing mortality of red snapper in the northern GOM (Gillig et al. 2000).  However, if fishing mortality was the limiting factor for red snapper and habitat was not important, we would not expect differences in fish age resulting from reef age (i.e. all reefs whether fished or not would show similar age distributions).  Red snapper enter the fishery around age-2, (recreational size minimum = 406 mm, commercial = 330 mm), with the catch predominately consisting of 2 to 4 year old fish.  If fishing mortality was effectively
limiting red snapper, these ages would be harvested and drastically decreased when analyzing
the age distribution. However, these ages represented 59 % (N=602) of the total catch,
indicating that fishing mortality was not controlling the red snapper population (Syc 2011).

One substantial difference between the study by Syc (2011) that suggests habitat limitations, and previous studies which suggested fishing mortality limitations was Syc�s use of fishery independent data. The previous studies mainly used fisher y dependent data for red snapper caught by recreational and commercial fishers (Szedlmayer and Shipp 1994, Baker and Wilson 2001, Patterson et al. 2001b, Wilson et al. 2001). This difference may account for differing results.  Syc (2011) suggested that fishing mortality probably had little influence on age distributions from artificial reefs sampled. In addition, it was possible to sample smaller red snapper that fishery dependent sampling programs cannot access due to size limitations on the fishery. The significant differences between red snapper abundances on the three reef years provide support for increased red snapper production from artificial reefs.

While a considerable amount of information is available concerning benthic habitats in the southeastern Atlantic, there is almost nothing published concerning how red snapper use various benthic habitats in the region (SAFMC Fisheries Ecosystem Plan 2008).

nodes.title: Depth Distribution
nodes.body:
Egg/Parturition- Collins et al. (2001) captured sexually mature female red snapper in spawning condition (hydrated oocytes) during 1999 off Alabama and the west coast of Florida at depths ranging from 23.8 -122.0 m.
Sedberry et al. (2006) captured adult female red snapper in spawning condition in the southeastern Atlantic over a depth range of 24-67 m in MARMAP trawls from South Carolina to Melbourne off eastern Florida. A spawning aggregation of red snapper was observed at Scamp Ridge off South Carolina at a depth of 53 m (Schobernd and Sedberry 2009).  Presumably, eggs occur within the epipelagic (euphotic) zone extending from 0-200 m (Lyczkowski-Shultz and Hanisko 2007).
Larva-The consistent presence of larval red snapper collected in SEAMAP plankton samples during summer and fall surveys between the 100 m and 200 m contour in both the western and eastern GOM supports the contention of Collins et al. (2001) that red snapper spawn over a wide depth range, i.e., from the mid-shelf to the continental slope (Lyczkowski-Shultz and Hanisko 2007).  Hence, larval red snapper occur in the epipelagic zone extending down to 200 m.
Young of Year - Diamond et al. (2010) analyzed NMFS SEAMAP trawl survey data collected during summer and fall surveys in the GOM from 1987 to 2007.  The primary composite hot spots of age 0 red snapper captured during summer surveys started east of the Texas-Louisiana border and extended west toward the Mexican border, ranging from about the 20 m depth contour (isobath) to the 50 m depth contour (Diamond et al. (2010).
Juvenile- Juvenile (age-1) red snapper were mostly captured during summer SEAMAP trawl surveys in the GOM (Diamond et al. 2010).  Annual zones of higher abundance of age-1 red snapper (red and yellow zones) extended from the upper Texas coast (east of Galveston) to western Louisiana ranging from about the 10 m depth contour to the 60 m depth contour.
Adult-Red snapper are abundant at depths of about 4-110 m (Carpenter 1965) and have been caught at 7-146 m in the GOM (Moseley 1966, Rivas 1970). Red snapper were the second most abundant lutjanid captured in MARMAP surveys in the southeast Atlantic (Cueller et al. 1996). Although not as abundant as vermillion snapper, red snappers occurred 124 times (322 individuals) from depths ranging from 7-68 m. In the Carolinas, they are usually found at depths of 46 to 91 m over both low and high relief areas (Grimes et al. 1977).  Red snappers captured in MARMAP surveys ranged in length from 2 to 85 cm. The maximum size of red snapper is approximately 91 cm (Robins and Ray 1986).

Wilson and Nieland (2004) noted that the western GOM off Louisiana and Texas currently produced significant portions of the commercial and recreational harvests of red snapper, however, this was not always the case.  Annual commercial landings in the five states bordering the GOM indicate a shift in the fishery from the eastern to the more western GOM since 1970 concomitant with the placement of several thousand oil and gas platforms into the area. Quantitative estimates of red snapper have been derived both from assessments of the effects of platform removal via explosives and from hydroacoustic surveys of selected platforms.  Based both on these estimates and on the number of platforms, they estimated from 1.2 to 7.2 million live around platforms placed at depths of 20-100 m. Many of these are relatively young individuals of ages 2-4 years.

Petroleum platforms differ from traditional artificial reefs in that their vertical profile extends throughout the water column and provides habitat from the photic zone to the substrate (Wilson and Nieland 2004, Wilson et al. 2006). Historically, a major obstacle in deriving scientific data about the effect of deep water artificial reefs (and platforms) on fishes and other nekton was the difficulty  in quantifying abundance and species composition associated with these reef communities. Wilson et al. (2006) successfully used two complementary techniques, hydroacoustics and point count visual surveys, to estimate the abundance (biomass) and species composition of fishes at several of these structures (Stanley and Wilson 1995, 1996a, 1996b, 1997, 1998, 2000, 2003) and natural reefs (Wilson et al 2003).  In these studies dual-beam hydroacoustics provided estimates of acoustic biomass, density, size distribution, and the near field area of influence. A remotely operated underwater vehicle was used to determine species composition. They found from 10,000 to 30,000 fishes associated with individual platforms; the lowest numbers were found at the largest and deepest structures, leading them to question the value of deep water structures as artificial reefs. They reported that the density of fishes around platforms was ten times greater than open water and from two to three times greater than fish density associated with the upper portion of the West Flower Garden Bank off eastern Texas; species composition also differed between these two habitat types (Wilson et al 2003).

It is of interest that some oil and gas platforms in the eastern, central, and western portions of the GOM had substantial populations of red snapper, while others did not have any red snapper (Wilson et al. 2006).  The depths where reef fish species were observed at the platforms varied depending on the depths where the platforms were situated.  The composition of the platform fish community has been shown to change with location and water depth. Previous researchers have noted a zonation of the assemblage of fishes associated with platforms and have divided the shelf waters of the northern GOM into three zones: coastal (water depth < 27 m), offshore (water depth 27 to 64 m) and bluewater (water depth > 64 m) (Gallaway 1980; Gallaway et al.1981; Gallaway and Lewbel 1982). This was more recently confirmed by Stanley and Wilson (2000), who reported that, at a platform in 219 m of water, pelagic bluewater fishes were found principally in the upper 100 m of the water column and fish density was essentially zero below 100 m depth. At a platform situated at a water depth of 60m, they found fishes throughout the water column, but fish density was highest near the surface and adjacent to the bottom; the fish community was characterized as reef associated shelf species. At a nearshore platform at 20 m depth, fishes were found throughout the water column and the population was characterized as estuarine.

Platforms situated closer to shore at depths <27m, generally had red snapper (Wilson et al. 2006). Platforms at intermediate depth range (27-64 m) were observed to have higher densities of red snapper, while those situated in deeper water (>64 m) tended not to have red snapper associated with them (with one exception).  Generally, speaking red snapper tended to be found near the bottom depth ranges of the platforms. Smaller red snapper were stacked higher-up with larger snapper tending to aggregate around the platforms in deeper water (Render 1995, Wilson et al. 2006).

Red snapper are an important species for both commercial and recreational interests in the northern GOM and as such warrant some special discussion (Wilson et al. 2006).  Of all the habitats included in this study, red snapper were proportionally most dominant at the deeper low-relief feature in comparison to the more shallow high relief feature at Sonnier Bank. This finding is similar to that reported by Wilson et al. (2003) for toppled and partially removed artificial reef structures. Red snappers were proportionally abundant at several platforms in all three regions of the study area; most of these platforms were at the shallowest depths included in the survey design. Few red snappers were observed at those platforms in deeper water at the edge of the Outer Continental Shelf (OCS). The movements of red snapper over their potential 50 year lifespan can help to explain some of the observed distribution. After spending the best part of their first two years in shallow, inshore waters, red snapper begin an offshore migration in search of more suitable, deepwater habitats that might include reefs, lumps, depressions, and wrecks (Nieland and Wilson 2003). In the northern GOM, these suitable habitats include the many oil and gas platforms that have been sited at moderate depths in the nearshore waters. After a residence at the platforms of perhaps 5-8 years, the red snapper migrate away from the platforms and spend the rest of their lives in a relatively solitary existence at natural or anthropogenic, non-platform structures in deeper waters toward the edge of the OCS (Gitschlag et al. 2003, Nieland and Wilson 2003, Gallaway et al. 2009).

Allman and Fitzhugh (2007) also provided length at age data to support the contention that older red snapper are found in deeper water associated with commercial longline catches. Their observations about age differences among gears are consistent with other studies that show red snapper undergo a general ontogenetic shift in habitat and depth.  Nieland and Wilson (2000) reported that age-1 and younger fish dominated benthic habitats sampled by survey trawls, whereas age-2 and age-3 fish dominated the samples obtained by explosive removal of an oil platform. Nieland and Wilson (2000)  further indicated that commercial hook and line collections of red snapper in Louisiana waters revealed few age-2 fish, and in a follow-up paper they speculated that fish older than about age-6 become rare in the hook and line catches due to mortality and emigration from the platforms (Wilson and Nieland 2001).  Mitchell et al. (2004) also suggested older red snapper are less reef-obligate, based on research longline catches.

A comparison of the age, length, and species composition of the NMFS longline survey was conducted to explore the potential of a deepwater (>150 m) reservoir of large, older red snapper in the GOM (Walter and Ingram 2009).   There is concern that there may be a large biomass that is relatively less vulnerable to the fishery and �not seen� by the assessment model because these fish are not taken by the fishery. The age composition of red snapper and depths fished by the NMFS longline survey were compared with age composition and depths of the commercial fisheries from logbook reported depths. There was little evidence from the NMFS survey of a large biomass in GOM waters beyond 150 meters. A peak distribution of red snapper catches occurred between 50-100 m. The percent of positive sets where red snapper were caught were 0% (0-25 m), 5.61% (25-50 m), 24.78% (50-100 m), 8.57% (100-150 m), and 0% (150-450 m).  However, the age composition of the survey differed from that of the various fisheries, even though the fisheries span the depths where the NMFS longline survey encounters older fish. There were more older fish caught by NMFS longline surveys and by commercial longline vessels in the western GOM in comparison to the eastern GOM. It appears that older red snapper may be only partially selected for by the fisheries, particularly the handline fishery and to a lesser extent by the longline fishery. While the commercial longline fishery in the GOM does capture older fish, it is in a lower proportion in comparison to the NMFS longline survey, indicating that some biomass may be less selected for by these fisheries. Some caution should be taken in these conclusions as the age composition for the commercial fisheries only represents landed fish and not discards, which could be high if fishers do not possess red snapper quota. The results suggest that there could be additional older biomass relatively less vulnerable to the fisheries but that this reduction in vulnerability is likely a spatial rather than a depth-related process and it likely occurs in waters shallower than 150 m. This lends support to the dome-shaped selectivities estimated by the CATCHEM model for the commercial handline and eastern longline fisheries (SEDAR7 Update 2009).

Scott-Denton et al. (2011) used observer data to describe the commercial bottom longline and commercial vertical-line fisheries in the GOM. From July 2006 through December 2009, data were collected from 9,468 sets collected during 308 trips aboard 2005 reef fish vessels. Of 30,125 red snapper observed being caught, 2456 were taken on longlines and 27,669 were caught on vertical lines. Approximately 77% of the red snapper taken on vertical lines were caught in the western GOM, with the remaining taken in the eastern GOM. Hotspot analyses of the vertical line fishery for red snapper using GIS indicated that the highest CPUEs occurred from the Florida Panhandle to the Mississippi Delta, off the Louisiana-Texas border area, and off Corpus Christi. Low CPUEs occurred on the West Florida Shelf. The majority (65%) were kept. Based on visual observations, 24% were released alive, 10% were discarded dead, and 1% discarded in an unknown condition. Depths of red snapper capture ranged from 6.0 to 558 m. Most (29%) of red snapper were caught in waters <37 m, followed by 37-46 m (26%), 47-56 m (13%), 57-64 m (13%). The remaining depth zones comprised 19%.  The immediate minimum assumed mortality of red snapper was 27% in the longline fishery and 28% in the vertical line fishery.

Recently, red snapper fishermen have claimed that a cryptic portion of the red snapper population in the South Atlantic is not being fully exploited or largely missed by the fishery (Southeast Fisheries Science Center 2010).  The fishermen have suggested that the biggest and oldest red snapper exist in the deepest depths and are not accessible by hook and line gear. They note that currents in the deeper depths prevent effective fishing with vertical hook and line gear and that the distance vessels must travel offshore to get to the deeper depths can be cost prohibitive.

In the southeast Atlantic, Hester and Nelson (2010) analyzed landings data obtained from Dr. Jennifer Potts (leader of the Life History Working Group for the SEDAR 24  red snapper stock assessment) collected from recreational Charter boats (CB), Head Boat (HB), Private Recreational (PR) boats, and commercial boats (CM) from North Carolina to Florida. There were 759 data records with depth recorded by minimum and maximum depths fished, along with the sex, fork length (FL) in mm, total length (TL) in mm, and the calendar age of each fish.  Where a depth fished was not provided by fishing location (most of data for each fisheries), a depth was computed by averaging the minimum and maximum depths fished provided per trip. While there was a lot of scatter in the data, a positive regression was derived indicating that the total length increased with increasing depth.  Plots of mean age and median age by depth for all sectors demonstrated that older fish (up to about age 9) tended to occur in deeper water. Similarly, longer fish tended to occur in deeper water.

The median depth fished in the southeast Atlantic by HB was 89 ft (27 m), CB 127.5 ft (39 m), and CM 135 ft (41 m) (Hester and Nelson 2010).  The median size of red snapper in the catch for each fishery was found to be 561.5 mm TL for HB, 558.0 mm TL for CB, and 607.0 mm TL for CM.  Fishing effort frequency distributions also indicated the approximate depth ranges fished. For HB the range was 1-175 ft (1-53 m), CB 1-280 ft (1-85 m), CM 1-336 ft (1-102 m). While CM tended to fish in somewhat deeper water than the recreational boats combined and catch slightly longer red snapper, the mean differences were not large. The analyses supported assertions by the commercial fishermen that they fish closer to shore, than what had been assumed during the SEDAR15 (2009) stock assessment. There were not many older fish being caught and landed by these fisheries.

The Date Workshop (DW) report produced by the Life History Working Group (SEDAR24 DW Report 2010) presented two graphs (Figure 2.9.1a and 2.9.1b) that depicted the depth distribution of U.S. South Atlantic red snapper for fishing fleets combined. Figure 2.9.1a depicted the size (TL mm) versus depth. There is no increasing relationship of length with depth apparent from the graph. The second graph (Figure 2.9.1b) depicted the age of red snapper versus depth.  Approximately 30 fish ranging in age from age-30 to age-50 are included in the graph.  Most of these older fish were found at depths ranging from 150 to 300 ft (50-100m). The proportion of older fish in the plot declined at depths ranging from 300 to 400 feet (100-133 m).

Landings for red snapper using longline gear in the southeastern Atlantic have never been large (Southeast Fisheries Science Center 2010). The SAFMC prohibited the use of longline gear inside 91 m (300 ft) in 1992. In 1999, the council also prohibited vessels with longline gear aboard to possess red snapper (Snapper Grouper Amendment 9). Hence, there presently is no longline fishery directed at red snapper in the southeastern Atlantic, which could catch older red snapper in deeper water.

Logbook data from commercial vessels and recreational headboats were analyzed by NOAA/NMFS staff (Southeast Fisheries Science Center 2010).  Also limited depth data were collected for some headboat trips by observers. They noted that ideally one would have detailed depth of capture information for red snapper caught in all fishery sectors. Unfortunately, this was not the case. Plots were created that examined snapper fishing effort by depth and the relative proportion selected by age groups up to age 20. However, it was not stated at what depths the older fish were captured.

Accounts by fishermen have suggested that red snapper exhibit a seasonal migration from offshore to inshore to form spawning aggregations (Southeast Fisheries Science Center 2010). These aggregations have been termed �snapper bonanzas,� owing to the large daily catches produced during these events. Like other snapper-grouper species that form spawning aggregations, they are likely more vulnerable during this time. If the largest (and oldest) red snapper are moving inshore to form spawning aggregations and their vulnerability is increased during that time period, then the results suggesting a constantly increasing selectivity, peaking at the oldest ages, may be more accurate. The general conclusion drawn from the analysis was that dome-shaped selectivity likely was not appropriate for the commercial handline sector and might not be appropriate for the recreational sectors (Southeast Fisheries Science Center 2010). These conclusions were largely driven by the age at depth data, which suggested no significant trend in age 5+ fish with depth.

A peer review of the red snapper research and management in the GOM recommended the need to monitor the number and length frequencies of red snapper discards (MRAG Americas, Inc. 1997).  Onboard observers were suggested as the best way to estimate discard mortality rates. This led to research and monitoring programs on both recreational and commercial fishing vessels (MRAG Americas Inc.  1999).  Several studies have focused on depth as an important factor in determining discard mortality of red snapper due to the visible impact of barotraumas (Collier 2010).  Studies conducted in shallow water (<35m or <115 feet) estimated discard mortality rates of 20% or less (Parker 1985, Render and Wilson 1994, Patterson et al. 2002, Burns et al. 2006). Studies conducted in deeper waters generally estimated higher discard mortality rates ranging from 17% to 93% (Gitschlag and Renaud 1994, Render and Wilson 1994, Dorf 2003, Burns et al. 2004, Nieland et al. 2007, Burns 2009, Diamond and Campbell 2009, Stephen and Harris 2009). The increase in discard mortality with increasing depth is an expected result and has been described for red snapper and other snapper grouper species (Patterson et al. 2001, Burns et al. 2002, Patterson et al. 2002, Rudershausen et al. 2007, Stephen and Harris 2009).

To estimate discard mortality rates, a �sink or swim� approach was suggested in which onboard observers would note the short-term fate of discarded red snapper: whether or not the fish swam down out of site (Dorf 2003, Stephen and Harris 2009).  Another suggested method to determine mortality rate involved releasing red snapper in cages, then lowering them to depth.  This method was used by Gitschlag and Renaud (1994) and by Render and Wilson (1994).

Dorf  (2003) put observers on recreational headboats off Texas and collected data during 54 trips fishing at a mean depth of 40.2 m (range 13.4-95.4 m). Red snapper less than the 1999 federal minimum size in the GOM of 450 mm (18-in) TL made up 93.4% of the 3,863 snapper collected.  Those less than the Texas state minimum size of 375 mm (15-in) made up 64.0% of the catch. When brought on board, 70.2% of snapper appeared normal and 26.1% had protruding stomachs. Of the discarded red snapper, 60.6% were released alive and swam down, 22.8% swam erratically, 15.2% floated, and 1.4% were discarded dead.  Galveston had the highest discard: landing ration (211:1) and smallest mean fish sixe (0.7 kg, 343 mm). Port Aransas had the lowest discard: landing ratio (5.2:1) and the largest mean fish size (0.9 kg, 387 mm).

Venting fish to reduce the effects of barotraumas and reduce discard mortality of red snapper has been researched.  Red snapper caught in shallow water experience little benefit from venting (Render and Wilson 1994, Render and Wilson 1996, Burns et al. 2002, Burns et al. 2008). In fact, venting fish may cause increased mortality for a variety of species (Wilde 2009, 2011). However, vented red snapper caught in waters deeper than 42 m increased survival compared to non-vented red snapper (Burns et al. 2008).  Smaller red snapper, which survive barotraumas better than larger fish, are normally found in shallower water while larger fish are typically found in deeper water (Burns et al. 2008).

Hook type has been discussed as a potential mechanism to reduce discard mortality.  However, Burns et al. (2008) found that there was not a significant decrease in discard mortality for red snapper caught on circle hooks compared to J hooks.  SEDAR7 (2005) stated red snapper discard mortality decreased by 50% for fish caught with circle hooks compared to those caught with J hooks.  A decrease in mortality of red snapper with circle hooks was also noted by Koenig (Burns et al. 2002) and by Rummer (2007).

Nieland et al. (2007a) sampled red snapper from commercial landings from the GOM off Louisiana from October 2001 to May 2004.  Red snapper ages (N=2,867) estimated from counts of annuli on otoliths ranged from 1 to 14 years; however, the vast majority (97.7%) of these were ages 2 to 6 years and the modal age was 3 years. Total lengths of all specimens were less than 600 mm TL. They also investigated the fate of red snapper regulatory discards (individuals <382 mm [15 inch] TL) during 16 trips on working commercial vessels; over two-thirds of 4,839 red snapper assigned among four discard fate categories (ranging from alive and vigorous to dead) were returned to the water either in moribund or dead condition.  Mortality among regulatory discards was very high and related to depth of capture. Among the discards, 778 (16%) swam down vigorously, 714 (15%) swam down slowly or erratically, 1,765 (36%) were alive but could not swim down, and 1,582 (33%) were dead.  There was a significant positive relationship between the percent mortality (proportion of discards in categories 3 and 4) and capture depth (across depth range 10-90 m) for all fishing opportunities where five of more discards were assessed.

Among 399 potential discards retained for age and length analyses, 86% were between 12 and 15 inches (305-381 mm) TL and 85% were 2 years of age (Nieland et al. 2007a). They concluded that the minimum size regulation appears to do little to protect juvenile red snapper from commercial fishing mortality. Heavy red snapper mortality, which begins as bycatch mortality in shrimp trawls, continues as discard mortality at sub-legal lengths when they first recruit to the offshore fishing grounds, and persists as harvest mortality among the youngest legal year- and size-classes. If the minimum size limit is intended to provide a respite from such mortality, a reconsideration of the utility of the minimum length regulation of the commercial harvest of red snapper (in the GOM) may be warranted.

In addition to the direct mortality monitored, �sink or swim� indicators suggest that red snapper experience a delayed mortality associated with injuries and stress obtained from capture (Diamond and Campbell 2009).  The ability of a fish to submerge after discarding is often used as a proxy for survival, but this practice underestimates total discard mortality because delayed mortality is overlooked.  Fishery managers need a way to link �sink or swim� indicators, or variables observed during capture and release, with delayed mortality rates.  Diamond and Campbell (2009) conducted a cage study of red snapper off the coast of Texas to estimate delayed mortality rates and to find factors that could link immediate and delayed mortality, between surface and bottom waters.  Immediate mortality (17%) was predicted by the interaction of depth and the differences in temperature between surface and bottom waters. Lactate levels were also significant predictors of immediate mortality in fish whose blood was tested. Delayed mortality (64%) was predicted primarily by a condition index consisting of the presence or absence or injuries, symptoms of barotraumas, and fish behaviors immediately after capture. Specific categories included bleeding, protruding intestines, everted stomach, exopthalmia, the presence or absence of flapping or gilling behaviors, and problems with cage submergence.  The majority of fatalities occurred within 24 h after fish were placed in the cages. Their mortality estimates indicated that red snapper discard mortality was significantly underestimated in the 2005 stock assessment for red snapper (SEDAR7 2005).  Diamond and Campbell (2009) concluded that the use of indices that relate the condition of an individual fish at capture to its probability of delayed mortality is an excellent method for linking immediate and delayed mortality and will likely be applicable to many species that are subject to catch-and-release fishing.

The key to a successful catch and release (CAR) program is that fish actually survive the CAR experience (Rummer 2007).  Management strategies are typically designed assuming CAR is below 20%.  Recent field studies suggest this may be possible for red snapper retrieved from depths ranging from 20-40 m (Patterson et al. 2001b, Burns et al. 2004) but rates may be greater than 70% if red snapper are retrieved from deeper depths (Burns et al. 2002). Logbook records from commercial vessels suggest rates may range upwards of 72-78% (Poffenberger and McCarthy 2004).  CAR mortality depends on a multitude of factors. However, the main underlying cause of CAR mortality is directly related to depth of capture.

The most effective way to manage a fishery that succumbs so seriously to CAR mortality is not via size limits, seasonal closures, and bag limits (Rummer and Bennett 2005, Rummer 2007). All combinations seem problematic; either the socioeconomics of the red snapper fishery or the potential for population growth and recovery are negatively impacted.  Rummer (2007) proposed that it would seem logical to impose fishery restrictions to discrete areas such that fish populations can be safeguarded from all fishing and CAR activity, therefore protecting age, size, sex classes and ratios simultaneously.  For fish like red snapper, where overfishing is widespread and CAR mortality is high, marine protected areas (MPAs) and/or no take reserves (NTRs) were proposed as having the greatest potential for overall conservation and sustainability of red snapper fisheries.

Estimated Discards SEDAR24
Observers working for the Gulf and South Atlantic Fisheries Foundation (GSAFFI) gathered data on the amount of discarding and discard mortality on snapper-grouper species caught on commercial hook-and-line (HH) vessels in the southeast Atlantic (GSAFFI 2008, 2010).  The data were collected on HH vessels fishing in Latitude zones 30 to 33 stretching from northern Florida to southern North Carolina.  A relatively high proportion of the red snapper catch taken in 2007 was below the 50 cm minimum size.  In terms of numbers, 97.7% of the catch of red snapper taken in 2007 was considered to be discarded bycatch (GSAFFI 2008).   Detailed information concerning CPUEs for red snapper kept and discarded was presented by statistical zones for Latitudes 30-33 for 2008 and for 2009 (GSAFFI 2010).  During 2008, the percentages discarded ranged from 57.7-77.9% during the first trimester, 58.4-73.3% in the second trimester, and 21.0-42.0% in the third trimester.  During, 2009, there was a decrease in the proportion of red snapper discarded which appears to be related to a decline in abundance of red snapper below the 50 cm minimum size limit. The proportion discarded across zones 30-33 ranged from 15.5-27.5% during the first trimester, 15.9-28.5% during the second trimester, and 3.8-10.2% during the third trimester.  Overall, the percent discarded during 2008 and 2009 averaged 34.8% (GSAFFI 2010). These data were provided to NMFS for use with the SEDAR24 stock assessment.

The GSAFFI reports demonstrate that discarding rates of red snapper can be very high when there are high numbers of undersized red snapper due to periodic recruitment.  The length frequency for red snapper during 2007 demonstrates high recruitment of undersized fish ranging from 30-50 cm TL (GSAFFI 2008).  Tabulated mean catch rates (CPUEs) for both kept and discarded red snapper indicate that most of this recruitment occurred off northeast Florida and off Georgia with lower mean CPUEs off South Carolina and North Carolina (GSAFFI 2010).  A decrease in mean CPUEs of discarded fish occurred, while mean CPUEs of kept fish increased by the third quarter of 2008. This trend continued into 2009 with mean CPUEs of kept fish increasing, while mean CPUES of discarded fish decreased.  The simplest explanation for this is that growth of the recruits during 2008 allowed more fish to be kept and fewer fish to be discarded as they increased in size to exceed the minimum size limit of 50 cm (20 inches) TL. This pattern is also apparent with length frequencies for red snapper measured from 2007 to 2009 by at-sea observers on headboats off Florida and to a lesser extent off Georgia (Sauls and Wilson 2010).

nodes.title: Discard Moralities South Atlantic
nodes.body:
The estimates of discard mortality used in SEDAR15 (2007) were 90% for the commercial fishery and 40% for the recreational fishery in the southeast Atlantic (SEDAR24 DW Report 2010).  The recreational estimate (40%) matched the discard mortality estimate for red snapper from the GOM for fish caught in waters deeper than 20 m (SEDAR7 2005).  A working paper was developed for SEDAR24 which includes a comprehensive discussion of discard mortality (Collier 2010).  To account for an increasing discard mortality rate with depth, three models were investigated to describe these depth effects.  Two of the models (Burns et al. 2002, Diamond et al. unpublished) used a logistic regression function to model the mortality rate and one used a linear trend (Nieland et al. 2007a). The plenary decided to use the depth model presented in Burns et al. (2002) to estimate discard mortality (SEDAR24 DW Report 2010).  The discard mortality estimate for the commercial fishery was 48%. The mortality rate chosen for both the recreational headboat fishery and the recreational charterboat fishery was 41.3%.  The private boat mortality rate estimate used in SEDAR24 was 38.8%.

The plenary decided to develop discard mortality estimates based on the relationship of discard mortality with depth (Burns et al. 2002). This method, used observer data having depth information for released fish (GSAFFI 2008, 2010). These observer data were collected during 2007-2009 between latitudes 30 and 33. Estimates of mortality were obtained by calculating a weighted average mortality from the Burns et al. (2002) equation, weighted by the depth profile. The profiles were computed in 25 ft intervals while the mortality estimates from Burns et al. (2002) were computed at the mid-points of these intervals. These estimates were relatively insensitive to interval width since approximately the same result (same whole percent) was obtained with 1 ft intervals from the observer data. To represent discard mortality of red snapper discarded from 1992-2009, the WG recommended the commercial mortality estimate based on discarded fish (48%).

In August 2001, the Southeast Fisheries Science Center (SEFSC) initiated a program to collect discard data from commercial fishing vessels landing federally managed species in the GOM and US South Atlantic (McCarthy 2010). A reporting form was developed as a supplement to the mandatory coastal logbook forms. Discard data from the SEFSC coastal fisheries logbook program were used to calculate the number of red snapper that were discarded in the U.S. South Atlantic during the period January 1, 2001 through December 31, 2009.  Fishing gear strata included handline, electric reel (bandit rig) trolling, longline, trap, gillnet and diving. Selected fishers were required to complete a supplemental discard form for every trip they made. To calculate species specific discard rates, discard data were matched to the effort data reported to the coastal logbook program.

A delta lognormal model was used to calculate the yearly least square means of the red snapper discard rate (McCarthy 2010).  This method combined separate general linear model (GLM) analyses of the proportion of trips that discarded red snapper and the discard rates of trips that discarded red snapper to construct a single standardized discard rate.  Total discards for each year were then calculated using a ratio estimator: yearly least square means (discard rate)*reported yearly total effort.

Discard mortalities (in units of 1000 fish) were modeled with the Baranov catch equation, which required estimates of discard selectivities and release mortality probabilities (SEDAR 24, 2010). Discards were assumed to have fleet-specific mortality probabilities, as suggested by the data workshop (commercial lines, 0.48; for-hire, 0.41; private, 0.39). Annual discard mortalities, as fit by the model, were computed by multiplying total discards (tabulated in the DW report) by the fleet-specific release mortality probability. For for-hire and private fleets, discard time series were assumed to begin in 1983, with the start of the 12-inch size limit; for the commercial lines fleet, discards were modeled starting in 1992 with the 20-inch size limit. Discards from the commercial dive fleet were assumed negligible and not modeled. Using these methods the numbers discarded per year were added to the reported fisheries landings data that were used to compute fishing mortalities.

Actual red snapper discards may be higher than the calculated totals presented by McCarthy (2010). In the limited observer data available discarded red snapper were more common than
retained red snapper (60% to 40% of 644 fish) (SEDAR24 DW 2010). Self-reported discards obtained from logbooks were reported in numbers of fish and lack length information making a similar comparison with landings data difficult. Discards and landings of red snapper from the commercial fishery, however, appear to be relatively low, particularly when compared to the recreational fishery. The total commercial discards from McCarthy (2010) may represent a minimum estimate of the number of red snapper discarded from the commercial fishery. The conclusion of the Commercial Work Group was that the SEDAR 24-DW01 report by McCarthy (2010) represents the best available information on commercial red snapper discards.

nodes.title: Temperature
nodes.body:
Egg/Parturition- Collins et al. (2001) captured sexually mature (mature ovaries with hydrated oocytes) female red snapper off Alabama and the west coast of Florida in the GOM at locations with bottom temperatures of 20.6oC and ranging from 26.8-29oC.
A spawning aggregation of red snapper was observed at Scamp Ridge off South Carolina in the southeast Atlantic at a bottom temperature of 20.9oC (Schobernd and Sedberry 2009).
Larva-Lyczkowski-Schultz and Hanisko (2007) tabulated the range of temperatures where red snapper were caught in surface neuston nets in the GOM during the Summer Groundfish (SG) surveys and the Fall Plankton (FP) surveys from 2000 to 2003.  Surface water temperatures ranged from 27.1-31.0oC (mean=29.4oC) for SG, and ranged from 25.4-30.3oC (mean=29.2oC) for FP.
Young of Year-
Juvenile-High value habitat for juvenile red snapper in the western GOM determined from a habitat suitability index (HSI) model was characterized as temperatures ranging from 24-26oC (Gallaway et al. 1999).
Adult-A spawning aggregation of red snapper was observed at Scamp Ridge off South Carolina at a bottom temperature of 20.9oC (Schobernd and Sedberry 2009).

nodes.title: Salinity
nodes.body:
Egg/Parturition- A spawning aggregation of red snapper was observed at Scamp Ridge off South Carolina at a bottom salinity of 36.5 g/L (Schobernd and Sedberry 2009).  Presumably, eggs occur near the surface over the same salinity range documented for larvae caught with neuston nets (Lyczkowski-Schultz and Hanisko  2007)
Larva- Lyczkowski-Schultz and Hanisko (2007) tabulated the range of salinities where red snapper were caught in surface neuston nets in the GOM during the Summer Groundfish (SG) surveys and the Fall Plankton (FP) surveys from 2000 to 2003.  Surface water salinities ranged from 24.2-35.7 psu (mean=32.5 psu for SG, and ranged from 27.2-36.6 psu (mean=34.7 psu) for FP.
Young of Year-
Juvenile-High value habitat for juvenile red snapper in the western GOM determined from a habitat suitability index model occurred at salinities around 35 g/L (ppt) (Gallaway et al. 1999).
Adult- A spawning aggregation of red snapper was observed at Scamp Ridge off South Carolina at depth of 53 m and a bottom salinity of 36.5 g/L (Schobernd and Sedberry 2009).

nodes.title: Dissolved Oxygen
nodes.body:
Egg/Parturition-No information found.
Larva- Lyczkowski-Schultz and Hanisko (2007) tabulated the range of dissolved oxygen levels where red snapper larvae were caught in surface neuston nets in the GOM during the Summer Groundfish (SG) surveys and the Fall Plankton (FP) surveys from 2000 to 2003.  Surface water dissolved oxygen levels ranged from 4.7-6.7 mg/L (mean=5.7 mg/L) for SG, and ranged from 5.5-6.6 mg/L (mean=6.1 mg/L) for FP.
Young of Year-
Juvenile- Seasonal habitat suitability index (HSI) models were developed for juvenile red snapper (age-0 and age-1) in the western GOM (Gallaway et al. 1999). Habitat factors considered in the analysis included water temperature, salinity, and dissolved oxygen at the bottom; depth and density of offshore petroleum platforms; and low-relief bottom structures.  High value habitat for juvenile snapper was characterized by depths between 18 and 64 m, water temperatures of 24-26oC, salinities around 35 g/L, and dissolved oxygen levels of at least 5 mg/L.  Density of low-relief structures was not a significant habitat element, and an inverse relationship was found between juvenile red snapper abundance and the density of offshore platforms. Results of the model analysis suggest that the step-like expansion of the hypoxic area (dissolved oxygen <= 2 mg/L) offshore of the mouth of the Mississippi River and west to the Texas border, which first occurred in 1993, reduced the habitat carrying capacity for juvenile red snapper in this region by up to 25%, averaging 19%. Gallaway et al. (1999) suggested that this environmental change may limit the level to which overfished GOM red snapper can be rebuilt to historical levels.
