nodes.title: FOOD HABITS
nodes.body: Trophic Mode: Juvenile and adult red snapper are carnivorous.

nodes.title: Feeding
nodes.body:
Larvae-Newly hatched larvae in the laboratory began actively feeding on a culture of algae and rotifers 3 days after hatching and were 2.5 mm SL 4 days after hatching (Rabalais et al. 1980).   Snapper larvae demand sufficient quantities of small prey organisms at the onset of first-feeding (Lan 2001, Ogle and Lotz 2000, Lemus et al. 2004, Rhodes and Phelps 2008). Copepod nauplii have proved to be an appropriate prey for red snapper larvae being cultured (Ogle et al. 2002, Lemus et al. 2002, Ogle et al. 2005).  Little information exists concerning what larval red snapper feed on in the ocean.
                                                                                                                                                                                                               Young of Year-
Juvenile-Small zooplankters were common prey of juveniles up to 150 mm FL, but the fish probably start to prefer larger prey when they are about 100 mm FL (Bradley and Bryan 1976).  Stomachs of juveniles most frequently contained shrimp throughout the year in the Gulf of Mexico (Camber 1955, Bradley and Bryan 1976). Other crustaceans (including crabs), fish and squid were found in 2-10% of the sampled fish. The types of prey that contributed the greatest percentage by volume to the diet of juveniles were squid, octopuses, and shrimp. Juveniles and adults eat a large variety of species of mollusks, crustaceans, and fishes.
Adult-Camber (1955) reported that adult red snapper in the GOM took the following prey (in decreasing order of frequency of occurrence); shrimp, small reef fish, crabs, and gastropods. He stated that tunicates may be taken in the spring.
Futch and Bruger (1976) stated that red snapper may feed over sand, shell, or mud bottoms next to reefs or other rocky bottoms. Many of the prey of red snapper are found over level bottoms adjacent to the reefs, rather than on the reefs themselves (Oavis 1975).

nodes.title: Food Items
nodes.body:
Larva- No information found.
Young of Year-
Juvenile One of the most comprehensive early red snapper diet studies was conducted by Bradley and Bryan (1975). They described the diets by season, of trawl-collected (open sand-mud habitat) and hook-and-line reef �rough bottom areas� red snapper from off the Texas coast.  They described the diets of 258 open-habitat and 190 reef habitat red snapper (25-325 mm FL) and found that juvenile red snapper were dependent on shrimp, crabs, and crustaceans.  They described a change in juvenile red snapper diet as fish size increased.  Young red snapper depended almost exclusively on invertebrates, and showed a gradual increase in vertebrate prey with growth.  However, they did not separate out the proportions of juveniles sampled over reef versus open habitats.
Lee (1998) and Szedlemayer and Lee (2004) examined the diets and habitat shift of juvenile red snapper from open sand-mud habitat (little or no relief) to artificial reef habitat (1 cubic meter concrete or PVC blocks), from June 1993 through December 1994.  In 1994, fish settled over open habitat from June to September, then began shifting to reef habitats. The shift was almost complete by December (visual surveys using SCUBA). Stomachs were examined from 1639 fish ranging from 18-280 mm SL. Of these, 850 had empty stomachs, and 346 from open habitat and 443 from reef habitat contained prey. Small red snapper (<60 mm SL) fed mostly on chaetognaths, copepods, shrimp, and squid. Larger red snapper (60-280 mm SL) shifted feeding to fish prey, greater amounts of squid and crabs, and continued feeding on shrimp.  Red snapper diets separated by habitat types rather than fish size for the size ranges that over-lapped habitats.  These diet shifts were attributed to feeding more on reef prey than on open-water prey. Thus, the shift in habitat shown by juvenile red snapper was reflected in their diet and suggested differential habitat values based not just on predation refuge but on food resources as well.
Wells et al. (2008c) used stable isotopes and stomach content analyses to describe the diet of red snapper in the northern GOM.  Approximately 1000 fish were collected over two years to test the possible effects of ontogeny, habitat, and a non-trawl reef permit area on red snapper diets. Stable isotopes of carbon, nitrogen, and sulfur were measured in both red snapper and potential primary producers. Ontogenetic shifts in diet occurred with increasing red snapper size-at-age, resulting in higher carbon13 and higher nitrogen15 isotope values and lower sulfur34 isotope values in larger fish.  Stomach content results supported ontogenetic shifts in diet by showing a change in diet from zooplankton, mysid shrimp, and squid for juvenile (ages 0 to 1) to diets dominated by benthic crustaceans and fishes for adults (ages 2+).  Habitat-specific differences in isotopes and stomach contents of similarly sized fish were identified; however, feeding differences, both in carbon13 and in prey identified in stomach contents, were detected, but were minimal.  Red snapper from outside a single non-trawl reef permit area had higher nitrogen15 isotope values and lower sulfur34 values than for conspecifics inside the non-trawl reef permit area.  The analyses of stable isotopes demonstrated that red snapper (ages 0 to 2) rely on sand and mud-associated prey regardless of the habitat from which they were collected, suggesting that the importance of shell and natural reef habitats was more important for red snapper survival than for additional prey resources. Juvenile red snapper occupying sand and mud recruit to structured habitats, such as shell-rubble to obtain refuge from predators, while obtaining prey items such as fish, from adjacent sand and mud areas.
Adult- Most red snapper diet studies have found that as individuals grow, there is a shift in their diet from invertebrates and zooplankton to a dependency on fish (Moseley et al. 1966, Bradley and Bryan 1975, Szedlemeyer and Lee 2004). A few studies (e.g., Camber 1955) have reported that large red snapper continue to eat demersal crustaceans. Pelagic zooplankton contributed to the diet of all size classes of red snapper examined by McCawley and Cowan (2007), decreasing only for snapper larger than 500 mm FL. Moseley concluded that it was inefficient for red snapper larger than 110 mm SL to exist on zooplankton. However, Siegel (1983) found that adult red snapper up to 550 mm SL off Alabama continued to consume significant amounts of pelagic zooplankton, especially larval decapods and stomatopods.
Gallaway et al. (1981, 2009) reported the gut contents of red snapper at oil and gas platforms in winter contained mainly fish (small carangids, mainly platform associated rough scad). In spring, the diet was dominated by fish (unidentified fish 23.5%, Atlantic cutlass fish 19.3%, and carangids-probably scad 18.6%, and mantis shrimp 29.5%. In fall, crustaceans (shrimp, 53.2% and crabs 17.2%f or a total of 70.4%) and fish (26.6%) dominated the diets.  Clearly, soft-bottom prey were a major component of the diet, but reef associated fish were taken when abundant.

Siegel (1983) described red snapper food habits from habitats sampled offshore Alabama and some samples from Louisiana and Florida.  For adults, fish and crabs constituted the main part of the diet.  Of interest, all sizes of adults were noted to consume crabs, rock shrimp, penaeid shrimp, larval decapods, and larval mantis shrimp.

Ouzts and Szedlmayer (2003) examined the diets of red snapper collected from the artificial reef area offshore Alabama among four diel feeding periods (dawn, day, dusk, and night) and among three standard size classes small (200-299 mm SL), medium (300-399 mm SL), and large (400-499 mm SL). A total of 432 stomachs were examined, of which 164 contained prey.  Prey items were assigned a habitat association based on the literature, the authors� observations, and expert opinion. Small red snapper fed mostly on reef and sand prey types, medium red snapper fed on similar portions of reef, sand and mixed habitat prey types; and large red snapper fed mainly on prey observed to use a variety of habitats.  Red snapper were found to feed throughout the 24-hr cycle, with mean gut fullness being significantly lower at dusk than for the day period. Fish were the dominant prey throughout the 24-h cycle. The second-most important prey group changed with period: shrimp were codominant for dawn, tunicates for day, and crabs were codominant for dusk and night periods.

As previously described, the study by Szedlemayer and Lee (2004) focused on food habits of juvenile (< 200 mm SL) red snapper from open bottom and artificial reefs offshore of Alabama.  However, 61 specimens were collected from reefs that ranged from 200-250 mm SL. For these fish, the principal prey categories on a volumetric basis were fish (59.7%), shrimp (27.8%), and crabs (12.5%). For the fish-prey category approximately 65% were reef associated taxa.  Reef associated shrimp species constituted 54.2% as compared with 42.4% from open-bottom habitats. The Szedlemeyer and Lee (2004) findings indicate that adult red snapper (200-250 mm SL) fed on both reef and open habitat prey types.  Even if, all crabs and all the shrimp but pistol and cleaner shrimp are  treated as soft-bottom species, reef prey still constituted about 46% of the diet based on this data set (Gallaway et al. 2009).
McCawley et al. (2006) collected diel food habitat data for red snapper in the Alabama reef areas during July and August 2000. A total of 109 red snapper stomachs were collected from fish 295-560 mm FL.  Of these 46 contained prey. When examined on a diel basis red snapper appeared to feed throughout the day and night, with no obvious pattern in feeding periodicity.  McCawley et al. (2006) concluded that less than 2% of the red snapper diet organisms came from reef-associated organisms, based upon the defined habitat associations of the identified prey organisms.
McCawley (2003) and McCawley and Cowan (2007) examined the stomach contents of 656 red snapper ranging from 207 to 913 mm FL. Of these, 268 (40.9%) contained identifiable prey, 262 (39.9%) were empty, 63 (9.6%) contained only bait, and 63 (9.6%) contained only unidentified material.  All the fish examined were considered to be adults.  The unidentified material category contributed the largest proportion of red snapper diet by % weight (35.9%), followed by crab (20.2%), fish (19.5%), adult mantis shrimp Squilla empusa (12.6%), and pelagic zooplankton (8%).
On a seasonal basis, McCawley and Cowan (2007) found that fish was present in red snapper diets in all seasons (comprising between 34.5% and 31.8% by weight after the unidentified material was excluded), but they did not contribute the greatest amount by % weight in any season. The diets in summer and winter by % weight was composed of adult mantis shrimp (33.0% and 33.4% respectively), in fall of crabs (35.1%), and spring of pelagic zooplankton (45.6%). Demersal crustaceans (crabs and adult mantis shrimp) were present in all seasons comprising between 41.9% and 54.4% by weight of the diet in summer, fall and winter. During the spring, red snapper fed on high numbers of pelagic zooplankton. Statistical analyses indicated that red snapper were feeding on nearly the same kinds of organisms year around. Appendices 1 to 3 in the paper by McCawley and Cowan (2007) summarize the findings of the various red snapper diet studies.
McCawley and Cowan (2007) estimated that only 1.3% of the red snapper diet (excluding unidentifiable material) consisted of reef associated organisms. In contrast, the dominant components of the diets were species associated with sand and mud habitats (41.2%) and the water column (31%, mainly mantis shrimp and larval fish). Their interpretation of these data was that adult red snapper were almost, if not entirely trophically independent of the reefs on which they lived. In contrast, Gallaway et al. (2009) concluded that many red snapper food habit studies show substantial feeding on reef prey types, which supports the contention that red snapper are obtaining significant food resources from reef habitats.
The recruitment of age-0 red snapper to high-relief habitats such as artificial reefs or natural reefs may also be limited by predation from larger, older red snapper or by predation from other reef-associated species (Bailey et al. 2001, Piko and Stedlmayer 2007, Mudrak and Stedlmayer 2012).  Age-0 red snapper were excluded from complex habitat (concrete blocks) when older red snapper were added to a tank (Bailey et al. 2001).  In caging experiments conducted in the field, higher abundance of red snapper occurred on reefs when predators were excluded; in captivity, age-0 red snapper spent more  time associated with complex habitat when a predator (Gulf flounder Paralichthys albigutta) was present (Piko and Szedlmayer 2007).

Chapin et al. (2009) assessed the survival and movement of hatchery-reared red snapper on artificial habitats in the northern GOM.  Hatchery-reared red snapper were released onto artificial reef habitats.  The fish showed 12.7% survival after 7 months on small habitats (0.86 cubic meters) and 3.1% survival after 8 months on large habitats (3.9 cubic meters). Emigration was estimated by the movement of fish to unstocked habitats and accounted for 76.8% of the decline in abundance at release sites after 26 days. Age-0 fish showed higher survival and growth rates on small habitats (27.6% at 26 days; 0.33 mm per day) compared with large habitats (13.2% at 34 days; 0.26 mm per day) which may be due to increased predation and competition on the large habitats.  Fish became evenly distributed among adjacent habitats 26 days after release, indicating that stocking densities at release habitats were above carrying capacities.  These observations suggested that providing additional habitat around red snapper release sites would increase survival.

Based on the life history of red snapper and the potential effects of predators on reef fish recruitment, the proximity of larger artificial reefs and their associated reef fish communities may affect new recruitment of juvenile red snapper (Mudrak and Szedlmayr 2012).   Small artificial reefs were placed near to (15 m) and farther away (500 m distant) from larger artificial reefs at a site off Alabama.  Divers used visual surveys to identify and count all fish present on the small reefs and estimated fish lengths.  Significantly higher abundances of age-0 red snapper were detected on the small distant reefs (500 m) than on the small nearby (15 m) reefs.  Significantly higher densities of rock seabass and pygmy filefish were observed on the small distant reefs compared with the small nearby reefs.  Mean species richness was significantly higher on the small distant reefs than on the small nearby reefs. The study indicated that if artificial reefs are built to provide habitat for juvenile red snapper, they should not be placed in areas immediately adjacent to existing adult habitat, conversely habitats intended for adult fish should not be placed near important red snapper nursery areas.

Nowling et al. (2011) used otolith microchemistry to successfully discriminate between red snapper collected from artificial reefs and those collected from oil and gas platforms. A total of 98 otoliths were analyzed by inductively coupled plasma-mass spectrometry (ICPMS) from collections made from both artificial reefs and oil and gas platforms in Alabama and Louisiana over a two-year period from 2002 to 2003. A suite of 15 selected stable isotopes were analyzed, because they were most likely to be present at oil and gas platforms and in the metals and other materials used in artificial reefs, and in the circulating heavy �muds� used while drilling wells. Linear and stepwise discriminate analyses were performed to show that by using subsets of all the elements measured, it was possible to discriminate among artificial reefs and oil and gas platforms at average misclassification rates in the order of 10%.

Sluis (2011) conducted a similar otolith microchemistry study using 17 elements to determine habitats of origin for red snapper collected off Texas, Louisiana, and Florida.  Specimens collected off Destin, Florida, off Louisiana, and off Texas exhibited elemental signatures indicating they had come from regions with oil and gas platforms. Specimens collected off Tampa, Florida did not have an oil and gas platform elemental signature.  Maximum likelihood estimates (MLE) based on region-specific baseline data indicate that red snapper collected from Destin, Florida were estimated to predominately originate from Louisiana (82.1%) and secondarily from Alabama (16.1%).  Red snapper collected from Tampa, Florida were also estimated as originating from Louisiana (53.6%) with more influence from Alabama (37.8%).

nodes.title: REPRODUCTION
nodes.body:
Gender-White and Palmer (2004) found that red snapper sampled off North Carolina to Key West
had a sex ratio that did not differ significantly from 1:1.  They are gonochoristic. The sex ratio had
not changed since 1986.  White et al. (2010) presented computations that did not differ from the
expected 1:1 ratio of male to female red snapper.
Mode-Red snapper are batch spawners periodically releasing eggs into the water column (Rabalais et al. 1980).

nodes.title: Domain-
nodes.body:
Fertilization-External fertilization of eggs by male sperm.
Spawning Strategy: The f ish spawn primarily away from reefs (Bradley and Bryan 1975). Spawning was reported at depths of 18-37 m over a firm sand bottom with 1ittle relief in the GOM (Beaumariage and Bullock 1976).

Sedberry et al. (2006) captured adult red snapper in spawning condition in the southeastern Atlantic over a depth range of 24-67 m and a temperature range of 18.05-27.59oC  in MARMAP bottom trawls from South Carolina to eastern Florida off Melbourne.  Examination of sexually mature ovaries of female red snapper collected by MARMAP found that spawning occurred at depths 23-27 m and latitudes 27o-33oLatitude in the southeastern Atlantic from South Carolina to Florida (White et al. 2010). Maps were presented depicting the spatial distributions of spawning females clustered off South Carolina, Georgia, and northeastern Florida. Two maps show capture locations for young-of-year (age-0) red snapper situated on the inner continental shelf off of South Carolina and North Carolina. The total number of age-0 red snapper collected with MARMAP trawls from 1979 to 2000 was 31 fish.
Schobernd and Sedberry (2009) reported observing a large school of at least 20-30 red snapper, which appeared to be a spawning aggregation, situated at Scamp Ridge off South Carolina, at 19:29 Eastern Daylight Time (EDT) on August 2, 2002. The school was seen from a submersible at a depth of 53 m, with a bottom temperature of 20.9oC and salinity of 36.5 g/L.

Phelps et al. (2009) noted that brood behavior in hatchery tanks can give some indication of anticipated spawning.  A few hours before sunset, male red snapper were observed to follow a female with a swollen abdomen, swimming close to her vent area. Spawning behavior included fish schooling and slow swimming, interrupted by sudden group swimming and rushing toward the water surface.  This pattern was repeated several times.  Spawning occurred mainly in the late afternoon/evening hours. Several fertilized spawns with egg development in the blastula stage were collected in the late afternoon to early evening hours, before lights started dimming off (at approximately 1900 hrs). Fertilized eggs were found in the egg collector 30 min to 2 hr after the spawning behavior was observed.  Floating eggs were carried by the water current from the spawning tank to the egg collector. Jackson et al. (2006) examined the abundance of hydrated eggs in ovaries of wild-caught red snapper along the northern GOM and concluded that spawning peaks around 1600 hours.

Reproductive Periodicity: In general, red snapper spawn in summer and fal1 in the GOM. They have one peak spawning period in Florida waters and two peaks in Texas. Individual fish probably spawn several times during the spawning season (several egg stages occur simultaneously in the ovaries); the protracted spawning season and variation in gonadosomatic indices in fish of similar size during the season are consistent with this hypothesis (Collins et al. 1987).

Information on spawning seasonality as well as size and age at maturity are available for the northern GOM (Bradley and Bryan 1975, Wilson et al. 1994, Collins et al. 1996, Woods 2003, Woods et al. 2003), the southern GOM (Brul� et al. 2004), and the southeastern Atlantic (White and Palmer 2004).  Prior to 2008, the only information on reproduction for the SE GOM was 30 years old (Futch and Bruger 1976). More recently, a detailed study of the east and west coasts of Florida was conducted by Brown-Peterson et al. (2008).

Geary et al. (2007) reported that spawning occurred from April through late August at three banks off Texas. Peaks were generally unimodal with the majority of recruits from June and July hatch dates. This is roughly two weeks later than the peak in the hatch date reported by Rooker et al. (2004).  Szedlmayer and Conti (1999) reported that peaks in hatch date distributions of red snapper in the northwestern gulf vary by several weeks between consecutive years. Gonadal analysis suggests that red snapper spawning occurs in the northwest GOM from April through October, suggesting that a second pulse of recruits may enter the fishery in the late fall (Collins et al. 2001).

Despite the lack of significant genetic differences, Jackson e t al. (2007) reported maturity schedules and size-specific fecundity were significantly different between red snapper populations east and west of the mouth of the Mississippi River. They suggested early maturity at smaller size in the eastern GOM may be a genotypic response to high fishing mortality having selectively removed later maturing genotypes, a response that would not be apparent in selectively neutral genetic markers such as mitochondrial DNA (MtDNA) or nuclear DNA microsatellites (Pruett et al. 2005, Saillant and Gold 2006). Regardless of the causative factor, the fact that regional differences exist implies some degree of isolation between the eastern and western GOM. Patterson et al. (2007) asserted that regional differences in size at age reported by Fisher et al. (2004) further support that population structure exists in GOM red snapper, which has not been revealed by traditional fisheries genetics applications (Pruett et al. 2005, Gold and Saillant 2007).

White and Palmer (2004) collected otoliths and gonadal tissues from red snapper sampled between Cape Lookout, North Carolina and Key West, Florida during 1979-2000. The mean size of red snapper from fishery-dependent samples were 594 mm TL and ranged from 70-976 mm TL. Fish sampled from fisheries-independent gear had a significantly smaller mean TL (426 mm, range = 121-866 mm) than fishery dependent samples. The mean size of red snapper was significantly smaller in the 1980s when compared to the 1990s, regardless of gear type. The overall sex ratio was not significantly different from the expected 1:1, regardless of gear type.  The smallest mature female was 287 mm TL and the largest immature female was 435 mm TL, with an estimate of length at 50% maturity of 378 mm TL. Histological examination of the gonads indicated that female red snapper were in spawning condition from May through October, with a peak between June and September.  The gonadosomatic index (GSI) for females ranged from a low of 0.35 in November and December to a high of 2.67 in June. Males were found to be in spawning condition thoughout the year.

Brown-Peterson et al. (2008) collected red snapper from recreational-for-hire boats at two distinct areas of Florida to examine potential differences in their reproductive biology.  Samples were obtained from the Florida East Coast (St. Augustine to Melbourne N=66) from June to November of 2004 and 2005, and from the Dry Tortugas (N=81) during May, June, and August 2004-2005. There was a significant relationship between length and batch fecundity of red snapper from the East Coast but not from the Dry Tortugas. Relative frequency estimates were low in Dry Tortugas fish (27 � 11 eggs/g) relative to 235 � 56 eggs/g in East Coast fish, but similar to those reported from Alabama. Spawning frequency estimates varied from every 2.2 days on the East Coast to every 4.3 days in the Dry Tortugas. The apparent regional differences in reproductive biology among Florida red snapper may require region-specific management plans for this species.

Parental Care: None reported.

Seasonal Energetics: Wakeman et al. (1979) studied oxygen consumption, energy consumption,
and growth of red snapper.

nodes.title: Juvenile-
nodes.body:
Adult- Authors of early studies of GOM red snapper reproductive biology concluded that fish began reaching sexual maturity at a small size (<300 mm TL) and had protracted spawning seasons extending through the summer months (Bradley and Bryan 1975, Futch and Bruger 1976, Moseley 1966).  Collins et al. (1996) were the first to estimate batch fecundity in red snapper and to establish that the spawning season extended from April through October in both the eastern and western GOM.  Red snapper usually show partial sexual maturity when 1 year old and show full maturity when about 2 years old and 375 mm in fork length (FL) (Moran 1988).

Length at maturity has been reported to be 320 mm FL (Camber 1955), and between 190 and 300 mm SL (Moseley 1966).  Wilson et al. (1994) presented preliminary estimates of maturation at 290 mm FL.  Age-at-maturity has been reported as greater than 2 years old in the GOM (Futch and Bruger 1976).

Ovary analysis has also varied among studies. While authors prior to 1976 (Camber 1955, Moseley 1966, Bradley and Bryan 1975) used macro-assessment of gonad maturation, later authors (Futch and Bruger 1976, Wilson and Nieland 1994, Collins et al. 1996) used histological techniques to determine stages of oocyte maturation.  Histology is a more effective method for staging oocytes because it allows a detailed view of cross-sectioned and stained oocytes (Jackson et al. 2007).

Jackson et al. (2007) used red snapper collected during the spawning season off Alabama and
Louisiana, to describe maturation schedules of red snapper. Progression of oocyte maturation to
vitellogenesis was used to define and identify sexually mature females. Combined data showed
that smallest mature red snapper was 267 mm FL and was two years old. The smallest with
hydrated oocytes, indicative of imminent spawning, or postovulatory follicles, indicative of recent
spawning, were 285 and 297 mm FL respectively, and both were two years old.  Red snapper off
Alabama reached maturation at smaller sizes and younger ages than those sampled off Louisiana.
Growth rates did not differ between the two regions. Such differences in maturation schedules
may document an important stock response to reductions in populations size.
A comparison of maturity schedules indicated that red snapper captured off Alabama reached 50%    maturity before 275 mm FL and before they were 2.5 years old, and raw data showed 100% maturity by 575 mm FL (Jackson et al. 2007).  Females captured off Louisiana reached 50% maturity before 325 mm FL and before they were 2.5 years old, and raw data showed 100% maturity by 625 mm FL and 6.5 years old. Compared to Alabama, Louisiana female red snapper progressed more slowly to reach 100% maturity over size- and age-classes.
In the southeast Atlantic, White and Palmer (2004) noted that male red snapper reach maturity as early as age-1 or 200 mm TL, with all males mature by age-3 or 378 mm TL.  Females can be mature by age-2 or 287 mm TL, with all females mature after age-4 or 435 mm TL. The gonadosomatic index (GSI) of female red snapper peaked in June and remained high until September.
White et al. (2010) used data obtained from the NOAA/NMFS Marine Resources Monitoring, Assessment and Prediction (MARMAP) program to assess reproductive condition in red snapper in the southeastern Atlantic for the SEDAR24 stock assessment. The youngest sexually mature female red snapper was age-2 and the oldest was age-4. The smallest mature female was 265 mm TL, and the largest immature female was 435 mm TL.  Age at 50% maturity was 1.87 yr and length at 50% maturity was 370 mm.  Mature females were present in 0% of the age-1 class, 54% of age-2, 86% of age-3, 93% of age-4, and 100% of females age-5 or older.  Mature males were present in 50% of age-1 class, 93% of age-2, 97% of age-3, 100% of age-4, 97% of age-5, and 100% of males age-6 or older.  All male red snapper were mature at 451 mm TL and larger.
Fecundity:  Fecundity of fish sampled in northwest Florida ranged from 0.2 million  eggs for a female about 3 years old and 386 mm FL to 9.3 million for a fish about 12 years old and 754 mm FL (Collins et al. 1987).

Only limited fecundity information is available for red snapper along the Atlantic coast of the U.S. (SEDAR24 DW Report 2010). The relationship between batch fecundity (BF) and TL (BF = 9548*TL � 5,224,104; r2 = 0.67) was estimated for 12 specimens, 560-937 mm (Brown-Peterson et al. 2009). The small sample size and the lack of specimens < 560 mm made this equation of minimal use for the SEDAR24 assessment. An estimate of fecundity at age was available from the GOM, but was not as predictive as an estimate of fecundity at length (see Woods 2003; Fitzhugh et al. 2004) because batch fecundity reaches an asymptote at an age of approximately 10-12 yr.

Given the lack of a usable fecundity estimate from the Atlantic region, three proxies to estimate fecundity were considered: 1) gonad weight versus age, 2) gonad weight versus whole fish weight, and 3) gonad weight versus total length (SEDAR24 DW Report 2010).  The first proxy (gonad weight versus age; was not considered adequate because of a large gap in the age data, and, secondly, the linear nature of the relationship was inconsistent with the non-linear relationship evident between gonad weight and fish size (whole weight or TL) as fish grow. The second proxy is probably a better option, given the need to relate gonad weight to spawning biomass. The gonad weight (Wg) - whole fish weight (Wf) relationship is expressed as a power function:

Wg = 3.1416x10-5 Wf 1.743; SEa = 3.1836x10-5, SEb = 0.1107.

The gonad weight (Wg) - total length (Lt) relationship, third proxy, is expressed as a power function:

Wg = 1.207x10-11 Lt 4.524; SEa = 3.16x10-11, SEb = 0.3923.

The Life History Working Group for SEDAR24 recommended the use of the second proxy, gonad weight � fish weight, as an estimate of fecundity in the assessment (SEDAR24 2010). Recommendation was accepted at plenary session of Data Workshop.

nodes.title: Development
nodes.body:
Egg/Parturition-In the laboratory, initial hatching began 20 h after fertilization (Minton et al. 1983), and about 50% of the eggs hatched within 25 h of fertilization (Rabalais et al. 1980).
Larva-	Newly hatched larvae in the laboratory averaged 2.2 mm SL (Rabalais et al. 1980). The larvae began actively feeding on a culture of algae and rotifers 3 days after hatching and were 2.5 mm SL 4 days after hatching.
                                                                                                                                                      Young of Year-                                                                                                                         Juvenile-                                                                                                                                        Adult-Porch et al. (2007a) modeled batch fecundity (BF) on size and age of red snapper for use in stock assessments in GOM waters. Batch fecundity is a principal determinant of the reproductive potential of indeterminate spawners.  BF appears to increase geometrically with length and asymptotically with age based upon combined data from reproductive sampling programs by NMFS in the GOM and MARFIN in the southeastern Atlantic. As the life history pattern of red snapper sets up a potential disconnection between size and age, Porsch et al. (2007a) modeled their interaction as explanatory variables of BF.  Visual analysis suggested a dome-shaped relationship between BF and age within a given size-class. To test this, a log-linear model and a new �standardized� age model (where the effect of age depends explicitly on the size of fish) were fitted to the data.  These analyses suggest that the effect of age, while statistically significant, was relatively small (the models with age and length terms explaining only slightly more of the variation in BF than a simple power function of length). The age effect seems to be most pronounced for fish that are exceptionally small or exceptionally large given their age, which constitute a small fraction of the sample and presumably also a small fraction of the population at large.  Hence, it seems unlikely that including this interaction would have any important ramifications for stock assessments of red snapper. Nevertheless, the effect of age on BF remains open to the degree that old fish (i.e., greater than age 13) were rare in the combined data set and tended to exhibit lower BF values than predicted. Age effects of other reproductive determinants remain to be evaluated but the authors found hydrated females to be of greater size-at-age than non-hydrated red snapper suggesting an age-length interaction on batch fecundity.

Mating/Spawning Duration: Only limited information is available for red snapper along the Atlantic coast of the U.S.   Brown-Peterson et al. (2009) reported that spawning occurs every 2.2 days based on a sample of 66 specimens collected during June through November. Estimates from the GOM revealed that spawning frequency increases until about Age 6; little information is available for older ages (Woods 2003, Fitzhugh et al. 2004).

Sex Ratio: Red snapper are gonochoristic with an equal sex ratio of 1:1 (Brown-Peterson et al. 2009, White et al. 2010)

nodes.title: Length Range
nodes.body:
Egg/Parturition- Red snapper eggs averaged 0.82 mm in diameter (range: 0.77-0.85 mm) (Rabalais et al. 1980).

Larva- Newly hatched larvae in the laboratory averaged 2.2 mm SL (Rabalais et al. 1980). The larvae began actively feeding on a culture of algae and rotifers 3 days after hatching and were 2.5 mm SL 4 days after hatching.  A total of 96 hatchery-reared red snapper larvae ranged in body length (BL) from 1.9 to 26.1 mm BL, and a total of 118 wild caught-larvae ranged from 2.6 to 20 mm BL (Drass et al. 2000).  Body length (BL) is equivalent to notochord length or standard length (SL) depending on the stage of development of the larvae (Leis 1987).

Daily growth rates observed by Geary et al. (2007) of 1.09 mm per day at Freeport Rocks, 1.01 mm per day at Heald Bank, 1.01 mm per day at Sabine Bank) off Texas overlap the upper end of red snapper observed by Rooker at al. (2004) of 0.78-0.88 mm per day, and 0.54-0.86 mm per day found by Szedlemayer and Conti (1999).

Young of Year-The age-0 larvae undergo metamorphosis and settle to the bottom when they are 16-19 mm TL and 26 to 30 days of age in the GOM (Rabalais et al.1980, Szedlmayer and Conti 1999, Rooker et al. 2004, Gallaway et al. 2009).  Settlement was observed in July and the newly settled fish (most <40 mm TL) were found over open or low relief habitat off Alabama (Szedlemayr and Lee 2004). Age 0 red snapper enter the GOM penaeid shrimp trawl fishery at about 67 days of age and 50 mm TL (Galloway et al. 2009). Age-0 fish began moving onto reefs as they reached sizes approaching 100 mm TL and by December were found on the reefs from which age-1 fish had abruptly disappeared (Stedlmayer and Lee 2004).

Juvenile-Wells (2007), also working offshore Alabama, observed an increase in mean size of age-1 red snapper corresponding to a shift from sand (96.1 mm TL) to low-relief shell (127.0 mm TL) to high relief habitat (172.3 mm TL).

Nieland and Wilson (2003) analyzed size frequency distributions of red snapper killed by explosives at an oil and gas platform off Louisiana. A peak in the size frequency distribution indicated that age-2 red snapper ranged from 250-380 mm TL.  Because of the 15 inch minimum size limit imposed by the GMFMC age-2 red snapper were not observed in size frequencies representing catches of red snapper taken from either the commercial or recreational fisheries.

Adults-Nieland and Wilson (2003) found a second peak in the size frequency of red snapper killed by explosives at an oil and gas platform off Louisiana. Age-3 red snapper ranged in size from 381-480 mm TL.  Adult red snapper in the GOM range in length up to 104 cm TL (Scott-Denton et al. 2011).

Red snapper initially grow quickly and then growth slows steadily as larger size associated with long life span is reached (Bradley and Bryan 1975). In the GOM, under-yearling fish grew 25 mm/month in August and September according to Bradley and Bryan (1975).
Length Conversions: The relations of SL to FL and FL to TL (lengths in mm) and N (sample size) were reported by Futch and Bruger (1976) as follows:

FL = 1.1585 SL + 13.3 (N = 21)
TL = l.0678 FL + 3.5 (N = 100)

Nelson and Manooch  (1982) reported the following relation:
TL = 1.0712 FL + 1.7 (N = 180).
Additional length-length relations are given in Parrack (1986b). 	Length- length relations show a high linear correlation  (Parrack 1986b).


Weight-Length Conversions: Length-weight relations calculated for severa1    areas in the gulf were similar  Parrack 1986b). The length-weight  relation  changed  at 190-300 mm SL (Moseley 1966).

(1982).
Florida   Males        Log10W = 3.008 log 10 FL -4.8104

nodes.title: Wet-Dry Weight Conversions
nodes.body:
Length at Age:  Scale annulus formation off the U.S. gulf coast is complete by
early summer for fish ages 2 and older (Parrack 1986). Annual growth of fish
of age 1 to 4 or 5 in the GOM ranged from 60 to 75 mm (Bradley Bryan 1975) and 90
mm (Moseley 1966).

nodes.title: Female-
nodes.body: Sexes Combined-Age-length keys for red snapper in the southeast Atlantic have been presented by Manooch et al. (1997, 1998), White and Palmer (2004), and McInerny (2007). Mean total lengths at age in the southeast Atlantic were presented by Manooch et al. (1997) and McInerny (2007).  McInerny presented a comparison of mean total lengths (TL) at age for the commercial fishery between 2003 and 2006 for Florida, and for North Carolina, South, Carolina, and Georgia combined (Table 5).  Table 6 presented a comparison of mean total lengths at age for the commercial fishery and for the recreational fishery off Florida between 2001 and 2006. In Table 7, McInerny (2007) presented a comparison of mean total lengths at age during the period of: a) no regulation, b) the fishery management plan (FMP), and c) after passage of Amendment 4.  Mean back-calculated total lengths at age for red snapper in the southeast Atlantic were presented  up to age-11 by Manooch et al. (1997), up to age-20 by McInerny (2007), and up to age 15 for various locations in the GOM (Louisiana, West Florida) and southeast Atlantic (Carolinas, East Florida) by Nelson and Manooch (1982). All of these studies cited presented mean lengths at age for the sexes combined.

nodes.title: Longevity
nodes.body:
Egg/Parturition- The early life history includes a planktonic egg stage for 18-27 hours (Rabalais et al. 1980; Minton et al. 1983).
Larva- The larval stage has a duration of 25-47 days (Leis 1987).
Young-of-Year- A benthic young-of-year stage occurs after the larvae undergo metamorphosis and settle to the bottom (Szedlemayer and Conti 1999). Size at settlement is about 1.7 cm.  Age-0 fish initially occur over sand, mud bottoms, then migrate to submerged banks of oyster shell (Lingo and Stedlmayer 2006, Piko and Stedlmayer 2007). Red snapper as small as 18 mm settled on relatively unstructured open shelf habitats in summer, but by the winter age-0 fish had recruited to artificial reefs that provided greater complexity and relief (Szedlemayer and Lee 2004).
Juvenile- A comparison of maturity schedules indicated that red snapper captured off Alabama reached 50% maturity before 275 mm FL and before they were 2.5 years old (Jackson et al. 2007).  Females captured off Louisiana reached 50% maturity before 325 mm FL and before they were 2.5 years old. Based on the age at which 50% of the fish are sexually mature, age-1 and age-2 red snapper can be classified as juveniles.
Adult- Maximum ages for red snapper derived from reading scales were age-4 in the northern GOM (Moseley 1966), age-13 off Louisiana (Nelson and Manooch 1982, age-9 off Alabama (Wade 1981), and age-11 off western Florida (Nelson and Manooch 1982). In the southeast Atlantic, Nelson and Manooch (1982) aged red snapper from east Florida and the Carolinas and found fish as old as 16 years using scales and otoliths.  Research by Beamish and McFarlane (1983) called into question the reliability of ages derived from scales and proposed the need for age validation studies.
Recent advances in otolith preparation methodology have allowed red snapper to be aged reliably in the GOM up to the following ages: 42 yr (Szedlemayer and Shipp 1994), 53 yr (Render 1995), 31 yr (Patterson 1999), 52 yr (Wilson and Nieland 1991), 47 yr (Allman et al. 2002), 53 yr (Mitchell et al. 2004), 55 yr (Baker and Wilson 2001), and 57 yr (Allman and Fitzhugh 2007).  Patterson et al. (2001b) found that the oldest female sampled was 34 years, and the oldest male was 33 years old.

Manooch and Potts (1997) aged red snapper from the southeast Atlantic up to 25 years old using sectioned otoliths. White and Palmer (2004) found that the age range determined from otoliths for fishery-independent samples in the southeast Atlantic was 1-22 years with a mean age of 3.1 years, and 1-45 years for fishery dependent samples with a mean age of 4.2 years.  The oldest red snapper aged using sectioned otoliths in the southeast Atlantic was 54 years old (McInerny 2007).

Potts et al. (2009) gathered otoliths to determine the age structure of red snapper collected from North Carolina to the east coast of Florida during the summer months of 2009.  All fish were collected with hook and line gear by recreational and commercial fishermen. The oldest red snapper caught off North Carolina was 12 yr, off South Carolina 20 yr, off Georgia 22 yr, and off northeast Florida 37 yr. Further studies are needed to determine whether older red snapper occur in deeper water offshore.
Aging Structures/Methods: Using scales to determine sizes at age, several studies found rapid growth in young fish. They grew from 137-177 mm TL at age 1 to 538-546 mm TL at age 5 and 784-794 mm TL at age 11 (Moseley 1966, Bradley and Bryan 1975, Nelson and Manooch 1982, Wade 1981).  They may reach 845 mm FL and 12 kg (Bradley and Bryan 1975) and an age of about 13 years (Nelson and Manooch 1982). Scale annulus formation off the U.S. GOM coast is complete by early summer for fish ages 2 and older (Parrack 1986).
A 35% decrease in the production in red snapper in the commercial GOM fishery from 1965 to 1975 prompted Futch and Bruger (1976) to further examine the age and growth of red snapper (Fisher 2007).  Among 240 red snapper taken off the west coast of Florida, they estimated red snapper ages of  1 to 5 yr from 200 readable whole otoliths; however, they postulated ages up to 20 yr for larger individuals whose otoliths were unreadable.
Bortone and Hollingsworth (1980) determined ages of red snapper using scale, otoliths, and vertebrae. They found that all three body parts had a statistically similar level of readability (between 75% and 80%). However, they only examined 46 red snapper.
Nelson and Manooch (1982) were used scales and also sectioned some otoliths to examine the age structure of red snapper in the northern GOM as well as the west-central Atlantic. They examined 2,151 scales (from both the GOM and SE Atlantic) and142 sectioned otoliths (Atlantic only) to examine the growth and mortality of red snapper along the southeastern U.S. and the northern GOM. They attempted to validate their ages using monthly mean marginal growth increments performed on scales (Fisher 2007).  This technique indicated that red snapper in the GOM form annuli during June and July. They were unable to perform marginal increment analyses on otoliths, because they did not have otoliths sampled throughout all 12 months of the year. However, 18 one-year-old red snapper sampled in the Carolinas during June all exhibited the beginning of new growth (translucence) at the otolith section edge, leading them to suggest that scale and otolith annuli form simultaneously.
A number of studies using sectioned otoliths have found greater longevity of red snapper than what was originally reported from age determinations using scales (Fisher 2007).  Szedlemayer and Shipp (1994) used counts of annuli on sectioned otoliths for 409 red snapper sampled with hook and line off Alabama. They reported a maximum age of 42 years, a substantial increase over the previously reported maximum age of 13 years determined from scales (Nelson and Manooch 1982).
Render (1995) estimated ages from sectioned otoliths for red snapper sampled from both the recreational and commercial fisheries off Louisiana. Render observed a maximum longevity of 53 years. He validated his age estimates through marginal increment analysis. The increased longevity estimates reported by Szedlemayer and Shipp (1994) and Render (1995) were available for the stock assessment conducted by Goodyear (1995).
A number of laboratories in the GOM region began routine annual aging programs of red snapper in an effort to track age structure trends over time for stock assessment purposes (Cowan et al. 1995, Wilson and Nieland 2001, Allman et al. 2002).  Wilson and Nieland (2001) tracked the age structure off Louisiana during eight years of variable collection effort from 1989 to 1998.  Allman et al. (2002) sampled commercial and recreational fisheries from Texas to the west coast of Florida in 1998 and 1999. A total of 8,169 otoliths were sectioned. Validation work was conducted using marginal increment analysis.
The consequences of incorrect age determination of red snapper was first pointed out by Rothschild et al. (1997) in their review of the red snapper GOM management plan. In particular some life history aspects of red snapper appeared to differ from typical long-lived marine species, such as their rapid growth and early maturity that were more consistent with short-lived species. Red snapper in the GOM mature as early as age two and show rapid growth within the first 10 years of life and fecundity increases with age (Szedlmayer and Shipp 1994, Collins et al. 2001, Woods et al. 2003). The inconsistency between red snapper life history and that of other long-lived species, and the lack of direct mark recapture studies, showed a need for further validation of annual increment formation in otoliths of red snapper, especially for older larger fish.
Szedlemayer (1998) studied the formation of daily otolith increments in age-0 red snapper after marking them with oxytetracycline dehydrate (OTC).   For wild red snapper, the mean otolith increment deposition rate was daily (0.97 increments per day) when growth rates were fast (0.63 mm FL, length of fish per day), but not daily (0.82 increments per day) when somatic growth was slow (0.2 mm length of fish per day). For reared larvae (N=8), increment deposition rates were daily (0.99 -1.03 increments per day), and growth rates ranged from 0.6 to 0.9 mm per day.  Growth rate affected increment deposition rate as a threshold function, i.e., when growth rate was <0.3 mm length of fish per day, deposition was less than daily, but above this level increment deposition did not exceed a daily rate. As growth rates increased increment widths increased.  Examination of a sub-sample (N=8) of the otoliths from the slowest growing wild fish by electron microscopy did not increase increment counts. Because red snapper are late spring-early summer spawners, young fish can expect maximum growth due to warm summer temperatures. Thus, daily ageing methods should be well suited for this species.
The use of bomb-radiocarbon was applied to validate otolith section ages in the GOM (Baker 1999, Baker and Wilson 2001).   Ages of red snapper ranged from 2 to 55 years with back-calculated years at birth ranging from 1943 to 1996.   Baker and Wilson (2001) stated that their radiocarbon chronologies based on accelerator mass spectrometry (AMS) provided evidence that otolith section-based age estimates for red snapper were valid.

A second age validation method applied to red snapper was radiometric testing, which measured the chemical disequilibria of 210 Pb (lead) to 226Ra (radium) (Wilson et al. 2001). Radiometric ageing of fish otoliths relies on the principal assumptions that (1) 226Ra is naturally incorporated into the otolith either at a constant rate or at a rate that is proportional to the mass increase of the otolith, (2) that the otolith remains a chemically closed system and there are no losses or gains of radionucleids (e.g., radon 222Rn), and (3) the initial activity ratio of 210Pb to 226Ra is close to zero.  Baker et al. (2001) showed that some of these assumptions were violated in red snapper otoliths.  In whole otoliths of both red snapper and red drum (Sciaenops ocellatus) 226Ra activity was inversely correlated with the otolith mass increase with age, validating the assumption that 226Ra accumulation in otoliths occurs at a rate proportional to that of calcium (Ca).  222Rn emanation from otoliths decreased as otolith mass increased.  222Rn loss occurred in all red snapper otolith samples (<=4.1%), and decreased with increasing size (age) of the otolith.
Although a validated aging method may have proved successful for a given study there is no guarantee that those structures will be interpreted the same by other readers (Campana 2001).  Allman et al. (2005) noted that while validation of aging methods is an important criterion in estimating growth and longevity, age interpretation remains largely subjective.  This subjectivity can pose a significant problem in aging red snapper otoliths due to challenges in interpreting the first annulus and in discerning annuli in older individual fish.
A measure of precision is a valuable means of assessing the reproducibility of age determinations beween individuals or laboratories (Campana 2001, Fisher 2007).  A number of the laboratories conducing red snapper age-growth studies have determined the average percent error (APE) to evaluate aging precision of red snapper (Render  1995, Patterson et al. 2001b, Wilson and Nieland 2001, Allman et al. 2002, Allman et al. 2005).
Wilson and Nieland (2001) noted that training and experience are critical to achieving accuracy and high between reader consensus on red snapper annulus counts due to the high level of difficulty of interpretation.
The Gulf States Marine Fisheries Commission (GSMFC) began to conduct yearly aging workshops in
2003 in an effort to bring together all aging laboratories in the GOM to discuss and standardize
processing and aging techniques (Mareska 2005, Fisher 2007).

Similar studies are being conducted in the Southeast Atlantic (White et al., 2010).  A red snapper aging
workshop was held during August 2009 in Charleston SC (Potts et al. 2009). Red snapper otoliths
(N=196) in a �reference� set from fishery-independent and fishery-dependent were aged during the inter-
laboratory workshop.  The average percent error (APE) for readers from South Carolina Department of
Natural Resources (SCDENR) was 9.13%.  Additonal red snapper otoliths (N=447) were aged with an
initial agreement of 67% and agreement within two annuli of 93% between two readers.  Ages
determined for red snapper otoliths ranged from 0 to 35 years.

The current ageing technique of counting annual growth increments on sectioned otoliths is often
difficult and subjective in young red snapper (Beyer and Szedlmayer 2010).  In particular, identification
of the first annulus is subject to reader identification and is a source of considerable error in aging young
fish (Holt and Arnold 1982, Wilson and Nieland 2001, Rooker et al. 2004,  Allman et al. 2005).

Interpretation of the putative first annulus in sectioned otoliths of red snapper has been a source of
debate among otolith readers throughout the GOM (Fisher at el. 2010).  The chemical marker alazarine
complexone was used to validate the periodicity of first  opaque annulus formation in red snapper otolith
sections.  Juvenile red snapper were immersed in 100 mg alizarin complexone per L seawater solution in
November 2005 and then reared in 6000 liter circular tanks until July 2006. Otoliths were then removed
from the fish and thin sectioned. All experimental otolith sections displayed a distinct fluorescent mark
ranging from 0.62 to 0.96 mm from the core when viewed under a microscope with a rhodamine filter.
The diffuse opaque annulus was located distally to the alizarine mark in all specimens (ranging from
0.88 to 1.51 mm).  The distal position of the presumptive first annulus relative to the alizarin mark in all
specimens indicates that this diffuse opaque annulus in red snapper sectioned otoliths forms during the
first winter after hatching. Translucent marginal edges of all otolith sections indicate that first annulus
formation is completed by mid-July.
A new method for determining the age of red snapper was developed involving shape analysis of otiliths (Beyer 2008, Beyer and Szedlemayer 2010).  Multidimensional scaling and non-parametric analysis showed significant shape differences of age-0, age-1, and age-2 fish.  Discriminant function analysis and cross-validation classification showed 65.6% correct age classification based on shape variables alone, and 86.7% correct age classifications with inclusion of otolith weight in the discriminant function.  Otolith shape can provide an objective method for ageing young red snapper.
The periodicity of otolith growth increments (opaque and translucent zones) from adult  red snapper was examined through a mark and recapture study conducted (2005-2010) and laboratory holding of hatchery-reared red snapper over a two year period (2002-2004) (Szedlmayer and Beyer 2011).  Wild red snapper (N=295) were caught on hook-and-line, marked with anchor tags, injected with oxytetracycline dihidrate (OTC), and released in the GOM off Alabama. Marked fish were recaptured up to 2.8 years after release (n=35) and sagittal otoliths were dissected, sectioned and examined under white and blue-violet light.  The number of opaque growth zones past the OTC mark was compared to time at liberty for each fish and supported an annual periodicity of growth increment formation. Also, most (87%) of the hatchery reared fish showed two opaque zones that supported an annual increment formation rate.  However, an unusual timing of opaque zone formation was shown for mark-recaptured fish.  Based on known timing of OTC marking, otoliths from mark-recapture fish showed opaque zone formation from late summer (August) to early winter (December). This fall formation of opaque zones is in contrast to previous studies and its timing may relate to the end of spawning for this species.

Research has been conducted to determine chemical signatures of red snapper otoliths associated with studies to determine differences in population demographics in the GOM (Patterson et al. 1998, 2001c, 2008; Gibson et al. 2010; Sluis  2011; Nowling et al.  2011). Some differences have been found indicating regional differences in age-0 red snapper between the eastern and western GOM (Patterson et al. 2008,  Sluis 2011).
Growth Equations: Ne1son and Manooch (1982) reported von Berta1anffy growth equations for fish from two areas in the GOM. They found that the von Bertalanffy growth curves for Louisiana, western Florida, eastern Florida, and the Carolinas differed statistically, as did the length-weight relations for fish from west Florida, east Florida, and the Carolina. However, the differences in growth curves were small and the differences in length-weight curves had little if any biological significance. Parrack (1986a) reported differences in growth curves between fish west of and fish east of the Mississippi Delta. This difference was inconclusive (Reef Fish Scientific Task Team and Special Scientific and Statistical Committee 1987).
A number of studies have developed von Bertalanffy growth equations for red snapper populations respectively in the GOM and southeast Atlantic (Collins et 1996, Nelson et al. 1985, Nelson and Manooch 1982, Manooch et al. 1998, Fisher et al. 2002, Szedlemayer and Shipp 1994, Wilson and Nieland 2001, Wilson et al. 2001, Patterson et al. 2001a, White and Palmer 2004, McInerny 2007, Saari 2011). Most of the studies fitted models for the sexes combined.  Wilson and Nieland (2001) and Fisher et al. (2002) developed separate models by sex of red snapper. Von Bertalanffy growth parameters for red snapper and other species of Lutjanidae were tabulated as part of a comparative study by Martinez-Andrade (2003).
Habitat varies greatly throughout the GOM and while numerous studies have aged red snapper, none have simultaneously compared the age and size structure and growth rates among standing and toppled oil and gas platforms with natural habitats (Saari 2011). The study examined the size and age structure and growth rates (using von Bertalanffy growth equations) of red snapper among three different habitats (shelf-edge banks, standing platforms, toppled platforms) and six recreational fishing regions of the GOM (South Texas, North Texas, Louisiana, Alabama, Northwest Florida, Central Florida). Across all of the habitats and regions, red snapper were small (mean TL = 526.84 mm, mean TW = 0.97 kg) and from younger age classes (mean age = 4.44 yr), representing the strong recruitments of 2004, 2005 and 2006, with few fish older than seven years (1.5%). Total length, weight, and age frequencies, and growth models differed significantly among the habitats. Red snapper from the banks were significantly smaller at age and slower growing than red snapper from the artificial habitats. Also, shelf-edge banks appeared to support a higher predominance of older red snapper compared to the artificial habitats. Demographic differences in red snapper size and age frequencies and growth parameters were found across the GOM. Small, fast-growing individuals dominated the recreational catches of South Texas, Northwest Florida, and Central Florida, whereas larger, slower-growing red snapper constituted the majority of the Alabama and Louisiana catches. Also, both of the Florida regions� catches were comprised of significantly younger red snapper than catches in the north-central and western regions. To prevent habitat- and region-specific overfishing and promote stock recovery, these differences should be weighed when evaluating future stock assessments and management decisions. It is also important for fisheries managers to note the absence of old red snapper in this study and its implications for the stock�s recovery status.

nodes.title: Commercial
nodes.body:
Gulf of Mexico
The red snapper is the most important fish in the GOM commercial snapper-grouper fishery between  Cape San Blas, Florida, and the mouth of the Rio Grande (Allen and Tashiro 1976); 4.6 million lb were landed commercially at U.S. ports in the GOM in 1985 (National Marine Fisheries Service 1986, Moran  1988).
From the 1880s to the 1950s, the red snapper fishery primarily operated out of Pensacola Florida (Collins 1885, Bortone et al. 1997, Shipp and Bortone 2008).  Although the fishery began in the 1840s, red snapper  was established as a major commercial product in the 1870s when the railroad system permitted the shipment of fishes from Pensacola to northern and inland markets. As early as 1883, it was evident that the number of red snapper was decreasing on the existing fishing grounds off Pensacola.  Snapper fishermen had to go further east each year to obtain a profitable catch. Many smacks sailed over 200 miles to the Florida Middle Ground. This area was also soon overfished.  New red snapper grounds were discovered off the Dry Tortugas in 1885. From 1895 to 1929, the discovery of a large red snapper fishery on the Campeche Banks off Mexico brought the period of the highest production for Pensacola�s red snapper industry.
Snappers and groupers are often taken together in the snapper-grouper fishery. Various fishing methods for snappers and groupers have been used or tested over the years.  Most commercial fishing is done with baited hooks and li nes on e1ectric and hydraulic reels which were too expensive until recently (Moran 1988). These are all classified as handlines in National Marine Fisheries Service fishery statistics.  From 2 to 40 hooks may be used with one reel (Allen and Tashiro 1976).  Ladyfish and squid are the most effective bait (Carpenter 1965); red snapper select fish and squid equally often (Futch and Bruger 1976). The industry has experimented with other fishing methods, but many were deficient; an otter trawl adapted for rough bottoms was effective (Smith 1948; Captiva and Rivers 1960; Nelson and Carpenter 1968).  An extensive bottom longline fishery that may take red snapper developed in the Gulf of Mexico since about 1980.  The longline fishery in the eastern gulf has been directed primarily at yellowedge grouper (Epinephelus flavolimbatus) (Parrack and Mclellan 1986).
Commercial   fishing grounds for red snapper are well offshore in the Gulf of Mexico (Moran 1988). In 1955, the most important fishing grounds had 1ong been the Campeche Banks off the Yucatan Peninsula, Mexico, which were the principa1    grounds fished by the west Florida fleet (Camber 1955; Hildebrand 1955). Fishing there by American boats was curtailed, however, since the extension of Mexico's fishery conservation zone to the 200-mi limit. Red snapper 1andings from foreign waters have composed less than 13% of the total U.S. landings since 1973 (Gulf of Mexico Fishery Management Counci1   1981). Western Florida landings varied widely over the years (Camber 1955).  They increased progressively as the fishery developed from  1880  to  1902,  stabilized  as  the Campeche Banks were exploited during 1902-28, dropped with reduced effort during  the  Great  Depression  of 1929-35,  increased  again  as  the economy began to recover in 1936-39, declined markedly with reduced effort from 1939 to 1945 during World War II, and then began to recover again around 1946 (Camber 1955).

In the early 1960's, large numbers of commercia1    vesse1 s were bui1t to fish for   ssnappers and	groupers (Carpenter 1965). The average number of handline vessels in western Florida was 180 in 1957-60; increased to 290 in 1961-65; leveled off at 260 in 1966-70; and increased again to 320 in 1971-74.  The average total number of handline fishermen in western Florida was 780 in 1957-60; increased to 1200 in 1961-65; and stabilized at 1030-1100 in 1967-74 (Florida Sea Grant College 1980; Gulf of Mexico Fishery Management Council 1981).

Porsch et al. (2007) noted that statistics on commercial landings of red snapper have been recorded by the National Marine Fisheries Sevice (NMFS) and its predecessors as far back as 1880. However, there are many gaps in the historical records. Censuses were conducted sporadically prior to 1949 and the water body were the catch was obtained was not recorded until 1963. Landings data obtained from several state and private agencies were used to supplement NMFS landings statistics. The data suggest a substantial red snapper fishery existed as early as 1872. The reconstructed landings are consistent with major events in the history of the fishery, but considerable uncertaintly remains over uncanvassed years between 1890 and the 1920s.

Landings for western Florida declined greatly during 1982-85 to the second-lowest level ever recorded. In 1983-85 catch per unit of effort (catch rate) was relatively high, but declined 26% during that period in the gulf east of the Mississippi River Delta for fish 3 years old and older in the bottom longline and the rod-and-reel fisheries (Parrack and McClellan 1986). Also, in 1983-85, a stock assessment showed that initial biomass (without recruits) declined 17% and recruitment biomass declined 98% in this area (Parrack and McClellan 1986).

The principal commercial fishing grounds used by fishermen from Alabama, Mississippi, Louisiana, and Texas are on the reefs offshore from those States. The average number of handline vessels in these four states was 150 in 1957-60 and 180 in 1961-65; declined to 90 in 1966-70; and leveled off at 80 in 1971-74. The average size of the vessels increased from 30 gross tons in 1957 to 61 gross tons in 1974 (Florida Sea Grant College 1980; Gulf of Mexico Fishery Management Council 1981). Landings peaked in the early 1960�s in Alabama and Texas, and in 1968 in Mississippi. Landings in Alabama, Texas, and Mississippi declined 73%-93% after these peaks in the 1960s, but Louisiana landings increased to a record high in 1984.  A recent stock assessment showed that estimated initial biomass (without recruits) declined 45%, but estimated recruitment biomass increased 21%, for red snapper west of the Mississippi River Delta between 1980 and 1985 (Parrack and McLellan 1986).

An increase in the number of fishing boats and trips may cause competition among boats, because the number of boats that can make a good catch in the prime fishing areas is limited; competition among boats reduces the catch per unit of fishing effort. On the Campeche Banks, the catch rate declined from 1937 to 1940, when the number of fishing trips (and probably the competition) increased, and then greatly increased from 1941 to 1945 when competition probably declined because of reduced fishing effort during World War II. The catch rate declined from 1948 to 1951, but competition probably also declined (Camber 1966).

The commercial red snapper fishery in the GOM during the 1970s ranked eighth in total weight, seventh in total value, and sixth in price per pound (NMFS 1986b, Moran 1988). The only species regularly exploited by offshore fisheries in the mid-1970s in the western gulf was the red snapper and the gulf menhaden, Brevoortia patronus (Hildebrand 1954). The red snapper was the most important of about 17 species in the U.S. snapper fishery (Allen and Tashiro 1976). In the northern GOM, it made up about 86% of the total value of the catch by the large vessels (56-69 ft long) in the snapper-grouper fisher that could reach distant fishing grounds, and in the southeastern gulf, it made up about 37% of the total value of the catch of all vessels in the fishery (Cato and Prochaska 1976). At the time of their study, the Campeche Banks were not fished substantially by American boats for political reasons. Total profits were greater for the larger vessels in the northern gulf because the value per pound was higher for red snapper than for the other species that predominated in thethe southern gulf (Cato and Prochaska 1976).

nodes.title: South Atlantic
nodes.body:
As early as 1886, red snapper were fished commercially on the east coast of Florida (Collins 1886).  Captain Latham fished on the east side of Florida, landing his catch
chiefly at Savannah, Georgia.  He generally fished for red snapper from off Cape
Canaveral southwards to the Indian River, in 12 to 15 fathoms (24-30 m) of water.
Comparatively few snapper were caught north of Cape Canaveral. The benthic habitat
fished was noted to differ from the west side of Florida. On the west coast, red snapper were generally caught in depressions of the sea bottom, commonly called �gullies�. On the east coast, the snapper were found most abundant on narrow coral ridges, which usually run parallel with the coast line, and are elevated 2 to 3 feet above the surrounding bottom. Some of these ridges were not more than 100 feet wide, while others may be 300 feet or more.  Red snappers were not so abundant on the east coast as they were on the west coast, but they averaged larger in size. A vessel carrying a crew of seven men made a trip of about two weeks, and an average fare (catch) was about 6,000 pounds (lbs.

A small commercial fishery for red snapper along the Atlantic coast has existed at least since
1902 when 155,000 pounds were landed, primarily in Georgia (SAFMC 2010).  The fishery continued at relatively low levels until after World War II. Landings jumped to approximately 250,000 pounds in 1945. By 1950, they had reached 363,000 pounds. Then, they fluctuated along a generally increasing trend through 1968, peaking at 974,000 pounds and declining to less than 100,000 pounds in 2006.  Commercial landings of red snapper in the south Atlantic increased from 1950 through the 1960s, reaching a peak in 1968 of 1,043,000 lbs (454 mt) (Manooch et al. 1998, White and Palmer 2004). From 1975 through 1998, annual landings fell from 721,100 to 60,949 lbs (White and Palmer 2004).  Eastern Florida landings dominated the catch through the middle 1970s after which a precipitous decline occurred.  During 1990-2001, 58% of the red snapper were landed in Florida (east coast), 6% in Georgia, 25% in South Carolina, and 11% in North Carolina.

nodes.title: Recreational
nodes.body:
Gulf of Mexico
The red snapper is one of the most desired species of sport fish in the GOM. Sport fishing grounds overlap commercial grounds (Moran 1988).  In 1965 and 1970, the weight of the commercial catch was less than that of the sport fish catch (Nakamura 1976).  Sport-fishing boats range from small 12-ft private boats to 85-ft party boats (head boats). The number of boats increased from 1956 to 1976 and probably partly displaced the inshore commercial fishery (Allen and Tashiro 1976, St. Amant 1976).

Between 1982 and 1985, the GOM sport fishery catch of red snapper declined by about 60% in Florida and 78% in Louisiana (Moran 1988). In western Florida, the commercial catch also declined sharply between 1982 and 1985. In Louisiana, the commercial fishery may have supplanted the recreational fishery over this period.

The largest annual sport catch for Louisiana from 1979 (when accurate statistics became available) to 1985 was about 2.7 million fish-the highest recorded for any gulf state for the same time period (Moran 1988). For that period, Alabama�s sport catch fluctuated with high catches about every other year; in years between 1979 and 1985, when the sport catch was higher (1979, 1981, and 1983), the commercial catch was also generally higher-except that the commercial catch peaked in 1982. A trend in the Texas catch could not be determined because too few data were available.  Mississippi�s catch remained low, and the commercial catch in 1985 was the lowest in 17 years. Regulations in 1988 in the U.S. waters of the GOM allowed a maximum of 5 fish less than 12 inches in Florida per trip for headboats.

In summary, the sport catch and commercial catch were sometimes positively correlated�possibly because both declined after heavy fishing pressure or because of a natural 30�month cycle in abundance (Camber 1955) � and sometimes negatively correlated, possibly because one fishery replaced the other (Allen and Tashiro 1976).

The red snapper ranked 19th in number of fish caught among groups of sport fish for which statistics  were
recorded in the GOM in 1985; about 2 million red snapper were caught by sport fishermen in the
  GOM that         year (National Marine  Fisheries  Service 1986a).

nodes.title: South Atlantic
nodes.body:
The South Atlantic recreational fishery is comprised of the private sector and for-hire sector (SAFMC  2010).  The private sector includes anglers fishing from shore (all land-based structures) and private/rental boats. The for-hire sector is composed of the charterboat and headboat (also called partyboat) sectors. Charterboats generally carry fewer passengers and charge a fee on an entire vessel basis, whereas headboats carry more passengers and payment is per person. The type of service, from a vessel- or passenger-size perspective, affects the flexibility to search different fishing locations during the course of a trip and target different species since larger concentrations of fish are required to satisfy larger groups of anglers.

In the U.S. south Atlantic, recreational landings peaked in 1985 at 619,000 lbs. In 2002, recreational fishermen
landed 390,908 lbs of red snapper (White and Palmer 2004).  Recreational snapper grouper harvest in the South Atlantic has been variable during the period 2003-2008, averaging slightly above 11 million pounds (SAFMC 2010). On average, the private/shore mode of fishing accounted for the largest harvests at around 7.62 million pounds (MP). Well below this harvest level are those of the charter mode at 1.92 MP and headboat at 1.63 MP. Harvests in each state  also fluctuated during the same period. On average, Florida accounted for most of the snapper grouper harvest in the South Atlantic at around 6.90 MP, followed by North Carolina at 2.21 MP, South Carolina at 1.51 MP, and lastly by Georgia at 0.62 MP.


Ecological Role:                                                                                                                        Species Stress: Based on 537 sectioned otoliths from red snapper collected in the southeast Atlantic from 1990-1996, Manooch and Potts (1997) found that red snapper length-at-age determinations were considerably smaller than the length-at-age estimates of red snapper determined from sectioned otoliths collected during 1974-1978 (Nelson and Manooch 1982).  The reduction in length-at-age found by Manooch and Potts (1997) may have been due to variation in sample sizes, differences in interpretation of the sectioned otoliths by investigators, or sustained heavy fishing pressure that may have selectively removed, over many generations, the faster growing individuals of the populations.
Nieland et al. (2007b) sampled 6,159 red snapper landed at a commercial dock in Cameron, Louisiana from October 1998 to May 2004 for morphometrics data and otoliths for age determination. The harvest was almost totally dominated by individuals of ages 2-6 years. Over the course of their sampling, they observed statistically significant decreases in mean total length (TL) of red snapper at ages 2-6 years.  The decline in mean sizes at age might be attributed to density-dependence wherein as the population increased in numbers there was a decrease in resources (food, habitat etc.) per individual fish, which might be manifested in a compensatory decrease in growth rate. Thus declines in red snapper mean TL age may be an expression of recovery from an overfished condition. Conversely, the heavy commercial and recreational harvest of young (juvenile and adult) red snapper in the northern GOM, many of them at the minimum TL required for retention, may have resulted in an inadvertent selection for the survival of slow-growing individuals.
Jackson et al. (2007) noted that red snapper in the GOM are managed as a unit stock and the fishery management plan is based on minimal data regarding reproductive output, and the size and age at sexual maturation is not certain. Differences in size and age at sexual maturity of red snapper between the northeast and north-central GOM were evaluated to test whether the population conforms to the unit stock hypothesis.  Red snapper were collected during the spawning season in 1999, 2000, and 2001 from the GOM off Alabama and Louisiana and were used to describe maturation schedules. Progression of oocyte maturation to vitellogenesis was used to define sexually mature females. Combined data showed the smallest mature red snapper was 267 mm FL and was two years old. The smallest with hydrated oocytes, indicative of imminent spawning, or postovulatory follicles, indicative of recent spawning, were 285 and 297 mm FL respectively, and both were two years old. Red snapper off Alabama reached maturation at smaller sizes and younger ages than those sampled off Louisiana.  Growth rates did not differ between the regions. Such differences in maturation schedules may document an important stock response by red snapper in the GOM to reductions in population size.  Jackson et al. (2007) stated that shifts in maturation schedules in red snapper may be attributable to genetic selection coincident with increased mortality.
Trippel (1995) reviewed fisheries literature worldwide and described situations where fish stock abundances have declined dramatically due to overfishing.  Evidence indicates that stocks comprised of a broad range of sizes and ages are able to spawn more eggs of a large range in size and that these eggs are spawned over a longer period of time than eggs produced by stocks comprised primarily of young fish.  He recommended that management should be pursued on the basis of reducing fishing pressure to levels that permit fish populations to reach older ages. The biological consequences of selective removal of large fish are now more clearly understood, and the excessive removal of fish can no longer be perceived as simply leading to a reduction in the number of eggs produced by the population. Important aspects of egg size and spawning time are also jeopardized by high levels of exploitation.
The truncated age structure and prevalence of faster growth rates of red snapper throughout the GOM are compensatory responses to overfishing that could severely hinder the population�s ability to recover (Saari 2011). Likewise, the temporal decrease in the length-at-age of red snapper and the precipitous decline in landings in the southeast Atlantic, and a low Spawning Potential Ratio (SPR) of 24-32% (SAFMC 2001) suggested that this species may have been overfished (SAFMC 2001, White and Potts 2004). Fisheries managers should consider these maladaptive responses in the stock when evaluating future assessments and management options, as well as the potential stock responses associated with future management options.

Size limits are commonly used to manage commercial and recreational fisheries (Stephen et al. 2010).  Minimum size limits, which are relatively easy to enforce, have been used to restrict total harvest, prevent growth overfishing, and allow individuals at least one spawning event before removal from the fishery. One widely acknowledged disadvantage of size limits is the mortality immediately at release for under-sized fish, but another emerging concern is that size-selective fisheries drive a phenotypic change in the life history traits of a population. Observed phenotypic changes can be driven by genetic and/or environmental influences. If the change is largely influenced by genetic changes, it may not be readily reversed.  Recent studies have shown that high levels of fishing pressure can change the size at age, age at maturation, and size at maturation of fish species.
