An advective field of currents was developed from a large database of drifter and moored currents, augmented by an operational model to fill gaps. The starting points for larval transport were the locations and day of the year of larval captures from the SEAMAP program ichthyoplankton surveys.  Because the field of currents was derived from near-surface observations and the depth distribution was uncertain, findings were expressed in terms of maximal transport pathways.  Transport pathways were principally vectored toward the west during September, October, and May under the influence of relatively strong climatological westward wind stress. Eastward pathways occurred in June, July, and August under the influence of weaker shoreward wind stress.  Westward transport pathways past the Mississippi delta were found near the delta, away from typical juvenile settlement habitat. Water movement from east to west across the Apalachicola peninsula occurred in the fall, suggesting the potential for genetic exchange from the eastern to the western Gulf.  Eastward water movement across the Apalachicola peninsula occurred in July, but only along the outer shelf.

Young of Year-Red snapper as small as 18 mm settled on relatively unstructured open shelf habitats in the GOM off Alabama in summer, but by the winter age-0 fish had recruited to artificial reefs that provided greater bottom complexity and relief (Szedlemayer and Lee 2004).

Juvenile-In Texas, juvenile red snapper moved offshore from shallow water (about 15-30 m) in summer to deeper water (35-60 m) in winter, based on depths of capture by trawl (Moseley 1966, Bradley and Bryan 1975). Bradley and Bryan (1975) reported ontogenetic movement of red snapper to structured habitats of increasing dimension occurred as an inshore to offshore migration throughout the juvenile stage. The movement may be a means of avoiding cooler inshore water in winter. The actual cue for movement, however was not a drop in temperature, because movement occurred before the temperature declined. Nelson and Manooch (1982) reported no size segregation between shallow (<35 m) and deep (>35 m) waters of the Carolinas.

Nieland and Wilson (2003) randomly sampled red snapper (n=300) killed using the explosive removal of an obsolete oil and gas platform off Louisiana.  Otolith-based aging revealed the majority of the fish were 2 and 3 years old (53% and 37% respectively), while virtually no age-1 fish were present in their sample.  Patterson et al. (2007) speculated that the lack of older fish at both platforms and artificial reefs may indicate that thigmotaxis or the threat of predation subsides with age and size, thus older fish display less site fidelity and greater movement (Patterson et al. 2001, Patterson and Cowan 2003, Strelcheck et al. 2007).  Alternatively, high fish mortality rates at platforms and artificial reefs may remove snapper very quickly from the population once fish recruit to the commercial or recreational fishery (Nieland and Wilson 2003, Patterson et al. 2007).

Adult: Adult red snapper remain in their reef habitations during cooler months. Tagging studies generally indicate little movement, particularly when the fish are released in water less than 14 m deep (Topp 1963, Beaumariage and Bullock 1976, Fable 1980). Adult red snapper sometimes move closer to shore in summer; they were collected in trawls in the lower parts of St. Andrews Bay system, Florida, in summer and fall but not in winter and spring (Ogren and Brusher 1977). Occasional tagged adults were caught 5-150 nautical miles from the point of release after 29-1,163 days of freedom (Beaumariage and Wittich 1966, Moe 1966, Beaumariage 1969).

Site fidelity (SF) provides an annual estimate of reef fish immigration or emigration from a reef (Gallaway et al. 2009).  For red snapper, 2- to 3-year-old fish at artificial reef structures in shallow water show high fidelity to a site on temporal scales of months to a year, albeit the probability of detecting ultrasonically tagged red snapper at a site one year after release was only 50% (Schroepfer and Szedlemayer 2006).

Mitchell et al. (2004) reported larger (median TL ranged from 545 to 815 mm among surveys), older red snapper were captured at higher rates in outer shelf habitats during experimental longline surveys in the eastern (off Alabama-Mississippi) and western (off Texas) GOM.  Fisheries-dependent data confirm that larger, older fish are captured more frequently in commercial-longline sectors operating offshore (Allman and Fitzhugh 2007).

The two main approaches that have been applied to estimate red snapper site fidelity are conventional and, more recently ultrasonic tagging (Patterson et al. 1997).  Szedlmayer (1997) conducted the first ultrasonic tagging experiment on red snapper on artificial reefs off Alabama. He concluded that red snapper displayed �high� site fidelity (SF) to artificial reefs, yet the mean time fish were detected was only 150 d for a species with a maximum longevity >50 years (Wilson and Nieland 2001).  While one fish was detected in the Szedlmayer study for 597 d, several others were lost from the study area. Both �stayers� and �movers� have important implications for population and connectivity (Diamond et al. 2007).  But, movers can no longer be tracked with ultrasonic receivers once they move beyond the range of the receivers.  Hence, the emphasis in red snapper ultrasonic tagging has tended to be weighted toward the stayers.  For example, Schroepfer and Szedlmayer (2006) concluded that ultrasonically tagged red snapper displayed high site fidelity to artificial reefs because 87% (13 out of 15) of the fish were detected within 200 m of the study sites 99% of the times they were detected. Westmeyer et al. (2007) reported even lower probability of detection at petroleum platforms off Louisiana after one year.   Site fidelity provides an annual estimate of reef fish immigration or emigration from a reef (Gallaway et al. 2009).
Conventional tagging studies are better suited for estimating dispersion distances and rates of movers (Patterson et al. 2007).  Among various studies, fish were captured at natural reefs, artificial reefs (including petroleum platforms), or both.  However, most of the existing tagging studies were conducted over artificial reefs sites in the north-central GOM (Szedlmayer and Shipp 1994, Patterson and Cowan 2003, Strelcheck et al. 2007). An exception is data from the Schlitz Tagging Program conducted off Florida in the 1960s (Beaumariage 1969, Moe et al. 1970). Fable (1980) also reported movement data for red snapper tagged over a variety of natural and artificial reefs off Texas, as did Diamond et. al. (2007).

A number of tagging studies have been conducted using red snapper in the GOM (Gallaway et al. 2009). Fable (1980) tagged 299 red snapper at natural reefs off Texas and 17 fish were recovered. Gallaway et al. (1980) reported very high short-term fidelity for red snapper at platforms in the Buccaneer Gas and Oil Field offshore of Galveston, Texas during the summer months.  Szeldlmayer and Shipp (1994) tagged and released 1,155 small red snapper at artificial reefs offshore of Alabama.  A total of 146 tagged fish were recovered, but only 37 of these had known recapture locations.  A total of 28 (74%) were recaptured within 2 km of their release site. Watterson et al. (1998) tagged red snapper at 9 artificial reefs off Alabama from March 1995 to January 1997. Eighty percent of recaptured fish that were not at liberty during Hurricane Opal were recaptured from 1.7 to 2.5 km from their site of release. Fish that were at liberty during Hurricane Opal (October 1995) showed greater movement.  The at-liberty fish moved on average 32.6 km, with 8 fish moving over 100 km, and 3 fish moving over 200 km.

Patterson et al. (2001b) continued the tagging study of Watterson et al. (1998) through August of 1999.  Hurricane George passed within 50 km of the tagging site during August 1999.  Of fish recaptured at tagging sites, 199 (97%) were captured  at the site where they had been released while 5 had changed location.  Patterson and Cowan (2003) used the data gathered by Patterson et al. (2001a) to estimate SF by modeling the rate of decline in recaptures at the tagging sites over time to obtain an annual instantaneous rate of decline (D).  They used the data to estimate the total mortality (Z), the total annual instantaneous emigration (Q), and the natural mortality (M). Estimated SF values ranged from 24.8% for all recaptures to 25.3% for all recaptures of fish that were released at their original captures, to 26.5% for recaptures for fish tagged and recaptured in the intervals between hurricanes.

Strelcheck et al. (2007) tagged 4,317 red snapper at 14 experimental reefs off coastal Alabama between January 1999 and October 2002.  Some 629 recaptures were reported, of which 412 (65%) were made by researchers at the original release site and 217 were reported by fishers. They concluded that observations of high site fidelity (SF) and low dispersal rates provided support for the hypothesis that artificial reefs offshore Alabama provide suitable habitat for adult red snapper.  In another conventional mark-recapture study, 5,614 red snapper were tagged between July 2002 and August 2005 (Diamond et al. 2007).  Tag returns provided location information for 82 fish. Of these, 54% moved an average distance of 20.4 km.  In a second program, over 9,000 fish were tagged aboard charter headboats, and private boats between 1983 and 2006.   In the latter case, 60 returns were analyzed. Most (72%) were recaptured at their release site, with 28% showing an average movement of 19.1 km.  Diamond et al. (2007) found that the spatial scale of movements was small enough to support the idea that red snapper stocks in the northern GOM are relatively isolated and that there may be a separate demographic stock off Texas.  Thus, all of these studies (Strelcheck et al. 2007, Diamond et al. 2007) support the view of limited movement and relatively high SF.

The issue of confidence about positional information for tagged fish reported by fishers has prompted a number of ultrasonic telemetry studies for red snapper (Szedlmayer 1997, Szedlemayer and Schropfer 2005, Schroepfer and Szedlmayer 2006, Peabody and Wilson 2006, Topping 2009, Topping and Szedlmayer 2011).  Szedlemayer (1997) reported residence times on artificial reefs of 17-597 days, and Szedlemayer and Schroepfer (2005) estimated red snapper were resident on an artificial reef for a mean time of 212 days, with one fish staying at one reef for up to 597 days.  Using the published information along with new ultrasonic tagging studies, Schroepfer and Szedlemayer (2006) used event analysis described by Allison (1995) to provide a newer estimate of residence time on reefs. The median residence time increased to 373 days.

Topping and Szedlmayer (2011) estimated residence time, SF, and movements of red snapper at 6 sites in the northern GOM using long-term telemetry monitoring. Event analysis was used to estimate SF and residence, based on right-censoring fishing and natural mortality.  Median residence time was 542 days, ranging from 1 to 1,099 d, with 72% of the fish staying at least 1 yr at the site.  Some fish (N=12) showed seasonal and directed movements to other sites (up to 8 km away) and returned to original sites 7 mo later. Diel movements away from the structure tended to occur at night. Site fidelity and residence times of red snapper were greater than in any previous study and show the importance of artificial reefs for this species.
Two tagging studies on red snapper have been conducted in the southeastern Atlantic: one by South Carolina Department of Natural Resources (SC DNR) and the other by Mote Marine Lab (Burns et al. 2008, SEDAR24 WG Report 2010). SC DNR�s tagging of red snapper began in 1990 and is ongoing. Through this study, 1,568 red snapper have been tagged by recreational fishermen with 176 fish returned (11.2% return rate). Few fish tagged have been over the 20 inch size limit (1.6%). Of the fish that have been recaptured, 2.4% of the red snapper were greater than the legal size limit at the time of tagging and 25.6% of the red snapper were greater than the legal size limit at the time of recapture.

In the largest tagging study, Burns et al. (2004) of Mote Marine Laboratory tagged and released 5,272 red snapper in the GOM (from Naples, FL, to the eastern border of Texas) and Atlantic (from Cape Canaveral, FL, to Georgia) over a 13 yr period. Approximately 40% of these fish were tagged in the Atlantic. Forty-four percent of the specimens were recaptured within 1.9 km of the tagging site. Less than 10 of the 410 recapture events showed movement>100 miles and movement between the Gulf of Mexico and the Atlantic coast is not mentioned in the report.

Mote Marine Lab has been tagging red snapper off Florida since 1997, and 4,124 have been tagged with 443 fish returned (10.7%) (Burns and Brown-Peterson 2008).  Few fish have been tagged over the 20 inch size limit (1.6%). Of the fish that have been recaptured, 3.6% of the red snapper were greater than the legal size limit at the time of tagging and 32.5% of the red snapper were greater than the legal size at the time of recapture.

Burns and Brown-Peterson (2008) tagged red snapper on both the east and west coasts of Florida. Plotting red snapper tag and recapture location showed the majority of the fish were site faithful, although some moved longer distances. The largest movement distance recorded was 362.4 km or 225 miles over a period of 48 months. Additionally, tag recaptures from the Mote Marine Laboratory database show a red snapper traveling from off Pensacola (Florida panhandle) to St. Augustine (Atlantic coast). Movement on the east coast tended to be more often from north to south and vice a versa due to the narrow shelf whereas west coast fish could expand over the much broader shelf. The general direction of movement, determined by fish tagged in the Florida Panhandle, was to the east and southeastern in the GOM. This is consistent with a clockwise direction along the Gulf coast reported for red snapper in previous studies (Render and Wilson 1993, Ingram and Patterson 2001, Patterson et al 2001a). This may indicate that re-recruitment to the southwest Florida coast may have come from the northern Gulf of Mexico.

Diamond et al. (2007) provided a list of factors that have been suggested to be important in affecting the percentage of fish that move compared to the percentage that remain at a site. These included size or age of fish (Moseley 1966), depth of capture (Beaumariage 1969, Watterson et al. 1998), seasonal patterns due to water temperature or reproductive condition (Topp 1963, Beaumariage 1969, Watterson et al. 1998), hurricanes (Watterson et al. 1998, Patterson et al. 2001a, Peabody 2004).  The accuracy of positional data reported for tag returns by fishers can also be an issue regarding site fidelity (SF).

It has also been hypothesized that SF of reef-associated organisms is dependent on prey availability and the availability of suitable refuge, i.e., the resource mosaic hypothesis (Frazer and Lindberg 1994) and density-dependent habitat selection (Lindberg et al. 2006). Reef-associated fish species that rely on benthic prey as the primary component of their diet  may create a gradient of prey depletion (or feeding halo) around the reefs, resulting in negative feedbacks to reef fish energetic, residence times, and local abundance, particularly when the feeding halos of adjacent reefs overlap (Lindberg et al. 2006, Gallaway et al. 2009). The degree of prey depletion and negative feedback can alter the potential for sustained productivity of an artificial reef or reef complex. Bioenergetic demands increase as foraging area increases, resulting in increased emigration from resource-depleted reefs to reefs containing a greater abundance of prey.

Once red snapper grow to about 8 years old, they are large enough to be invulnerable to most predation and occur over open habitat as well as at reef habitat (Gallaway et al. 2009).  In the western GOM, these older fish are most abundant in longline sets at depths between 55 and 92 m. In this region, the zone of highest abundance of early red snapper larvae (Lyczkowski-Shultz and Hanisko 2007) corresponds to the depth distribution of 8+ year adults taken on longlines (Mitchell 2004, Gallaway et al. 2009).

Gallaway et al. (2009) presented histograms depiciting the relative frequency of age groups of red snapper residing at offshore oil and gas platforms, artificial reefs, and over soft bottom in deeper water in the northern GOM.  Explosive removals determined that the most frequent age groups (N=16,505) found to be present on oil and gas platforms were age-2 (34%) and age-3 (29%) (Gitschlag et al. 2003).  Age-4 was the only other age group representing as much as 10% of the population.  Similar data for the age structure of red snapper at oil and gas platforms were presented by Nieland and Wilson (2003). Szedlemayer (2007) determined the ages for 3,415 red snapper collected from 94 different artificial reefs off Alabama. Age-1 comprised about 14%, age-2 (36%), and age-3 comprised 25% of the total population.  Red snapper on the Flower Gardens Banks (N=780) were predominantly ages 3, 4, and 5 (Zastrow 1984).  In contrast red snapper sampled by Mitchell (2004) caught using longlines over soft bottom in deeper water were predominantly comprised of red snapper ranging from 8 to over 17 years of age (Gallaway et al. 2009).

Gallaway et al. (2009) finished their review of red snapper life history by concluding that prior to the proliferation of offshore oil and gas platforms and artificial reefs (e.g., pre-1980s), young new recruits occurred over open substrates between age 0 and age 2.  In this habitat, natural mortality was high due to the lack of cover affording protection from predation, and the fish were subject to shrimp trawl bycatch as well. Age-2 red snapper were commonly taken in shrimp trawls along with age-0 and age-1 fish until about 1990, which demonstrated their abundance in open habitats (Goodyear  1995). After this stage, natural reefs in the northern GOM would then harbor red snapper age 3 and greater.  They suggested that recruitment of the age 0-2 fish to the natural reefs was inhibited by the presence of adult or larger fish occupying the reefs. After age-8, red snapper would increase their foraging range to include soft-bottom habitat in deeper water, because they reached a size that reduced population predation.

sections.heading: Substrate
sections.content:
Egg/Parturition- Not applicable since eggs are planktonic (Rabalais et al. 1980, Minton et al. 1983).
Larva- Not applicable since larvae are planktonic (Rabalais et al. 1980, Minton et al. 1983, Lyczkowski-Shultz and Hanisko 2007).
Young of Year- In the northwestern Gulf of Mexico (GOM), Szedlemeyer and Conti (1999) observed newly settled age-0 red snapper on open bottom (sand and mud) as well as low-relief shell habitat. However settlement was significantly higher on shell ridges. Rooker et al. (2004) collected newly settled red snapper on shell ridges, but observed large numbers of settlers on mud habitats away from low-relief shell ridges suggesting factors other than structure may be critical during the early post-settlement period.
A number of studies have demonstrated that age-0 and age-1 red snapper are abundant over sand, mud, and shell-rubble substrates in the U.S. GOM.  Red snapper were sampled at three natural banks on the inner continental shelf of Texas (Geary et al. 2007). Digital side-scan sonar and multibeam data were used to define inshore (mud), ridge (shell), and offshore (mud) habitats for Freeport Rocks, Heald Bank, and Sabine Bank in 2003 and Freeport Banks on 2004.  Results indicate that both shell and inshore and offshore mud habitats associated with these natural banks serve as settlement habitat for red snapper, and all three habitats have the potential to function as nursery areas for this species.  Settlement sizes and ages reported by Geary et al. (2007) were similar to those of previous studies off Mississippi and Alabama (Workman et al. 2002, Szedlemeyer and Conti 1999) and off Texas (Rooker et al. 2004).  Unfortunately, these benthic habitats are the same areas fished by the GOM fisheries for pink, brown, and white shrimp (Patterson et al. 2005, Bentley et al. 2005).
Shrimp trawling in the U.S. GOM from Florida to Texas is conducted over sand, mud, and submerged beds of oyster shell (Wells et al. 2008a, b).  Wells et al. (2008a) analyzed the spatial distribution and abundance of age-0 red snapper over sand, low-relief shell rubble, high-relief shell rubble, and at high-relief habitats within a de facto non-trawl area and in similar habitats where commercial shrimp trawling occurred.  Age-0 red snapper were most dense over sand and low-relief shell rubble habitats and moved to higher-relief shell rubble and natural habitats by age-1.  Habitat-specific growth rates of age-0 fish were highest over sand (range 0.05-1.03 mm per day).  Densities of age-0 red snapper were highest over trawled sand, but higher over non-trawled shell rubble by 6 months of age (age-0.5+).  Red snapper collected over sand  and low-relief shell rubble areas exposed to trawling had truncated size distributions, higher mortality estimates, and lower production potential (the latter evaluated with G-Z and P-B ratios) compared with fish over non-trawled areas of similar habitat. The results suggest that juvenile red snapper residing over non-trawled areas may have a higher probability of survival than fish in areas exposed to commercial shrimp trawling.
Research indicates that structured habitats are essential nursery areas for age-0 red snapper (Szedlemayer and Conti 1999). Laboratory experiments indicate both wild and hatchery-reared juvenile red snapper show associations with structure, (i.e., artificial reefs, Masuda et al. 2003) and shell habitats (Szedlmayer and Howe 1997).
Sampling trawls deployed by Rooker et al. (2004) and Geary et al. (2007) contained mesh bags that retained recently settled young-of-year red snapper for which biogenic structures such as worm tubes may provide sufficient structure in soft sediments (Workman et al. 2002).  Furthermore, mud habitats were immediately adjacent to shell rubble habitats and may have served as foraging areas.  Patterson et al. (2005) reported red snapper juvenile (YOY?) density in sand habitats was significantly correlated with sponge biomass. Hence, they concluded sponges provided habitat complexity at a scale sufficient for juvenile (YOY?) snapper.  Similarly, Workman and Foster (1994) reported juvenile (YOY?) snapper in sand habitats typically were associated with objects such as squid egg cases, woody debris, or discarded drink cans, that fish used for either  refuge or orientation (Patterson et al. 2007).
Research has been conducted to discriminate between nursery areas for age-0 red snapper in the northern GOM using otolith microchemistry (Patterson et al. 1998,  2001c).   More recently Sluis (2011) was able to assign juvenile (age1 and/or age-2) red snapper to either artificial reefs or oil and gas platforms based on otolith microchemistry.
Red Snapper Bycatch In GOM Shrimp Trawl Fisheries
Regulation of GOM red snapper did not start until 1984 with the implementation of the reef fish management plan by the Gulf of Mexico Fisheries Management Council (GMFMC) (Hood et al. 2007).  The first stock assessment of GOM red snapper occurred in 1988 and concluded that the stock was overfished and that overfishing was occurring (Goodyear 1988). The assessment also noted that the GOM shrimp fishery contributed heavily to the red snapper fishing mortality (F) by harvesting age-0 and age-1 red snapper as bycatch.  A second red snapper stock assessment was conducted by Goodyear and Phares (1990). This assessment concluded that the stock condition was less than one percent of the target 20% spawning stock biomass ratio (SSBR). To rebuild the stock by 2000, a complete closure of the directed fishery would be required and there would also need to be a 60% reduction in shrimp trawl bycatch of juvenile red snapper.
It is well documented that juvenile red snapper are a significant portion of shrimp trawl bycatch in the GOM with some 20 million estimated to have been taken in shrimp trawling in 1989 (Nichols et al. 1990). Warren (1994) estimated that the capture of juvenile red snapper in shrimp trawl bycatch was 34 million fish per year. More recent estimates of juvenile snapper bycatch in the shrimp trawl fishery vary from 25 to 45 million per year (SEDAR7  2005).  Although a portion of these fish may survive capture; the vast majority do not survive and are discarded (Gutherz and Pellegrin 1988).  Goodyear and Phares (1990) estimated that 90% of the fishing mortality of age-0 and age-1 red snapper in the GOM results from shrimp trawl bycatch.
This led to the requirement that shrimp fishing vessels must install bycatch reduction devices (BRDs) to increase the escapement of juvenile red snapper from the trawls (Gallaway and Cole 1999). Beginning in May 1998, the National Marine Fisheries Service (NMFS) required that BRDs be installed on trawls used in the commercial shrimp fishery.  BRDs were mandated for use in the U.S. GOM shrimp fishery to reduce shrimp trawl mortality of juvenile red snapper. Conditional survival of juvenile red snapper from shrimp trawl bycatch had been estimated to be in the order of 12%. The BRDs were believed to be capable of reducing the bycatch mortality by more than 50%.  Hence, BRDs were mandated by GMFMC to support rebuilding the red snapper stock in the GOM by the target date of 2019.  Research programs were initiated to evaluate whether BRDs were capable of reducing bycatch mortality by more than 50% (Parsons and Foster 2007).
Branstetter (1997) coordinated evaluations of various types of BRDs using observers on commercial shrimp trawlers in the GOM and southeastern Atlantic. In the western GOM, red snapper occurred in 393 of 719 total fisheye tows and 201 or 403 expanded mesh tows. Their distribution tended to be offshore of the 10 fathom (20 m) contour except off south Texas where near-shore captures of red snapper were not uncommon. Reduction levels of red snapper by BRDs were strongly correlated to seasons and the associated size of the fish on the shrimp grounds.  Based on the data gathered, the smallest fish (age-0) recruit to the shrimp grounds in the late summer-early fall at a size of about 50 mm FL.  If smaller fish (<50 mm FL) recruit to the grounds earlier, they did not occur in the final catch. It may be that these fish pass though the meshes of the cod-end. The juveniles continue to reside in these regions through age-1 (mean size about 175 mm FL). (For stock assessment purposes all fish become age-1 at the start of the calendar year i.e., at 6 months of age, but for the purposes of this discussion, ages represent biological ages where spawning birthdates are mid-summer). Quarterly stratification of the red snapper length-frequencies taken in both the �control� and �BRD� net indicated that during the first calendar quarter the majority of individuals were small age-0 fish less than 120 mm FL, and at this size there was very little reduction.  As the year progressed, and these fish increased in size to larger than 110 mm FL, reductions increased, but only for fish larger than 110 mm FL. By mid-summer, when most red snapper on the shrimp grounds were larger than 100 mm, reductions were substantial. During the fall, when the next year-class began recruiting, overall reductions were reduced again because of the limited reduction of these smaller fish, but there were still good reductions for the few larger fish.
Research studies into swimming performance and behavior of red snapper in relation to bycatch reduction have been published (Engas et al. 1999, Workman and Foster 2002, Parsons and Foster 2007).  This size-limited reduction has a kinematic basis (Branstetter 1997, Engas et al. 1999).  Fish smaller than 100 mm cannot sustain a swimming speed to overcome the speed of the trawl, thus they tire and are pushed to the back of the cod end during and extended tow time.  Red snapper 60-100 mm can sustain a swimming speed of only about 0.2-0.3 meters per second, and have a burst speed of about 0.6-1.0 meters per second, whereas the trawl is being pulled forward at about 1.3 meters per second (2.5 nautical miles per hour). Once the juvenile red snapper attain a size of 110 mm, they can produce the needed sustainable swimming speed to keep a constant position with the net, and seek escape routes.
Parsons and Foster (2007) found a significant effect of fish size and season on red snapper critical swimming speeds using a Brett style swim tunnel. For fish ranging between 6 and 17 cm SL, critical swimming speeds ranged from about 35-70 cm/s, depending upon the season. However, critical swimming speeds did not differ between day and night. This was important, since most shrimp trawling in the GOM occurs at night. A Vortex Generating Bycatch Reduction Device (VGBRD) was used to evaluate red snapper behavior during day and during the night.  During daylight, 79.2% of red snapper exited the VGBRD in an average of 4.1 minutes. However, during night-time tests, only 17.6% of the red snapper exited the VGBRD in an average of 5.0 minutes.  Behavioral tests revealed a strong negative phototactic response in dark adapted red snapper. Furthermore, they found that when the VGBRD was illuminated with LED lights placed downstream of the exit, 96% of red snapper exited the device in 7.1 minutes. In color/contrast choice experiments, red snapper unerringly associated with the dark colored (black or dark green) panel placed on the bottom of the experimental tank.  In another set of experiments, they found that red snapper displayed a strong optomotor response, i.e., the tendency to following and match speeds with a moving pattern.  They concluded that illumination, color/contrast, and/or the optomotor response may improve BRD performance.
Modeling conducted by Goodyear (1995) of both NMFS SEAMAP bottom trawl data and commercial shrimp trawl data collected by on-board observers found that age-0 and age-1 red snapper predominated in the catches. Goodyear estimated that 310.7 million red snapper were captured in commercial shrimp trawls from 1982 to 1992 with 138.5 million (44%) being age-0 and 172.2 million (56%) being age-1.
A study was conducted by LGL Ecological Research Associates to assess the feasibility of meeting the 60% escapement requirement using BRDs on shrimp trawls (Gallaway et. 1998).  They reanalyzed the SEAMAP bottom trawl data, the commercial observer data, and shrimp fishing effort in a general linear model and estimated that 198.1 million red snapper had been captured in shrimp trawls from 1982 to 1992.  They estimated that 129.4 million (65%) red snapper were age-0 and 68.8 million (35%) were age-1.  The revised estimates averaged on the order of 30 to 47% lower than the NMFS estimates by Goodyear (1995).  Nevertheless, the estimated bycatch levels were high (26 to 32 million per year).  The age structure of the bycatch consisted of a much larger fraction of age-0 fish and fewer age-1 fish than had been estimated by Goodyear (1995).  Gallaway et al. (1998) concluded that BRDs did not effectively exclude age-0 red snapper, and that existing stock recovery policy based on the NMFS model bycatch estimates derived from using BRDs to reduce shrimp trawl mortality of juvenile red snapper may be ineffective.
Gallaway and Cole (1999) estimated that the maximum potential exclusion of juvenile (age-0 and age-1) red snapper with the use of BRDs was only about 25-27%, not the 59% that had been previously estimated (Wattson et al. 1997a 1997b).  If rebuilding required a 50% reduction in bycatch mortality of age-0 and age-1 red snapper, Gallaway and Cole (1999) concluded that the use of BRDs by itself would not produce the mortality reductions necessary to meet this objective. Bycatch reduction of juvenile red snapper from BRDs is currently estimated to be below 15% (Foster 2005, Hood et al. 2007).
Beginning in May 1998, NMFS required that BRDs be installed in penaeid shrimp trawl gear in the GOM (Gazey et al. 2008). Changes in observer protocols were introduced, one of which was that all red snapper collected in shrimp trawls would be enumerated and measured when possible.  This yielded a time series of catch data and length frequency data from the GOM commercial shrimp fishery.
Bycatch estimates (Nichols 2005a, 2005b) were improved by both the new red snapper observer data and by the development of an improved bycatch model. The red snapper length data gathered by observers in the GOM were used to make subjective estimates of the age-0 and age-1 fractions in the bycatch (Nichols 2005c). Nichols et al. (2005) also used seasonal SEAMAP trawl survey data to estimate the instantaneous natural mortality (M) was 0.6 for age-1 red snapper. This value was used in conjunction with the ratio of age-0 to age-1 mortality used by Goodyear (1995) to infer that M for age-0 red snapper was 1.0 (SEDAR7 2005). These values were used in the SEDAR7 (2005) stock assessment as the best estimates of the M for age-0 and age-1 red snapper in the GOM. Cordue (2005) recommended that future red snapper stock assessments should model post-recruitment density-dependent mortality �as this is critical for determining the impact of penaeid shrimp bycatch on red snapper rebuilding.�
Gazey et al. (2008) analyzed NMFS�s post-1998 Observer file and constructed a length-based, age-structured model (Fournier et al. 1998) to objectively estimate the growth and mortality parameters and age composition of the commercial shrimp trawl bycatch of red snapper in the western GOM using 81 length frequency datasets (a total of 239,521 fish were measured) collected from July 1999 to February 2007.  Important findings of the modeling include: (1) the shrimp trawl bycatch during the first and the third trimesters is dominated (86-87%) by age-0 fish, (2) the growth pattern of age-0 and age-1 fish suggest the fish form an annulus during the winter months, (3) the natural mortality of age-0 fish appears to be double (a minimum 70% increase) the value used in the last stock assessment (done in 2005), and (4) the evidence of density-dependent juvenile mortality derived from the length-based, age-structured model was overwhelming (i.e., density-dependent mortality indices derived from the model supported the concept that survival of age-0 and age-1 red snapper were related to the availability of benthic habitat). Inclusion of these findings in the red snapper stock assessment has the potential of substantially alter management practices.
Shrimp Fishing areas Southeast Atlantic
The commercial fishing area for penaeid shrimp (white, brown and pink) species in the South Atlantic is mainly concentrated from Pamlico Sound and Ocracoke Inlet, North Carolina to Fort Pierce, Florida (SAFMC-FEP 2008). There is another fishery off the Florida Keys where the main target is pink shrimp. Commercial shrimp catches in all four states are taken from internal waters, state waters out to three miles and from the EEZ. Most of the shrimp in these states are caught by otter trawls (SAFMC 1996b).
In North Carolina, the important shrimp fishing areas are Pamlico Sound, Core Sound, major rivers and off the southern coast, south of Ocracoke Inlet. The brown shrimp fishery is the most important fishery followed by the white shrimp fishery in the fall and the pink shrimp fishery in the spring. Trawling often occurs in the EEZ off South Carolina prior to the opening of the territorial sea and during the open state trawling season. The summer to winter white shrimp fishery is the most important shrimp fishery for South Carolina vessels.

In Georgia, shrimp fishing takes place along the entire coast. Shrimp are harvested in estuarine and nearshore waters of each coastal county (SAFMC-FEP 2008). Georgia law allows for state waters to be opened for the harvest of food shrimp from May 15 until December 31. On average, Georgia waters are open from Mid-June through January. White shrimp comprise the largest annual portion of the commercial catch, yielding approximately 80% of all harvested shrimp. It is harvested in state waters during late summer, fall, winter, and spring months. The brown shrimp comprises approximately 18% of the annual catch. During the summer, brown shrimp may comprise upwards of 70% of the total harvested shrimp. Pink shrimp make up less than 2% of the total catch.

The most important fishing area along Florida�s east coast is the northeastern part of the state, between Fernandina Beach and Melbourne, just south of Cape Canaveral (SAFMC-FEP 2008).  Along Florida�s east coast, the shrimp fishery is characterized by brown shrimp dominating the summer fishery and white shrimp dominating the fall and winter fisheries. Pink shrimp are harvested in Biscayne Bay generally during the period November through May.

Commercial bait shrimp fishery
The commercial bait shrimp fishery is much larger in Florida than in the other South Atlantic states. Live shrimp for bait are caught in Dade County and in six counties around the St. Johns River. A variety of gear is used in this fishery, but otter trawls (St. Johns) and roller frame trawls (Biscayne Bay) are the most commonly used. Wing nets are used in Volusia County for live bait shrimp harvest. There is very little effort directed specifically for commercial bait shrimp in either North Carolina or South Carolina.  In Georgia, however, the commercial bait shrimp fishery is the state�s fourth most valuable commercial fishery. Targeting smaller shrimp than the food shrimp industry, the commercial bait shrimp fishery is restricted to designated zones inside the estuary.

Red snapper Shrimp Trawl Bycatch Southeast Atlantic
Young Of Year-Very little data has been collected concerning the spatial distributions and relative abundance of age-0 red snapper in the southeast Atlantic (Rindone et al. 2012). While BRDs were installed on shrimp trawls associated with the shrimp fisheries from North Carolina to Florida in the southeast Atlantic, no young-of-the year (age-0) or juvenile (age-1) red snapper have been reported as bycatch (Scott-Denton and Nance 1996, Branstetter 1997, Murray et al. 1992, Rulifson et al. 1992, Watson et al. 1999, R. Pugliese pers. comm. SAFMC,  2012).  Red snapper were either absent or rare in the shrimp trawl catches monitored by observers.  Trawl catches by weight were dominated by estuarine and/or near-shore species such as Cannonball Jellyfish, White Shrimp, Spot, Atlantic Menhaden, Other jellyfish, Brown Shrimp, Atlantic Croaker, Southern Kingfish, Blue Crab, and Star Drum (SAFMC 1996).
Branstetter (1997) presented maps depicting the locations where commercial shrimp trawling using BRDs was conducted in the GOM and southeast Atlantic from 1993 to 1996. Most of the trawling depicted using BRDs in the GOM was conducted over the middle continental shelf over sand, and mud substrates. Most of the trawling depicted in the southeast Atlantic was located near shore. Red snapper were common in shrimp trawls monitored by observers in the GOM, but not in the southeastern Atlantic.  The most likely explanation for the absence of age-0 and age-1 red snapper in commercial shrimp trawl catches in the southeast Atlantic is that the shrimp fisheries are conducted near shore; while post-larval settlement of red snapper occurs farther offshore, similar to patterns mapped in the GOM (Diamond et al 2010).
The absence of age-0 and age-1 red snapper associated with fisheries-independent trawling conducted by MARMAP further offshore in the southeastern Atlantic may be related to the mesh sizes used in the trawls (White et al. 2010).  The Yankee Trawl used has a mesh of 5.1 cm in the cod end, and 1.3 cm in the cod end liner. Age-0 and age-1 red snapper may be able to escape through this mesh size.
Juvenile- Several studies have indicated that juvenile red snapper use inshore low-relief habitats during early life and migrate to high relief habitat in deeper waters as they grow (Bradley and Bryan 1975, Szedlemayer and Howe 1997, Szedlemayer and Conti 1999, Workman et al. 2002, Patterson et al. 2005).  Field studies have found that juvenile red snapper (>60 mm SL) recruit to artificial reef structures in the GOM (Workman et al. 2002, Szedelmayer and Lee 2004).
Wells (2005) and Wells and Cowan (2007) studied the abundance and spatial distributions of red snapper off the north-central GOM on the Alabama and Mississippi inner continental shelf.  Seabed characterization was performed with digital side-scan sonar and with sediment box-cores. They found that juvenile red snapper were predominantely collected over low-relief sand habitats, which is similar to the findings by Rooker et al. (2004) and Patterson et al. (2005).

Wells et al. (2008b) described habitat-specific differences in community structure, highlighting the differences between trawled and non-trawled areas of the northern GOM continental shelf. They characterized fish and invertebrate community structure over sand, shell-rubble, and natural reef substrata, and assessed the effects of trawling on sand and shell-rubble habitats and their associated communities during quarterly trawl surveys over a 2-year period. Fish and invertebrate communities differed significantly among habitat types, and with respect to trawling exposure.  Habitat characteristics were quantified with video transects sampled with a remotely operated vehicle, and included percentage coverage of tubeworms, bryozoans, anemones, corals, and algae, significantly affecting fish community structure. Diversity indices differed among habitats, with the highest Shannon diversity (H�) and Pielou�s evenness (J�) over shell-rubble, specifically non-trawled shell-rubble. In addition, higher values of H� and J� were found over trawled sand relative to non-trawled sand habitats.  Length frequency distributions of several abundant fish species showed truncated size distributions over trawled and non-trawled habitats and were both habitat- and species-specific. Median lengths of juvenile (age-1) red snapper were significantly lower over trawled sand (97.4 mm TL) in comparison to non- trawled sand (123.8 mm TL), and significantly lower over trawled shell (125.2 mm TL) in comparison to non-trawled shell (143.8 mm TL) habitat.  Numerically, red snapper displayed an affinity for reef habitats both outside and within non-trawled habitats, providing further support for the view that red snapper have an affinity for structured habitats over the sizes found in this study (mean TL 155 mm � 2mm SE).
Juvenile snapper display a strong thigmotaxis, seeking structured environments (Workman et al. 1994, Szedlemayer and Howe 1997, Bailey et al. 2001, Franks et al. 2004). Szedlemayer and Howe (1997) reported juvenile red snapper selected oyster shell versus sand habitat in tank trials, while Patterson et al. (2005) reported highest juvenile densities in trawl samples off Alabama and Mississippi came from high-relief (2-3 m) shell rubble ridge habitats. Seemingly contrary results were presented by Rooker et al. (2004) and Geary et al. (2007) that demonstrated that juvenile red snapper were in high densities in relatively unstructured mud habitats, and Patterson et al. (2005) reported moderately high juvenile densities occurred in sand habitats off Alabama and Mississippi. It is not clear whether these were young-of-year (age-0) red snapper or juvenile (age-1 and age-2) red snapper.
Adult-Adult red snapper are common in submarine gullies and depressions where food may accumulate and over coral reefs, rock outcrops, and gravel bottoms in the Gulf of Mexico (Stearns 1885, Klima 1976). Usually fewer fish are supported by smooth bottom without high relief than by bottom with three-dimensional structures, such as offshore oil and gas rigs, artificial reefs, and wrecks (Johnston et al. 1976, Sonnier et al. 1976).
Wells and Cowan (2007) found that sub-adult and adult red snapper were found over higher relief habitats such as the shell-rubble and natural hard bottom reef habitats.  They showed both significantly higher abundance and larger size over the reef habitat.   No seasonal effects were observed. Red snapper accounted for 59% of the overall similarity within reef fish assemblages and 20% of the total dissimilarity between shell and reef fish assemblages. It has been suggested that red snapper recruit to these high-relief habitats at about 18 months of age or 20 cm TL (Gallaway et al. 1999).

sections.heading: Artificial Reefs
sections.content:
Ontogenetic habitat shifts in red snapper habitat utilization is complicated due to the proliferation of artificial reefs deployed in the north-central GOM and the vast number of oil and gas platforms, which function as artificial reefs, erected in the northwestern GOM (Wilson and Nieland 2004, Westmeyer et al. 2007, Patterson et al. 2007).
Gallaway et al. (1981) characterized the food habits of red snapper at the Buccaneer Gas and Oil Field located offshore from Galveston, Texas, at depths of about 10 fathoms (20 m).  They suggested that red snapper moved away from the platforms during the late night to early morning period to feed over soft bottoms.  Hastings et al. (1976) obtained similar results for lutjanids at research platforms in the northeastern Gulf.  Peabody (2004), Peabody and Wilson (2006), and McDonough (2009) also suggested that nocturnal movements of red snapper away from Louisiana platforms was related to feeding behavior.
Dufrene (2005) characterized the inner-shelf area offshore eastern Louisiana to panhandle Florida and suggested that this benthic habitat was about 15% shell (submerged oyster shell banks) and 85% soft sand, mud substrate. The vast majority of the inner shelf in this area is composed of sand, mud, and silt, with little or no vertical relief (Gallaway et al. 2009).
On a larger spatial scale, Parker et al. (1983) estimated that 2,571 square kilometers of natural reef habitat (3.3% of the bottom) is present at depths between 18 and 91 m in the region between Pensacola, Florida and Pass Cavala, Texas.  Of this, only 1.6% (1,285 square kilometers) was comprised of reefs having relief >1m (Parker et al. 1983, Gallaway et al. 2009). If one adds natural reefs further offshore not assessed by Parker et al. (1983) the total area with high-relief natural reefs becomes 1, 578 square kilometers (Gallaway et al. 2009).  Thus, high-relief natural reefs constitute about 2% of the shelf area.
Some 4,000 offshore oil and gas platforms are located across the shelf of the western GOM and provide on the order of 12 square kilometers of artificial reef habitat (Gallaway et al. 2009). Platforms differ from natural reefs in many ways but a unique feature is that that they span the entire water column. Offshore petroleum platforms extend from the beach to the abyss, from Alabama to southern Texas. The highest platform densities occur in shallow and mid-shelf areas.
The construction of oil and gas platforms in the GOM as well as other artificial reefs has corresponded to changes in habitat distribution patterns for red snapper (Gallaway et al. 2009).  In 1960, there were about 351 offshore oil and gas platforms in the northern GOM, but these increased to 1,520 by 1970, and reached 2,540 by 1980. From 1990 to the present, the number of platforms has averaged about 4,000, considering both new installations as well as removals. They proposed that the increased construction of oil and gas platforms as well as other artificial reef habitats has provided protective habitat for age 2 fish that would otherwise have suffered high mortality over open habitats. Although fishing mortality can be high at these new habitats (Nieland and Wilson 2003), Gallaway et al. (2009) suggested that prior to their construction mortality was even higher for age 2 fish over open habitat. This being the case, they suggested that the removal of production platforms and other artificial reefs will likely result in a large reduction in red snapper available to the directed fisheries. They concluded that the existing literature is consistent with the premise of density-dependent natural mortality in red snapper for at least age 0 and age 1 fish, and likely for older fish as well. If this aspect is incorporated in the assessment models, management advice may be substantially altered.
An area of 3,108 square kilometers offshore Alabama has been designated for artificial reef placement and it is estimated that on the order of 10,000 small reefs occur in this area (Gallaway et al. 2009). Collectively, these reefs equate to a total area of 0.1 square kilometers. This is the largest of the artificial reef areas. The area of artificial reef habitat in the western GOM is small compared to the area of natural reefs.  However, artificial reef habitats (especially oil and gas platforms) located in near-shore and mid-shelf zones appear to be used by age-2 red snapper much more than their proportional area would suggest.
Age-2 Population Size at Platforms -1992
Stanley (1994) showed that an average of 5,304 (95% CI = 2,756) red snapper occupied each major platform during the winter 1992.  Gallaway and Cole (1997) used the Stanley (1994) estimate along with platform distribution, size and count data along with red snapper age composition data to estimate 3 million (95% CI = 1.7 to 4.2 million) age-2 red snapper were present around oil platforms throughout the entire GOM at the beginning of 1992.
Goodyear�s (1995) red snapper stock assessment estimated the total age-2 red snapper population in the GOM at the beginning of 1992 was 3.7 million fish. Collectively, these data suggest 70-80% of the total age-2 red snapper population were living around offshore platforms in 1992 (Gallaway and Cole 1997, Gallaway et al. 2009).
Age-2 Population Size at Platforms -1995
Gitshchlag et al. (2003) provided data from explosive platform removal studies in 1995 that suggested, on average that 775 (95% CI =482-1,062) red snapper were present at each offshore platform, large and small combined. These data when multiplied times the number of platforms present in the GOM in 1995 (4,000) times the fraction of fish that were age-2 suggested that 1.1 million age-2 red snapper were present at offshore platforms in 1995. The SEDAR7 (2005) red snapper stock assessment suggested that the total age-2 red snapper population in the western GOM in 1995 was 1.6 million fish. These data suggest that approximately 70% of all age-2 red snapper were living around offshore platforms in 1995 (Gallaway et al. 2009).
Thus, results from at least two independent studies (Stanley 1994, Gitschlag et al. 2003) suggest that a high proportion of the age-2 red snapper population in the western GOM reside at offshore oil and gas platforms (Gallaway et al. 2009).
The main finding summarized by Gallaway et al. (2009) was that submerged oyster shell present in the northern GOM acts as essential habitat protecting age-0 and age-1 red snapper from predation. Without this benthic habitat, most of these �recruits� would not survive.  Likewise, artificial reefs created off Alabama, and oil and gas platforms created off Mississippi, Louisiana and Texas provide high-relief benthic habitat that enhances the survival of age-2 red snapper. Prior to the creation of artificial reefs and oil and gas platforms, they suggested there was a high mortality on age-2 fish due to predation.  The general absence of high-relief natural reefs inshore and on the mid-continental shelf tended to limit the survival of these early life-stages of red snapper.
Shipp (1999) and Shipp and Bortone (2009) have proposed that the creation of artificial reefs and oil and gas platforms have tended to enhance the production of red snapper. It was the transformation of the substratum from a predominantly sandy mud habitat to one having increased areas of hard bottom with high-relief that relieved the �bottleneck� that had previously prevented red snapper from increasing in abundance.  Artificial reefs may attract fish but, in addition they also provide increased habitat that relieves a �bottleneck� in the life history that previously restricted population abundance.  Shipp and Bortone (2009) called this concept the habitat limitation hypothesis.
Some studies have indicated attraction because red snapper were mostly feeding on prey from pelagic environments and open sand-mud habitats (McCawley et al. 2006, Wells et al. 2008b), while others have indicated significant feeding on reef species and artificial reefs were enhancing prey resources (Ouzts and Szedlmayer 2003; Szedlmayer and Lee 2004; Redman and Szedlmayer 2009).

Further evidence of the habitat limitation hypothesis rather than purely attraction was provided by Stedlemayer and Shipp (1994). They demonstrated a marked increase in abundance of early-juvenile (age-0) red snapper within the Alabama artificial reef area following large-scale artificial reef placement. Thus, the increased population of this area was likely attributable to a habitat-related recruitment increase and not a result of migration from other areas.
Stedlmayer (2007) concluded that based on fisheries-independent studies on artificial reefs off Alabama that his group had conducted over the previous decade (Szedlmayer 2000, Szedlemayer and Furman 2000, Stedlmayer et al. 2004) that red snapper populations may be in better condition compared to past assessments.  Using SCUBA surveys on shell/block artificial reef habitats, mean total mortality (Z) was estimated as Z=2.3 for age-0 to age-1 red snapper, similar to previous estimates of Z=1.98 (Nichols et al. 2005) and Z=2.12 (Nance 1998) derived from SEAMAP shrimp trawl data.  Natural mortality (M) was estimated by Stedlmayer (2007) based on the difference between total mortality (Z) and fishing mortality (F), with the present estimate M=1.9 for age-0, M=0.6 for age-1, and M=0.35 for ages 2 to 54.  Combining ages, growth rates, mortalities, and length-weight relation, the estimated transitional spawning potential ratio (SPR) was estimated = 0.21 at F=0.19, and maximum yield was attained when F was increased to 0.3. The main difference is that the Stedlmayer (2007) stock assessment used age-specific estimates for M obtained from benthic habitat surveys rather than stock assessment models not tied to habitat-related information.
Shipp and Bortone (2009) concluded that if the habitat limitation hypothesis is correct, it will be necessary to maintain or even increase the amount of artificial reef habitat to keep pace with fishing pressure. Programs such as �rigs to reefs� efforts off Louisiana and Texas would have to be continued, as would reef construction off Alabama.
All previous GOM stock assessments have concluded that red snapper in the GOM are overfished and undergoing overfishing. However, recent published studies (Stedlmayer 2007, Gazey et al. 2008, Gallaway et al. 2009, Shipp and Bortone 2009) have shown that red snapper are density-dependent and that age 0 and age 1 fish have a much higher natural mortality rate than was used in previous stock assessments. By using a density-dependent model and a higher natural mortality for age 0 and age 1 fish, it appears  that red snapper stock are neither overfished nor undergoing overfishing (Griffin and Woodward 2010). Also, because the natural mortality for age 0 and age 1 fish are much higher than originally assumed, shrimp trawls have less effect on red snapper reaching age 2+ than previously thought. Future stock assessments need to consider density-dependent models and higher natural mortality rates for age 0 and age 1 red snapper.
Cowan et al. (2011a) disagreed with the habitat limitation hypothesis proposed by Shipp and Borton (2009) and with what they called �faith-based fisheries management� of red snapper.  While there were a number of concerns outlined in the paper, Cowen et al. (2011a) took exception to the idea that available habitat for age-1+ fish and older red snapper can limit population size.  They claimed that the premise that year class success in red snapper is not determined until the fish are between 1.5 and 2 years old (the time that they begin to inhabit reefs as sub-adults) was inconsistent with a periodic (bet-hedging) life history strategy.
Some believe that the availability of interstices (i.e., small hiding spots) for newly settled post-larvae and juveniles can be limiting; those individuals not finding refuge suffer high predation rates (Cowan et al. 2011a).  In this case, mortality is thought to be density-dependent (Forrester 1990; Holbrook et el. 2000; Forester and Steele 2000, 2004). But, Cowan et al. (2011a) asserted that age-0 red snapper rarely recruit directly to high-relief natural or artificial reefs; that they settle on sand/mud substrates and transition to more structured habitat with size and age. It is this transition that makes them susceptible to shrimp trawling.
Others believe that the supply of ref fish larvae is limiting, with good year classes being determined by density independent factors that occur while larvae are planktonic prior to settlement on the reefs (citations in Cowan et al. 2011a).
In neither of the above scenarios is habitat for adults limiting; many studies have shown that adult fish usually do not saturate reefs (citations in Cowan et al. 2011a).  In nature, however, it is unlikely to be a simple dichotomy, as more than one factor can be limiting at different life stages (multiple causalities).
Cowan et al. (2011a) argued that the amount of habitat for adult red snapper, especially artificial habitats that account for <5% (Stanley and Wilson 2003) of total useable habitat as compared to suitable natural habitats, probably does not limit recruitment or population size.  They argued that artificial reefs may increase carrying capacity, but this may be negated because they attract predatory fish and fishermen. They inferred that red snapper life history was inconsistent with the notion that habitat limitation (Gallaway et al. 2009, Shipp and Bortone 2009) is a strong actor in regulating population size in this species.
A number of arguments against the habitat limitation hypothesis and against the concept that artificial reefs enhance production of red snapper were presented by Cowan et al. (2011a). Perhaps all that can be concluded is that many changes have occurred concurrently, making it difficult to differentiate which factors (fishing pressure, shrimp trawling, impact of hurricanes, management measures, artificial reefs) have been most important in allowing red snapper populations to increase in the GOM.  Given that offshore shrimp fishing effort (early 2010) was down by as much as 75-85% (SEDAR15 Update  2009) owing to recent coastal storm damage, economic woes, high fuel prices and cheap imported shrimp, bycatch has been declining for the last several years, especially since 2002, and the directed fishery (that also has been impacted by high fuel prices) has recently been constrained by the 2006 Magnuson-Stevens Reauthorization Act (MSRA) to lower total allowable catches (TACs).  Simply put, the recovery formula long prescribed in the agency assessment has finally been realized, although recent estimates of natural mortality (M) for age-0 and age-1 red snapper may diminish the role that bycatch reduction can play in recovery of the stock. Even so, recent sampling off Louisiana and the Florida panhandle (Dance 2008, SEDAR7 Update, 2009) indicates that the increase in numbers is mostly comprised of 3-7 year old fish, but numbers are indeed increasing. Given that artificial reefs and especially oil and gas platforms have been in place for many years (Shipp and Bortone 2009), it seems counterintuitive to award credit to artificial structures for the beginning stages of a stock recovery that is just now becoming apparent.
Results of both the Gazey et al. (2008) study and the work presented by Brooks (SEDAR7 Update, 2009) indicate there is a strong likelihood that natural mortality (M) for juvenile red snapper in the GOM is density-dependent and perhaps quite a bit higher than was assumed during SEDAR7 (2005).  Density-dependent mortality was not incorporated into the assessment (SEDAR7 Update, 2009) for two principal reasons. First, doing so would be a radical departure from an update versus a benchmark assessment. And secondly, there was no time to explore coding the CATCHEM model to incorporate density-dependent mortality into the assessment.

A review of several published studies, along with the above investigations indicates that natural mortality (M) may have been underestimated in SEDAR7 (2005) for age 0 and 1 red snapper in the GOM (SEDAR7 Update, 2009). The estimates of M from these studies ranged from 0.98 to 3.7 for age 0 and from 0.6 to 1.4 for age 1 red snapper. The lower ranges are the values used in SEDAR 7 (2005). However, none of the studies were able to distinguish natural mortality from emigration; therefore, it is possible that some of the M values reviewed were too high. Accordingly, the continuity run maintained the SEDAR7 values, whereas two alternative models utilized a value twice that of SEDAR7 (2005).

Syc (2011) compared the age of red snapper to known age of artificial reefs off Alabama. The size and age of red snapper were sampled from April through November 2010 and compared with the age of the artificial reefs at the site of capture.  Artificial reefs were deployed in 2006 (N=20, 4 year old reefs), 2009 (N=10, 1 year old reefs) and 2010 (N=10, 0.5 year old reefs). Red snapper were sampled with hook-and-line and a fish trap. After sampling was completed, SCUBA divers estimated the remaining red snapper densities at sample reefs using visual surveys, photographs, and video recordings. Syc found significantly older fish on older reefs.  This finding supports previous telemetry studies that showed long-term residency of red snapper on artificial reefs (Topping and Stedlmayer 2011). This relation between reef age and fish age supports previous studies that indicated red snapper production from artificial reefs (Szedlmayer and Shipp 1994; Szedlmayer 2007; Gallaway et al. 2009).  The increased production is likely due to an increase in available reef habitat, which was previously found to be a controlling factor affecting the density and growth of red snapper (Szedlmayer and Shipp 1994; Szedlmayer and Conti 1999; Gazey et al 2008).

Red snapper are recruited to the newly deployed reefs rapidly as juveniles (approximately age-1) and then reside on these reefs for several years (Syc 2011).  If these reefs were only attracting red snapper, there would be no correlation between fish age and reef age, since red snapper would simply be migrating to and from reefs.  In the present case (Syc 2011), the age distribution would have been random, with no clear dominate age classes. However, dominate age classes for each reef year were found and correlated with reef age, providing evidence that artificial reefs were producing rather than simply attracting red snapper.  If artificial reefs are enhancing the population and experiencing no fishing pressure, Powers et al. (2003) estimated that these reefs could increase production by 6.45 kg wet weight per 10 square meters in the first year.  Since the reefs used by Syc (2011) were not known to fishermen, fishing mortality was limited and following the rational of Powers et al. (2003), had the potential to increase production.

Several studies have suggested that red snapper populations are overfished and that habitat   limitation is not a controlling factor (Schrippa and Legault 1999, Patterson et al. 2001a, Cowan et al. 2011a). Clearly, there is significant fishing mortality of red snapper in the northern GOM (Gillig et al. 2000).  However, if fishing mortality was the limiting factor for red snapper and habitat was not important, we would not expect differences in fish age resulting from reef age (i.e. all reefs whether fished or not would show similar age distributions).  Red snapper enter the fishery around age-2, (recreational size minimum = 406 mm, commercial = 330 mm), with the catch predominately consisting of 2 to 4 year old fish.  If fishing mortality was effectively
limiting red snapper, these ages would be harvested and drastically decreased when analyzing
the age distribution. However, these ages represented 59 % (N=602) of the total catch,
indicating that fishing mortality was not controlling the red snapper population (Syc 2011).

One substantial difference between the study by Syc (2011) that suggests habitat limitations, and previous studies which suggested fishing mortality limitations was Syc�s use of fishery independent data. The previous studies mainly used fisher y dependent data for red snapper caught by recreational and commercial fishers (Szedlmayer and Shipp 1994, Baker and Wilson 2001, Patterson et al. 2001b, Wilson et al. 2001). This difference may account for differing results.  Syc (2011) suggested that fishing mortality probably had little influence on age distributions from artificial reefs sampled. In addition, it was possible to sample smaller red snapper that fishery dependent sampling programs cannot access due to size limitations on the fishery. The significant differences between red snapper abundances on the three reef years provide support for increased red snapper production from artificial reefs.

While a considerable amount of information is available concerning benthic habitats in the southeastern Atlantic, there is almost nothing published concerning how red snapper use various benthic habitats in the region (SAFMC Fisheries Ecosystem Plan 2008).
