sections.heading: Depth Distribution
sections.content:
Egg/Parturition- Collins et al. (2001) captured sexually mature female red snapper in spawning condition (hydrated oocytes) during 1999 off Alabama and the west coast of Florida at depths ranging from 23.8 -122.0 m.
Sedberry et al. (2006) captured adult female red snapper in spawning condition in the southeastern Atlantic over a depth range of 24-67 m in MARMAP trawls from South Carolina to Melbourne off eastern Florida. A spawning aggregation of red snapper was observed at Scamp Ridge off South Carolina at a depth of 53 m (Schobernd and Sedberry 2009).  Presumably, eggs occur within the epipelagic (euphotic) zone extending from 0-200 m (Lyczkowski-Shultz and Hanisko 2007).
Larva-The consistent presence of larval red snapper collected in SEAMAP plankton samples during summer and fall surveys between the 100 m and 200 m contour in both the western and eastern GOM supports the contention of Collins et al. (2001) that red snapper spawn over a wide depth range, i.e., from the mid-shelf to the continental slope (Lyczkowski-Shultz and Hanisko 2007).  Hence, larval red snapper occur in the epipelagic zone extending down to 200 m.
Young of Year - Diamond et al. (2010) analyzed NMFS SEAMAP trawl survey data collected during summer and fall surveys in the GOM from 1987 to 2007.  The primary composite hot spots of age 0 red snapper captured during summer surveys started east of the Texas-Louisiana border and extended west toward the Mexican border, ranging from about the 20 m depth contour (isobath) to the 50 m depth contour (Diamond et al. (2010).
Juvenile- Juvenile (age-1) red snapper were mostly captured during summer SEAMAP trawl surveys in the GOM (Diamond et al. 2010).  Annual zones of higher abundance of age-1 red snapper (red and yellow zones) extended from the upper Texas coast (east of Galveston) to western Louisiana ranging from about the 10 m depth contour to the 60 m depth contour.
Adult-Red snapper are abundant at depths of about 4-110 m (Carpenter 1965) and have been caught at 7-146 m in the GOM (Moseley 1966, Rivas 1970). Red snapper were the second most abundant lutjanid captured in MARMAP surveys in the southeast Atlantic (Cueller et al. 1996). Although not as abundant as vermillion snapper, red snappers occurred 124 times (322 individuals) from depths ranging from 7-68 m. In the Carolinas, they are usually found at depths of 46 to 91 m over both low and high relief areas (Grimes et al. 1977).  Red snappers captured in MARMAP surveys ranged in length from 2 to 85 cm. The maximum size of red snapper is approximately 91 cm (Robins and Ray 1986).

Wilson and Nieland (2004) noted that the western GOM off Louisiana and Texas currently produced significant portions of the commercial and recreational harvests of red snapper, however, this was not always the case.  Annual commercial landings in the five states bordering the GOM indicate a shift in the fishery from the eastern to the more western GOM since 1970 concomitant with the placement of several thousand oil and gas platforms into the area. Quantitative estimates of red snapper have been derived both from assessments of the effects of platform removal via explosives and from hydroacoustic surveys of selected platforms.  Based both on these estimates and on the number of platforms, they estimated from 1.2 to 7.2 million live around platforms placed at depths of 20-100 m. Many of these are relatively young individuals of ages 2-4 years.

Petroleum platforms differ from traditional artificial reefs in that their vertical profile extends throughout the water column and provides habitat from the photic zone to the substrate (Wilson and Nieland 2004, Wilson et al. 2006). Historically, a major obstacle in deriving scientific data about the effect of deep water artificial reefs (and platforms) on fishes and other nekton was the difficulty  in quantifying abundance and species composition associated with these reef communities. Wilson et al. (2006) successfully used two complementary techniques, hydroacoustics and point count visual surveys, to estimate the abundance (biomass) and species composition of fishes at several of these structures (Stanley and Wilson 1995, 1996a, 1996b, 1997, 1998, 2000, 2003) and natural reefs (Wilson et al 2003).  In these studies dual-beam hydroacoustics provided estimates of acoustic biomass, density, size distribution, and the near field area of influence. A remotely operated underwater vehicle was used to determine species composition. They found from 10,000 to 30,000 fishes associated with individual platforms; the lowest numbers were found at the largest and deepest structures, leading them to question the value of deep water structures as artificial reefs. They reported that the density of fishes around platforms was ten times greater than open water and from two to three times greater than fish density associated with the upper portion of the West Flower Garden Bank off eastern Texas; species composition also differed between these two habitat types (Wilson et al 2003).

It is of interest that some oil and gas platforms in the eastern, central, and western portions of the GOM had substantial populations of red snapper, while others did not have any red snapper (Wilson et al. 2006).  The depths where reef fish species were observed at the platforms varied depending on the depths where the platforms were situated.  The composition of the platform fish community has been shown to change with location and water depth. Previous researchers have noted a zonation of the assemblage of fishes associated with platforms and have divided the shelf waters of the northern GOM into three zones: coastal (water depth < 27 m), offshore (water depth 27 to 64 m) and bluewater (water depth > 64 m) (Gallaway 1980; Gallaway et al.1981; Gallaway and Lewbel 1982). This was more recently confirmed by Stanley and Wilson (2000), who reported that, at a platform in 219 m of water, pelagic bluewater fishes were found principally in the upper 100 m of the water column and fish density was essentially zero below 100 m depth. At a platform situated at a water depth of 60m, they found fishes throughout the water column, but fish density was highest near the surface and adjacent to the bottom; the fish community was characterized as reef associated shelf species. At a nearshore platform at 20 m depth, fishes were found throughout the water column and the population was characterized as estuarine.

Platforms situated closer to shore at depths <27m, generally had red snapper (Wilson et al. 2006). Platforms at intermediate depth range (27-64 m) were observed to have higher densities of red snapper, while those situated in deeper water (>64 m) tended not to have red snapper associated with them (with one exception).  Generally, speaking red snapper tended to be found near the bottom depth ranges of the platforms. Smaller red snapper were stacked higher-up with larger snapper tending to aggregate around the platforms in deeper water (Render 1995, Wilson et al. 2006).

Red snapper are an important species for both commercial and recreational interests in the northern GOM and as such warrant some special discussion (Wilson et al. 2006).  Of all the habitats included in this study, red snapper were proportionally most dominant at the deeper low-relief feature in comparison to the more shallow high relief feature at Sonnier Bank. This finding is similar to that reported by Wilson et al. (2003) for toppled and partially removed artificial reef structures. Red snappers were proportionally abundant at several platforms in all three regions of the study area; most of these platforms were at the shallowest depths included in the survey design. Few red snappers were observed at those platforms in deeper water at the edge of the Outer Continental Shelf (OCS). The movements of red snapper over their potential 50 year lifespan can help to explain some of the observed distribution. After spending the best part of their first two years in shallow, inshore waters, red snapper begin an offshore migration in search of more suitable, deepwater habitats that might include reefs, lumps, depressions, and wrecks (Nieland and Wilson 2003). In the northern GOM, these suitable habitats include the many oil and gas platforms that have been sited at moderate depths in the nearshore waters. After a residence at the platforms of perhaps 5-8 years, the red snapper migrate away from the platforms and spend the rest of their lives in a relatively solitary existence at natural or anthropogenic, non-platform structures in deeper waters toward the edge of the OCS (Gitschlag et al. 2003, Nieland and Wilson 2003, Gallaway et al. 2009).

Allman and Fitzhugh (2007) also provided length at age data to support the contention that older red snapper are found in deeper water associated with commercial longline catches. Their observations about age differences among gears are consistent with other studies that show red snapper undergo a general ontogenetic shift in habitat and depth.  Nieland and Wilson (2000) reported that age-1 and younger fish dominated benthic habitats sampled by survey trawls, whereas age-2 and age-3 fish dominated the samples obtained by explosive removal of an oil platform. Nieland and Wilson (2000)  further indicated that commercial hook and line collections of red snapper in Louisiana waters revealed few age-2 fish, and in a follow-up paper they speculated that fish older than about age-6 become rare in the hook and line catches due to mortality and emigration from the platforms (Wilson and Nieland 2001).  Mitchell et al. (2004) also suggested older red snapper are less reef-obligate, based on research longline catches.

A comparison of the age, length, and species composition of the NMFS longline survey was conducted to explore the potential of a deepwater (>150 m) reservoir of large, older red snapper in the GOM (Walter and Ingram 2009).   There is concern that there may be a large biomass that is relatively less vulnerable to the fishery and �not seen� by the assessment model because these fish are not taken by the fishery. The age composition of red snapper and depths fished by the NMFS longline survey were compared with age composition and depths of the commercial fisheries from logbook reported depths. There was little evidence from the NMFS survey of a large biomass in GOM waters beyond 150 meters. A peak distribution of red snapper catches occurred between 50-100 m. The percent of positive sets where red snapper were caught were 0% (0-25 m), 5.61% (25-50 m), 24.78% (50-100 m), 8.57% (100-150 m), and 0% (150-450 m).  However, the age composition of the survey differed from that of the various fisheries, even though the fisheries span the depths where the NMFS longline survey encounters older fish. There were more older fish caught by NMFS longline surveys and by commercial longline vessels in the western GOM in comparison to the eastern GOM. It appears that older red snapper may be only partially selected for by the fisheries, particularly the handline fishery and to a lesser extent by the longline fishery. While the commercial longline fishery in the GOM does capture older fish, it is in a lower proportion in comparison to the NMFS longline survey, indicating that some biomass may be less selected for by these fisheries. Some caution should be taken in these conclusions as the age composition for the commercial fisheries only represents landed fish and not discards, which could be high if fishers do not possess red snapper quota. The results suggest that there could be additional older biomass relatively less vulnerable to the fisheries but that this reduction in vulnerability is likely a spatial rather than a depth-related process and it likely occurs in waters shallower than 150 m. This lends support to the dome-shaped selectivities estimated by the CATCHEM model for the commercial handline and eastern longline fisheries (SEDAR7 Update 2009).

Scott-Denton et al. (2011) used observer data to describe the commercial bottom longline and commercial vertical-line fisheries in the GOM. From July 2006 through December 2009, data were collected from 9,468 sets collected during 308 trips aboard 2005 reef fish vessels. Of 30,125 red snapper observed being caught, 2456 were taken on longlines and 27,669 were caught on vertical lines. Approximately 77% of the red snapper taken on vertical lines were caught in the western GOM, with the remaining taken in the eastern GOM. Hotspot analyses of the vertical line fishery for red snapper using GIS indicated that the highest CPUEs occurred from the Florida Panhandle to the Mississippi Delta, off the Louisiana-Texas border area, and off Corpus Christi. Low CPUEs occurred on the West Florida Shelf. The majority (65%) were kept. Based on visual observations, 24% were released alive, 10% were discarded dead, and 1% discarded in an unknown condition. Depths of red snapper capture ranged from 6.0 to 558 m. Most (29%) of red snapper were caught in waters <37 m, followed by 37-46 m (26%), 47-56 m (13%), 57-64 m (13%). The remaining depth zones comprised 19%.  The immediate minimum assumed mortality of red snapper was 27% in the longline fishery and 28% in the vertical line fishery.

Recently, red snapper fishermen have claimed that a cryptic portion of the red snapper population in the South Atlantic is not being fully exploited or largely missed by the fishery (Southeast Fisheries Science Center 2010).  The fishermen have suggested that the biggest and oldest red snapper exist in the deepest depths and are not accessible by hook and line gear. They note that currents in the deeper depths prevent effective fishing with vertical hook and line gear and that the distance vessels must travel offshore to get to the deeper depths can be cost prohibitive.

In the southeast Atlantic, Hester and Nelson (2010) analyzed landings data obtained from Dr. Jennifer Potts (leader of the Life History Working Group for the SEDAR 24  red snapper stock assessment) collected from recreational Charter boats (CB), Head Boat (HB), Private Recreational (PR) boats, and commercial boats (CM) from North Carolina to Florida. There were 759 data records with depth recorded by minimum and maximum depths fished, along with the sex, fork length (FL) in mm, total length (TL) in mm, and the calendar age of each fish.  Where a depth fished was not provided by fishing location (most of data for each fisheries), a depth was computed by averaging the minimum and maximum depths fished provided per trip. While there was a lot of scatter in the data, a positive regression was derived indicating that the total length increased with increasing depth.  Plots of mean age and median age by depth for all sectors demonstrated that older fish (up to about age 9) tended to occur in deeper water. Similarly, longer fish tended to occur in deeper water.

The median depth fished in the southeast Atlantic by HB was 89 ft (27 m), CB 127.5 ft (39 m), and CM 135 ft (41 m) (Hester and Nelson 2010).  The median size of red snapper in the catch for each fishery was found to be 561.5 mm TL for HB, 558.0 mm TL for CB, and 607.0 mm TL for CM.  Fishing effort frequency distributions also indicated the approximate depth ranges fished. For HB the range was 1-175 ft (1-53 m), CB 1-280 ft (1-85 m), CM 1-336 ft (1-102 m). While CM tended to fish in somewhat deeper water than the recreational boats combined and catch slightly longer red snapper, the mean differences were not large. The analyses supported assertions by the commercial fishermen that they fish closer to shore, than what had been assumed during the SEDAR15 (2009) stock assessment. There were not many older fish being caught and landed by these fisheries.

The Date Workshop (DW) report produced by the Life History Working Group (SEDAR24 DW Report 2010) presented two graphs (Figure 2.9.1a and 2.9.1b) that depicted the depth distribution of U.S. South Atlantic red snapper for fishing fleets combined. Figure 2.9.1a depicted the size (TL mm) versus depth. There is no increasing relationship of length with depth apparent from the graph. The second graph (Figure 2.9.1b) depicted the age of red snapper versus depth.  Approximately 30 fish ranging in age from age-30 to age-50 are included in the graph.  Most of these older fish were found at depths ranging from 150 to 300 ft (50-100m). The proportion of older fish in the plot declined at depths ranging from 300 to 400 feet (100-133 m).

Landings for red snapper using longline gear in the southeastern Atlantic have never been large (Southeast Fisheries Science Center 2010). The SAFMC prohibited the use of longline gear inside 91 m (300 ft) in 1992. In 1999, the council also prohibited vessels with longline gear aboard to possess red snapper (Snapper Grouper Amendment 9). Hence, there presently is no longline fishery directed at red snapper in the southeastern Atlantic, which could catch older red snapper in deeper water.

Logbook data from commercial vessels and recreational headboats were analyzed by NOAA/NMFS staff (Southeast Fisheries Science Center 2010).  Also limited depth data were collected for some headboat trips by observers. They noted that ideally one would have detailed depth of capture information for red snapper caught in all fishery sectors. Unfortunately, this was not the case. Plots were created that examined snapper fishing effort by depth and the relative proportion selected by age groups up to age 20. However, it was not stated at what depths the older fish were captured.

Accounts by fishermen have suggested that red snapper exhibit a seasonal migration from offshore to inshore to form spawning aggregations (Southeast Fisheries Science Center 2010). These aggregations have been termed �snapper bonanzas,� owing to the large daily catches produced during these events. Like other snapper-grouper species that form spawning aggregations, they are likely more vulnerable during this time. If the largest (and oldest) red snapper are moving inshore to form spawning aggregations and their vulnerability is increased during that time period, then the results suggesting a constantly increasing selectivity, peaking at the oldest ages, may be more accurate. The general conclusion drawn from the analysis was that dome-shaped selectivity likely was not appropriate for the commercial handline sector and might not be appropriate for the recreational sectors (Southeast Fisheries Science Center 2010). These conclusions were largely driven by the age at depth data, which suggested no significant trend in age 5+ fish with depth.

A peer review of the red snapper research and management in the GOM recommended the need to monitor the number and length frequencies of red snapper discards (MRAG Americas, Inc. 1997).  Onboard observers were suggested as the best way to estimate discard mortality rates. This led to research and monitoring programs on both recreational and commercial fishing vessels (MRAG Americas Inc.  1999).  Several studies have focused on depth as an important factor in determining discard mortality of red snapper due to the visible impact of barotraumas (Collier 2010).  Studies conducted in shallow water (<35m or <115 feet) estimated discard mortality rates of 20% or less (Parker 1985, Render and Wilson 1994, Patterson et al. 2002, Burns et al. 2006). Studies conducted in deeper waters generally estimated higher discard mortality rates ranging from 17% to 93% (Gitschlag and Renaud 1994, Render and Wilson 1994, Dorf 2003, Burns et al. 2004, Nieland et al. 2007, Burns 2009, Diamond and Campbell 2009, Stephen and Harris 2009). The increase in discard mortality with increasing depth is an expected result and has been described for red snapper and other snapper grouper species (Patterson et al. 2001, Burns et al. 2002, Patterson et al. 2002, Rudershausen et al. 2007, Stephen and Harris 2009).

To estimate discard mortality rates, a �sink or swim� approach was suggested in which onboard observers would note the short-term fate of discarded red snapper: whether or not the fish swam down out of site (Dorf 2003, Stephen and Harris 2009).  Another suggested method to determine mortality rate involved releasing red snapper in cages, then lowering them to depth.  This method was used by Gitschlag and Renaud (1994) and by Render and Wilson (1994).

Dorf  (2003) put observers on recreational headboats off Texas and collected data during 54 trips fishing at a mean depth of 40.2 m (range 13.4-95.4 m). Red snapper less than the 1999 federal minimum size in the GOM of 450 mm (18-in) TL made up 93.4% of the 3,863 snapper collected.  Those less than the Texas state minimum size of 375 mm (15-in) made up 64.0% of the catch. When brought on board, 70.2% of snapper appeared normal and 26.1% had protruding stomachs. Of the discarded red snapper, 60.6% were released alive and swam down, 22.8% swam erratically, 15.2% floated, and 1.4% were discarded dead.  Galveston had the highest discard: landing ration (211:1) and smallest mean fish sixe (0.7 kg, 343 mm). Port Aransas had the lowest discard: landing ratio (5.2:1) and the largest mean fish size (0.9 kg, 387 mm).

Venting fish to reduce the effects of barotraumas and reduce discard mortality of red snapper has been researched.  Red snapper caught in shallow water experience little benefit from venting (Render and Wilson 1994, Render and Wilson 1996, Burns et al. 2002, Burns et al. 2008). In fact, venting fish may cause increased mortality for a variety of species (Wilde 2009, 2011). However, vented red snapper caught in waters deeper than 42 m increased survival compared to non-vented red snapper (Burns et al. 2008).  Smaller red snapper, which survive barotraumas better than larger fish, are normally found in shallower water while larger fish are typically found in deeper water (Burns et al. 2008).

Hook type has been discussed as a potential mechanism to reduce discard mortality.  However, Burns et al. (2008) found that there was not a significant decrease in discard mortality for red snapper caught on circle hooks compared to J hooks.  SEDAR7 (2005) stated red snapper discard mortality decreased by 50% for fish caught with circle hooks compared to those caught with J hooks.  A decrease in mortality of red snapper with circle hooks was also noted by Koenig (Burns et al. 2002) and by Rummer (2007).

Nieland et al. (2007a) sampled red snapper from commercial landings from the GOM off Louisiana from October 2001 to May 2004.  Red snapper ages (N=2,867) estimated from counts of annuli on otoliths ranged from 1 to 14 years; however, the vast majority (97.7%) of these were ages 2 to 6 years and the modal age was 3 years. Total lengths of all specimens were less than 600 mm TL. They also investigated the fate of red snapper regulatory discards (individuals <382 mm [15 inch] TL) during 16 trips on working commercial vessels; over two-thirds of 4,839 red snapper assigned among four discard fate categories (ranging from alive and vigorous to dead) were returned to the water either in moribund or dead condition.  Mortality among regulatory discards was very high and related to depth of capture. Among the discards, 778 (16%) swam down vigorously, 714 (15%) swam down slowly or erratically, 1,765 (36%) were alive but could not swim down, and 1,582 (33%) were dead.  There was a significant positive relationship between the percent mortality (proportion of discards in categories 3 and 4) and capture depth (across depth range 10-90 m) for all fishing opportunities where five of more discards were assessed.

Among 399 potential discards retained for age and length analyses, 86% were between 12 and 15 inches (305-381 mm) TL and 85% were 2 years of age (Nieland et al. 2007a). They concluded that the minimum size regulation appears to do little to protect juvenile red snapper from commercial fishing mortality. Heavy red snapper mortality, which begins as bycatch mortality in shrimp trawls, continues as discard mortality at sub-legal lengths when they first recruit to the offshore fishing grounds, and persists as harvest mortality among the youngest legal year- and size-classes. If the minimum size limit is intended to provide a respite from such mortality, a reconsideration of the utility of the minimum length regulation of the commercial harvest of red snapper (in the GOM) may be warranted.

In addition to the direct mortality monitored, �sink or swim� indicators suggest that red snapper experience a delayed mortality associated with injuries and stress obtained from capture (Diamond and Campbell 2009).  The ability of a fish to submerge after discarding is often used as a proxy for survival, but this practice underestimates total discard mortality because delayed mortality is overlooked.  Fishery managers need a way to link �sink or swim� indicators, or variables observed during capture and release, with delayed mortality rates.  Diamond and Campbell (2009) conducted a cage study of red snapper off the coast of Texas to estimate delayed mortality rates and to find factors that could link immediate and delayed mortality, between surface and bottom waters.  Immediate mortality (17%) was predicted by the interaction of depth and the differences in temperature between surface and bottom waters. Lactate levels were also significant predictors of immediate mortality in fish whose blood was tested. Delayed mortality (64%) was predicted primarily by a condition index consisting of the presence or absence or injuries, symptoms of barotraumas, and fish behaviors immediately after capture. Specific categories included bleeding, protruding intestines, everted stomach, exopthalmia, the presence or absence of flapping or gilling behaviors, and problems with cage submergence.  The majority of fatalities occurred within 24 h after fish were placed in the cages. Their mortality estimates indicated that red snapper discard mortality was significantly underestimated in the 2005 stock assessment for red snapper (SEDAR7 2005).  Diamond and Campbell (2009) concluded that the use of indices that relate the condition of an individual fish at capture to its probability of delayed mortality is an excellent method for linking immediate and delayed mortality and will likely be applicable to many species that are subject to catch-and-release fishing.

The key to a successful catch and release (CAR) program is that fish actually survive the CAR experience (Rummer 2007).  Management strategies are typically designed assuming CAR is below 20%.  Recent field studies suggest this may be possible for red snapper retrieved from depths ranging from 20-40 m (Patterson et al. 2001b, Burns et al. 2004) but rates may be greater than 70% if red snapper are retrieved from deeper depths (Burns et al. 2002). Logbook records from commercial vessels suggest rates may range upwards of 72-78% (Poffenberger and McCarthy 2004).  CAR mortality depends on a multitude of factors. However, the main underlying cause of CAR mortality is directly related to depth of capture.

The most effective way to manage a fishery that succumbs so seriously to CAR mortality is not via size limits, seasonal closures, and bag limits (Rummer and Bennett 2005, Rummer 2007). All combinations seem problematic; either the socioeconomics of the red snapper fishery or the potential for population growth and recovery are negatively impacted.  Rummer (2007) proposed that it would seem logical to impose fishery restrictions to discrete areas such that fish populations can be safeguarded from all fishing and CAR activity, therefore protecting age, size, sex classes and ratios simultaneously.  For fish like red snapper, where overfishing is widespread and CAR mortality is high, marine protected areas (MPAs) and/or no take reserves (NTRs) were proposed as having the greatest potential for overall conservation and sustainability of red snapper fisheries.

Estimated Discards SEDAR24
Observers working for the Gulf and South Atlantic Fisheries Foundation (GSAFFI) gathered data on the amount of discarding and discard mortality on snapper-grouper species caught on commercial hook-and-line (HH) vessels in the southeast Atlantic (GSAFFI 2008, 2010).  The data were collected on HH vessels fishing in Latitude zones 30 to 33 stretching from northern Florida to southern North Carolina.  A relatively high proportion of the red snapper catch taken in 2007 was below the 50 cm minimum size.  In terms of numbers, 97.7% of the catch of red snapper taken in 2007 was considered to be discarded bycatch (GSAFFI 2008).   Detailed information concerning CPUEs for red snapper kept and discarded was presented by statistical zones for Latitudes 30-33 for 2008 and for 2009 (GSAFFI 2010).  During 2008, the percentages discarded ranged from 57.7-77.9% during the first trimester, 58.4-73.3% in the second trimester, and 21.0-42.0% in the third trimester.  During, 2009, there was a decrease in the proportion of red snapper discarded which appears to be related to a decline in abundance of red snapper below the 50 cm minimum size limit. The proportion discarded across zones 30-33 ranged from 15.5-27.5% during the first trimester, 15.9-28.5% during the second trimester, and 3.8-10.2% during the third trimester.  Overall, the percent discarded during 2008 and 2009 averaged 34.8% (GSAFFI 2010). These data were provided to NMFS for use with the SEDAR24 stock assessment.

The GSAFFI reports demonstrate that discarding rates of red snapper can be very high when there are high numbers of undersized red snapper due to periodic recruitment.  The length frequency for red snapper during 2007 demonstrates high recruitment of undersized fish ranging from 30-50 cm TL (GSAFFI 2008).  Tabulated mean catch rates (CPUEs) for both kept and discarded red snapper indicate that most of this recruitment occurred off northeast Florida and off Georgia with lower mean CPUEs off South Carolina and North Carolina (GSAFFI 2010).  A decrease in mean CPUEs of discarded fish occurred, while mean CPUEs of kept fish increased by the third quarter of 2008. This trend continued into 2009 with mean CPUEs of kept fish increasing, while mean CPUES of discarded fish decreased.  The simplest explanation for this is that growth of the recruits during 2008 allowed more fish to be kept and fewer fish to be discarded as they increased in size to exceed the minimum size limit of 50 cm (20 inches) TL. This pattern is also apparent with length frequencies for red snapper measured from 2007 to 2009 by at-sea observers on headboats off Florida and to a lesser extent off Georgia (Sauls and Wilson 2010).

sections.heading: Discard Moralities South Atlantic
sections.content:
The estimates of discard mortality used in SEDAR15 (2007) were 90% for the commercial fishery and 40% for the recreational fishery in the southeast Atlantic (SEDAR24 DW Report 2010).  The recreational estimate (40%) matched the discard mortality estimate for red snapper from the GOM for fish caught in waters deeper than 20 m (SEDAR7 2005).  A working paper was developed for SEDAR24 which includes a comprehensive discussion of discard mortality (Collier 2010).  To account for an increasing discard mortality rate with depth, three models were investigated to describe these depth effects.  Two of the models (Burns et al. 2002, Diamond et al. unpublished) used a logistic regression function to model the mortality rate and one used a linear trend (Nieland et al. 2007a). The plenary decided to use the depth model presented in Burns et al. (2002) to estimate discard mortality (SEDAR24 DW Report 2010).  The discard mortality estimate for the commercial fishery was 48%. The mortality rate chosen for both the recreational headboat fishery and the recreational charterboat fishery was 41.3%.  The private boat mortality rate estimate used in SEDAR24 was 38.8%.

The plenary decided to develop discard mortality estimates based on the relationship of discard mortality with depth (Burns et al. 2002). This method, used observer data having depth information for released fish (GSAFFI 2008, 2010). These observer data were collected during 2007-2009 between latitudes 30 and 33. Estimates of mortality were obtained by calculating a weighted average mortality from the Burns et al. (2002) equation, weighted by the depth profile. The profiles were computed in 25 ft intervals while the mortality estimates from Burns et al. (2002) were computed at the mid-points of these intervals. These estimates were relatively insensitive to interval width since approximately the same result (same whole percent) was obtained with 1 ft intervals from the observer data. To represent discard mortality of red snapper discarded from 1992-2009, the WG recommended the commercial mortality estimate based on discarded fish (48%).

In August 2001, the Southeast Fisheries Science Center (SEFSC) initiated a program to collect discard data from commercial fishing vessels landing federally managed species in the GOM and US South Atlantic (McCarthy 2010). A reporting form was developed as a supplement to the mandatory coastal logbook forms. Discard data from the SEFSC coastal fisheries logbook program were used to calculate the number of red snapper that were discarded in the U.S. South Atlantic during the period January 1, 2001 through December 31, 2009.  Fishing gear strata included handline, electric reel (bandit rig) trolling, longline, trap, gillnet and diving. Selected fishers were required to complete a supplemental discard form for every trip they made. To calculate species specific discard rates, discard data were matched to the effort data reported to the coastal logbook program.

A delta lognormal model was used to calculate the yearly least square means of the red snapper discard rate (McCarthy 2010).  This method combined separate general linear model (GLM) analyses of the proportion of trips that discarded red snapper and the discard rates of trips that discarded red snapper to construct a single standardized discard rate.  Total discards for each year were then calculated using a ratio estimator: yearly least square means (discard rate)*reported yearly total effort.

Discard mortalities (in units of 1000 fish) were modeled with the Baranov catch equation, which required estimates of discard selectivities and release mortality probabilities (SEDAR 24, 2010). Discards were assumed to have fleet-specific mortality probabilities, as suggested by the data workshop (commercial lines, 0.48; for-hire, 0.41; private, 0.39). Annual discard mortalities, as fit by the model, were computed by multiplying total discards (tabulated in the DW report) by the fleet-specific release mortality probability. For for-hire and private fleets, discard time series were assumed to begin in 1983, with the start of the 12-inch size limit; for the commercial lines fleet, discards were modeled starting in 1992 with the 20-inch size limit. Discards from the commercial dive fleet were assumed negligible and not modeled. Using these methods the numbers discarded per year were added to the reported fisheries landings data that were used to compute fishing mortalities.

Actual red snapper discards may be higher than the calculated totals presented by McCarthy (2010). In the limited observer data available discarded red snapper were more common than
retained red snapper (60% to 40% of 644 fish) (SEDAR24 DW 2010). Self-reported discards obtained from logbooks were reported in numbers of fish and lack length information making a similar comparison with landings data difficult. Discards and landings of red snapper from the commercial fishery, however, appear to be relatively low, particularly when compared to the recreational fishery. The total commercial discards from McCarthy (2010) may represent a minimum estimate of the number of red snapper discarded from the commercial fishery. The conclusion of the Commercial Work Group was that the SEDAR 24-DW01 report by McCarthy (2010) represents the best available information on commercial red snapper discards.

sections.heading: Temperature
sections.content:
Egg/Parturition- Collins et al. (2001) captured sexually mature (mature ovaries with hydrated oocytes) female red snapper off Alabama and the west coast of Florida in the GOM at locations with bottom temperatures of 20.6oC and ranging from 26.8-29oC.
A spawning aggregation of red snapper was observed at Scamp Ridge off South Carolina in the southeast Atlantic at a bottom temperature of 20.9oC (Schobernd and Sedberry 2009).
Larva-Lyczkowski-Schultz and Hanisko (2007) tabulated the range of temperatures where red snapper were caught in surface neuston nets in the GOM during the Summer Groundfish (SG) surveys and the Fall Plankton (FP) surveys from 2000 to 2003.  Surface water temperatures ranged from 27.1-31.0oC (mean=29.4oC) for SG, and ranged from 25.4-30.3oC (mean=29.2oC) for FP.
Young of Year-
Juvenile-High value habitat for juvenile red snapper in the western GOM determined from a habitat suitability index (HSI) model was characterized as temperatures ranging from 24-26oC (Gallaway et al. 1999).
Adult-A spawning aggregation of red snapper was observed at Scamp Ridge off South Carolina at a bottom temperature of 20.9oC (Schobernd and Sedberry 2009).

sections.content:
Egg/Parturition-No information found.
Larva- Lyczkowski-Schultz and Hanisko (2007) tabulated the range of dissolved oxygen levels where red snapper larvae were caught in surface neuston nets in the GOM during the Summer Groundfish (SG) surveys and the Fall Plankton (FP) surveys from 2000 to 2003.  Surface water dissolved oxygen levels ranged from 4.7-6.7 mg/L (mean=5.7 mg/L) for SG, and ranged from 5.5-6.6 mg/L (mean=6.1 mg/L) for FP.
Young of Year-
Juvenile- Seasonal habitat suitability index (HSI) models were developed for juvenile red snapper (age-0 and age-1) in the western GOM (Gallaway et al. 1999). Habitat factors considered in the analysis included water temperature, salinity, and dissolved oxygen at the bottom; depth and density of offshore petroleum platforms; and low-relief bottom structures.  High value habitat for juvenile snapper was characterized by depths between 18 and 64 m, water temperatures of 24-26oC, salinities around 35 g/L, and dissolved oxygen levels of at least 5 mg/L.  Density of low-relief structures was not a significant habitat element, and an inverse relationship was found between juvenile red snapper abundance and the density of offshore platforms. Results of the model analysis suggest that the step-like expansion of the hypoxic area (dissolved oxygen <= 2 mg/L) offshore of the mouth of the Mississippi River and west to the Texas border, which first occurred in 1993, reduced the habitat carrying capacity for juvenile red snapper in this region by up to 25%, averaging 19%. Gallaway et al. (1999) suggested that this environmental change may limit the level to which overfished GOM red snapper can be rebuilt to historical levels.

sections.heading: FOOD HABITS
sections.content: Trophic Mode: Juvenile and adult red snapper are carnivorous.

sections.heading: Feeding
sections.content:
Larvae-Newly hatched larvae in the laboratory began actively feeding on a culture of algae and rotifers 3 days after hatching and were 2.5 mm SL 4 days after hatching (Rabalais et al. 1980).   Snapper larvae demand sufficient quantities of small prey organisms at the onset of first-feeding (Lan 2001, Ogle and Lotz 2000, Lemus et al. 2004, Rhodes and Phelps 2008). Copepod nauplii have proved to be an appropriate prey for red snapper larvae being cultured (Ogle et al. 2002, Lemus et al. 2002, Ogle et al. 2005).  Little information exists concerning what larval red snapper feed on in the ocean.
                                                                                                                                                                                                               Young of Year-
Juvenile-Small zooplankters were common prey of juveniles up to 150 mm FL, but the fish probably start to prefer larger prey when they are about 100 mm FL (Bradley and Bryan 1976).  Stomachs of juveniles most frequently contained shrimp throughout the year in the Gulf of Mexico (Camber 1955, Bradley and Bryan 1976). Other crustaceans (including crabs), fish and squid were found in 2-10% of the sampled fish. The types of prey that contributed the greatest percentage by volume to the diet of juveniles were squid, octopuses, and shrimp. Juveniles and adults eat a large variety of species of mollusks, crustaceans, and fishes.
Adult-Camber (1955) reported that adult red snapper in the GOM took the following prey (in decreasing order of frequency of occurrence); shrimp, small reef fish, crabs, and gastropods. He stated that tunicates may be taken in the spring.
Futch and Bruger (1976) stated that red snapper may feed over sand, shell, or mud bottoms next to reefs or other rocky bottoms. Many of the prey of red snapper are found over level bottoms adjacent to the reefs, rather than on the reefs themselves (Oavis 1975).

sections.heading: Food Items
sections.content:
Larva- No information found.
Young of Year-
Juvenile One of the most comprehensive early red snapper diet studies was conducted by Bradley and Bryan (1975). They described the diets by season, of trawl-collected (open sand-mud habitat) and hook-and-line reef �rough bottom areas� red snapper from off the Texas coast.  They described the diets of 258 open-habitat and 190 reef habitat red snapper (25-325 mm FL) and found that juvenile red snapper were dependent on shrimp, crabs, and crustaceans.  They described a change in juvenile red snapper diet as fish size increased.  Young red snapper depended almost exclusively on invertebrates, and showed a gradual increase in vertebrate prey with growth.  However, they did not separate out the proportions of juveniles sampled over reef versus open habitats.
Lee (1998) and Szedlemayer and Lee (2004) examined the diets and habitat shift of juvenile red snapper from open sand-mud habitat (little or no relief) to artificial reef habitat (1 cubic meter concrete or PVC blocks), from June 1993 through December 1994.  In 1994, fish settled over open habitat from June to September, then began shifting to reef habitats. The shift was almost complete by December (visual surveys using SCUBA). Stomachs were examined from 1639 fish ranging from 18-280 mm SL. Of these, 850 had empty stomachs, and 346 from open habitat and 443 from reef habitat contained prey. Small red snapper (<60 mm SL) fed mostly on chaetognaths, copepods, shrimp, and squid. Larger red snapper (60-280 mm SL) shifted feeding to fish prey, greater amounts of squid and crabs, and continued feeding on shrimp.  Red snapper diets separated by habitat types rather than fish size for the size ranges that over-lapped habitats.  These diet shifts were attributed to feeding more on reef prey than on open-water prey. Thus, the shift in habitat shown by juvenile red snapper was reflected in their diet and suggested differential habitat values based not just on predation refuge but on food resources as well.
Wells et al. (2008c) used stable isotopes and stomach content analyses to describe the diet of red snapper in the northern GOM.  Approximately 1000 fish were collected over two years to test the possible effects of ontogeny, habitat, and a non-trawl reef permit area on red snapper diets. Stable isotopes of carbon, nitrogen, and sulfur were measured in both red snapper and potential primary producers. Ontogenetic shifts in diet occurred with increasing red snapper size-at-age, resulting in higher carbon13 and higher nitrogen15 isotope values and lower sulfur34 isotope values in larger fish.  Stomach content results supported ontogenetic shifts in diet by showing a change in diet from zooplankton, mysid shrimp, and squid for juvenile (ages 0 to 1) to diets dominated by benthic crustaceans and fishes for adults (ages 2+).  Habitat-specific differences in isotopes and stomach contents of similarly sized fish were identified; however, feeding differences, both in carbon13 and in prey identified in stomach contents, were detected, but were minimal.  Red snapper from outside a single non-trawl reef permit area had higher nitrogen15 isotope values and lower sulfur34 values than for conspecifics inside the non-trawl reef permit area.  The analyses of stable isotopes demonstrated that red snapper (ages 0 to 2) rely on sand and mud-associated prey regardless of the habitat from which they were collected, suggesting that the importance of shell and natural reef habitats was more important for red snapper survival than for additional prey resources. Juvenile red snapper occupying sand and mud recruit to structured habitats, such as shell-rubble to obtain refuge from predators, while obtaining prey items such as fish, from adjacent sand and mud areas.
Adult- Most red snapper diet studies have found that as individuals grow, there is a shift in their diet from invertebrates and zooplankton to a dependency on fish (Moseley et al. 1966, Bradley and Bryan 1975, Szedlemeyer and Lee 2004). A few studies (e.g., Camber 1955) have reported that large red snapper continue to eat demersal crustaceans. Pelagic zooplankton contributed to the diet of all size classes of red snapper examined by McCawley and Cowan (2007), decreasing only for snapper larger than 500 mm FL. Moseley concluded that it was inefficient for red snapper larger than 110 mm SL to exist on zooplankton. However, Siegel (1983) found that adult red snapper up to 550 mm SL off Alabama continued to consume significant amounts of pelagic zooplankton, especially larval decapods and stomatopods.
Gallaway et al. (1981, 2009) reported the gut contents of red snapper at oil and gas platforms in winter contained mainly fish (small carangids, mainly platform associated rough scad). In spring, the diet was dominated by fish (unidentified fish 23.5%, Atlantic cutlass fish 19.3%, and carangids-probably scad 18.6%, and mantis shrimp 29.5%. In fall, crustaceans (shrimp, 53.2% and crabs 17.2%f or a total of 70.4%) and fish (26.6%) dominated the diets.  Clearly, soft-bottom prey were a major component of the diet, but reef associated fish were taken when abundant.

Siegel (1983) described red snapper food habits from habitats sampled offshore Alabama and some samples from Louisiana and Florida.  For adults, fish and crabs constituted the main part of the diet.  Of interest, all sizes of adults were noted to consume crabs, rock shrimp, penaeid shrimp, larval decapods, and larval mantis shrimp.

Ouzts and Szedlmayer (2003) examined the diets of red snapper collected from the artificial reef area offshore Alabama among four diel feeding periods (dawn, day, dusk, and night) and among three standard size classes small (200-299 mm SL), medium (300-399 mm SL), and large (400-499 mm SL). A total of 432 stomachs were examined, of which 164 contained prey.  Prey items were assigned a habitat association based on the literature, the authors� observations, and expert opinion. Small red snapper fed mostly on reef and sand prey types, medium red snapper fed on similar portions of reef, sand and mixed habitat prey types; and large red snapper fed mainly on prey observed to use a variety of habitats.  Red snapper were found to feed throughout the 24-hr cycle, with mean gut fullness being significantly lower at dusk than for the day period. Fish were the dominant prey throughout the 24-h cycle. The second-most important prey group changed with period: shrimp were codominant for dawn, tunicates for day, and crabs were codominant for dusk and night periods.

As previously described, the study by Szedlemayer and Lee (2004) focused on food habits of juvenile (< 200 mm SL) red snapper from open bottom and artificial reefs offshore of Alabama.  However, 61 specimens were collected from reefs that ranged from 200-250 mm SL. For these fish, the principal prey categories on a volumetric basis were fish (59.7%), shrimp (27.8%), and crabs (12.5%). For the fish-prey category approximately 65% were reef associated taxa.  Reef associated shrimp species constituted 54.2% as compared with 42.4% from open-bottom habitats. The Szedlemeyer and Lee (2004) findings indicate that adult red snapper (200-250 mm SL) fed on both reef and open habitat prey types.  Even if, all crabs and all the shrimp but pistol and cleaner shrimp are  treated as soft-bottom species, reef prey still constituted about 46% of the diet based on this data set (Gallaway et al. 2009).
McCawley et al. (2006) collected diel food habitat data for red snapper in the Alabama reef areas during July and August 2000. A total of 109 red snapper stomachs were collected from fish 295-560 mm FL.  Of these 46 contained prey. When examined on a diel basis red snapper appeared to feed throughout the day and night, with no obvious pattern in feeding periodicity.  McCawley et al. (2006) concluded that less than 2% of the red snapper diet organisms came from reef-associated organisms, based upon the defined habitat associations of the identified prey organisms.
McCawley (2003) and McCawley and Cowan (2007) examined the stomach contents of 656 red snapper ranging from 207 to 913 mm FL. Of these, 268 (40.9%) contained identifiable prey, 262 (39.9%) were empty, 63 (9.6%) contained only bait, and 63 (9.6%) contained only unidentified material.  All the fish examined were considered to be adults.  The unidentified material category contributed the largest proportion of red snapper diet by % weight (35.9%), followed by crab (20.2%), fish (19.5%), adult mantis shrimp Squilla empusa (12.6%), and pelagic zooplankton (8%).
On a seasonal basis, McCawley and Cowan (2007) found that fish was present in red snapper diets in all seasons (comprising between 34.5% and 31.8% by weight after the unidentified material was excluded), but they did not contribute the greatest amount by % weight in any season. The diets in summer and winter by % weight was composed of adult mantis shrimp (33.0% and 33.4% respectively), in fall of crabs (35.1%), and spring of pelagic zooplankton (45.6%). Demersal crustaceans (crabs and adult mantis shrimp) were present in all seasons comprising between 41.9% and 54.4% by weight of the diet in summer, fall and winter. During the spring, red snapper fed on high numbers of pelagic zooplankton. Statistical analyses indicated that red snapper were feeding on nearly the same kinds of organisms year around. Appendices 1 to 3 in the paper by McCawley and Cowan (2007) summarize the findings of the various red snapper diet studies.
McCawley and Cowan (2007) estimated that only 1.3% of the red snapper diet (excluding unidentifiable material) consisted of reef associated organisms. In contrast, the dominant components of the diets were species associated with sand and mud habitats (41.2%) and the water column (31%, mainly mantis shrimp and larval fish). Their interpretation of these data was that adult red snapper were almost, if not entirely trophically independent of the reefs on which they lived. In contrast, Gallaway et al. (2009) concluded that many red snapper food habit studies show substantial feeding on reef prey types, which supports the contention that red snapper are obtaining significant food resources from reef habitats.
The recruitment of age-0 red snapper to high-relief habitats such as artificial reefs or natural reefs may also be limited by predation from larger, older red snapper or by predation from other reef-associated species (Bailey et al. 2001, Piko and Stedlmayer 2007, Mudrak and Stedlmayer 2012).  Age-0 red snapper were excluded from complex habitat (concrete blocks) when older red snapper were added to a tank (Bailey et al. 2001).  In caging experiments conducted in the field, higher abundance of red snapper occurred on reefs when predators were excluded; in captivity, age-0 red snapper spent more  time associated with complex habitat when a predator (Gulf flounder Paralichthys albigutta) was present (Piko and Szedlmayer 2007).

Chapin et al. (2009) assessed the survival and movement of hatchery-reared red snapper on artificial habitats in the northern GOM.  Hatchery-reared red snapper were released onto artificial reef habitats.  The fish showed 12.7% survival after 7 months on small habitats (0.86 cubic meters) and 3.1% survival after 8 months on large habitats (3.9 cubic meters). Emigration was estimated by the movement of fish to unstocked habitats and accounted for 76.8% of the decline in abundance at release sites after 26 days. Age-0 fish showed higher survival and growth rates on small habitats (27.6% at 26 days; 0.33 mm per day) compared with large habitats (13.2% at 34 days; 0.26 mm per day) which may be due to increased predation and competition on the large habitats.  Fish became evenly distributed among adjacent habitats 26 days after release, indicating that stocking densities at release habitats were above carrying capacities.  These observations suggested that providing additional habitat around red snapper release sites would increase survival.

Based on the life history of red snapper and the potential effects of predators on reef fish recruitment, the proximity of larger artificial reefs and their associated reef fish communities may affect new recruitment of juvenile red snapper (Mudrak and Szedlmayr 2012).   Small artificial reefs were placed near to (15 m) and farther away (500 m distant) from larger artificial reefs at a site off Alabama.  Divers used visual surveys to identify and count all fish present on the small reefs and estimated fish lengths.  Significantly higher abundances of age-0 red snapper were detected on the small distant reefs (500 m) than on the small nearby (15 m) reefs.  Significantly higher densities of rock seabass and pygmy filefish were observed on the small distant reefs compared with the small nearby reefs.  Mean species richness was significantly higher on the small distant reefs than on the small nearby reefs. The study indicated that if artificial reefs are built to provide habitat for juvenile red snapper, they should not be placed in areas immediately adjacent to existing adult habitat, conversely habitats intended for adult fish should not be placed near important red snapper nursery areas.

Nowling et al. (2011) used otolith microchemistry to successfully discriminate between red snapper collected from artificial reefs and those collected from oil and gas platforms. A total of 98 otoliths were analyzed by inductively coupled plasma-mass spectrometry (ICPMS) from collections made from both artificial reefs and oil and gas platforms in Alabama and Louisiana over a two-year period from 2002 to 2003. A suite of 15 selected stable isotopes were analyzed, because they were most likely to be present at oil and gas platforms and in the metals and other materials used in artificial reefs, and in the circulating heavy �muds� used while drilling wells. Linear and stepwise discriminate analyses were performed to show that by using subsets of all the elements measured, it was possible to discriminate among artificial reefs and oil and gas platforms at average misclassification rates in the order of 10%.

Sluis (2011) conducted a similar otolith microchemistry study using 17 elements to determine habitats of origin for red snapper collected off Texas, Louisiana, and Florida.  Specimens collected off Destin, Florida, off Louisiana, and off Texas exhibited elemental signatures indicating they had come from regions with oil and gas platforms. Specimens collected off Tampa, Florida did not have an oil and gas platform elemental signature.  Maximum likelihood estimates (MLE) based on region-specific baseline data indicate that red snapper collected from Destin, Florida were estimated to predominately originate from Louisiana (82.1%) and secondarily from Alabama (16.1%).  Red snapper collected from Tampa, Florida were also estimated as originating from Louisiana (53.6%) with more influence from Alabama (37.8%).

sections.heading: REPRODUCTION
sections.content:
Gender-White and Palmer (2004) found that red snapper sampled off North Carolina to Key West
had a sex ratio that did not differ significantly from 1:1.  They are gonochoristic. The sex ratio had
not changed since 1986.  White et al. (2010) presented computations that did not differ from the
expected 1:1 ratio of male to female red snapper.
Mode-Red snapper are batch spawners periodically releasing eggs into the water column (Rabalais et al. 1980).

sections.heading: Domain-
sections.content:
Fertilization-External fertilization of eggs by male sperm.
Spawning Strategy: The f ish spawn primarily away from reefs (Bradley and Bryan 1975). Spawning was reported at depths of 18-37 m over a firm sand bottom with 1ittle relief in the GOM (Beaumariage and Bullock 1976).

Sedberry et al. (2006) captured adult red snapper in spawning condition in the southeastern Atlantic over a depth range of 24-67 m and a temperature range of 18.05-27.59oC  in MARMAP bottom trawls from South Carolina to eastern Florida off Melbourne.  Examination of sexually mature ovaries of female red snapper collected by MARMAP found that spawning occurred at depths 23-27 m and latitudes 27o-33oLatitude in the southeastern Atlantic from South Carolina to Florida (White et al. 2010). Maps were presented depicting the spatial distributions of spawning females clustered off South Carolina, Georgia, and northeastern Florida. Two maps show capture locations for young-of-year (age-0) red snapper situated on the inner continental shelf off of South Carolina and North Carolina. The total number of age-0 red snapper collected with MARMAP trawls from 1979 to 2000 was 31 fish.
Schobernd and Sedberry (2009) reported observing a large school of at least 20-30 red snapper, which appeared to be a spawning aggregation, situated at Scamp Ridge off South Carolina, at 19:29 Eastern Daylight Time (EDT) on August 2, 2002. The school was seen from a submersible at a depth of 53 m, with a bottom temperature of 20.9oC and salinity of 36.5 g/L.

Phelps et al. (2009) noted that brood behavior in hatchery tanks can give some indication of anticipated spawning.  A few hours before sunset, male red snapper were observed to follow a female with a swollen abdomen, swimming close to her vent area. Spawning behavior included fish schooling and slow swimming, interrupted by sudden group swimming and rushing toward the water surface.  This pattern was repeated several times.  Spawning occurred mainly in the late afternoon/evening hours. Several fertilized spawns with egg development in the blastula stage were collected in the late afternoon to early evening hours, before lights started dimming off (at approximately 1900 hrs). Fertilized eggs were found in the egg collector 30 min to 2 hr after the spawning behavior was observed.  Floating eggs were carried by the water current from the spawning tank to the egg collector. Jackson et al. (2006) examined the abundance of hydrated eggs in ovaries of wild-caught red snapper along the northern GOM and concluded that spawning peaks around 1600 hours.

Reproductive Periodicity: In general, red snapper spawn in summer and fal1 in the GOM. They have one peak spawning period in Florida waters and two peaks in Texas. Individual fish probably spawn several times during the spawning season (several egg stages occur simultaneously in the ovaries); the protracted spawning season and variation in gonadosomatic indices in fish of similar size during the season are consistent with this hypothesis (Collins et al. 1987).

Information on spawning seasonality as well as size and age at maturity are available for the northern GOM (Bradley and Bryan 1975, Wilson et al. 1994, Collins et al. 1996, Woods 2003, Woods et al. 2003), the southern GOM (Brul� et al. 2004), and the southeastern Atlantic (White and Palmer 2004).  Prior to 2008, the only information on reproduction for the SE GOM was 30 years old (Futch and Bruger 1976). More recently, a detailed study of the east and west coasts of Florida was conducted by Brown-Peterson et al. (2008).

Geary et al. (2007) reported that spawning occurred from April through late August at three banks off Texas. Peaks were generally unimodal with the majority of recruits from June and July hatch dates. This is roughly two weeks later than the peak in the hatch date reported by Rooker et al. (2004).  Szedlmayer and Conti (1999) reported that peaks in hatch date distributions of red snapper in the northwestern gulf vary by several weeks between consecutive years. Gonadal analysis suggests that red snapper spawning occurs in the northwest GOM from April through October, suggesting that a second pulse of recruits may enter the fishery in the late fall (Collins et al. 2001).

Despite the lack of significant genetic differences, Jackson e t al. (2007) reported maturity schedules and size-specific fecundity were significantly different between red snapper populations east and west of the mouth of the Mississippi River. They suggested early maturity at smaller size in the eastern GOM may be a genotypic response to high fishing mortality having selectively removed later maturing genotypes, a response that would not be apparent in selectively neutral genetic markers such as mitochondrial DNA (MtDNA) or nuclear DNA microsatellites (Pruett et al. 2005, Saillant and Gold 2006). Regardless of the causative factor, the fact that regional differences exist implies some degree of isolation between the eastern and western GOM. Patterson et al. (2007) asserted that regional differences in size at age reported by Fisher et al. (2004) further support that population structure exists in GOM red snapper, which has not been revealed by traditional fisheries genetics applications (Pruett et al. 2005, Gold and Saillant 2007).

White and Palmer (2004) collected otoliths and gonadal tissues from red snapper sampled between Cape Lookout, North Carolina and Key West, Florida during 1979-2000. The mean size of red snapper from fishery-dependent samples were 594 mm TL and ranged from 70-976 mm TL. Fish sampled from fisheries-independent gear had a significantly smaller mean TL (426 mm, range = 121-866 mm) than fishery dependent samples. The mean size of red snapper was significantly smaller in the 1980s when compared to the 1990s, regardless of gear type. The overall sex ratio was not significantly different from the expected 1:1, regardless of gear type.  The smallest mature female was 287 mm TL and the largest immature female was 435 mm TL, with an estimate of length at 50% maturity of 378 mm TL. Histological examination of the gonads indicated that female red snapper were in spawning condition from May through October, with a peak between June and September.  The gonadosomatic index (GSI) for females ranged from a low of 0.35 in November and December to a high of 2.67 in June. Males were found to be in spawning condition thoughout the year.

Brown-Peterson et al. (2008) collected red snapper from recreational-for-hire boats at two distinct areas of Florida to examine potential differences in their reproductive biology.  Samples were obtained from the Florida East Coast (St. Augustine to Melbourne N=66) from June to November of 2004 and 2005, and from the Dry Tortugas (N=81) during May, June, and August 2004-2005. There was a significant relationship between length and batch fecundity of red snapper from the East Coast but not from the Dry Tortugas. Relative frequency estimates were low in Dry Tortugas fish (27 � 11 eggs/g) relative to 235 � 56 eggs/g in East Coast fish, but similar to those reported from Alabama. Spawning frequency estimates varied from every 2.2 days on the East Coast to every 4.3 days in the Dry Tortugas. The apparent regional differences in reproductive biology among Florida red snapper may require region-specific management plans for this species.

Parental Care: None reported.

Seasonal Energetics: Wakeman et al. (1979) studied oxygen consumption, energy consumption,
and growth of red snapper.

sections.heading: Juvenile-
sections.content:
Adult- Authors of early studies of GOM red snapper reproductive biology concluded that fish began reaching sexual maturity at a small size (<300 mm TL) and had protracted spawning seasons extending through the summer months (Bradley and Bryan 1975, Futch and Bruger 1976, Moseley 1966).  Collins et al. (1996) were the first to estimate batch fecundity in red snapper and to establish that the spawning season extended from April through October in both the eastern and western GOM.  Red snapper usually show partial sexual maturity when 1 year old and show full maturity when about 2 years old and 375 mm in fork length (FL) (Moran 1988).

Length at maturity has been reported to be 320 mm FL (Camber 1955), and between 190 and 300 mm SL (Moseley 1966).  Wilson et al. (1994) presented preliminary estimates of maturation at 290 mm FL.  Age-at-maturity has been reported as greater than 2 years old in the GOM (Futch and Bruger 1976).

Ovary analysis has also varied among studies. While authors prior to 1976 (Camber 1955, Moseley 1966, Bradley and Bryan 1975) used macro-assessment of gonad maturation, later authors (Futch and Bruger 1976, Wilson and Nieland 1994, Collins et al. 1996) used histological techniques to determine stages of oocyte maturation.  Histology is a more effective method for staging oocytes because it allows a detailed view of cross-sectioned and stained oocytes (Jackson et al. 2007).

Jackson et al. (2007) used red snapper collected during the spawning season off Alabama and
Louisiana, to describe maturation schedules of red snapper. Progression of oocyte maturation to
vitellogenesis was used to define and identify sexually mature females. Combined data showed
that smallest mature red snapper was 267 mm FL and was two years old. The smallest with
hydrated oocytes, indicative of imminent spawning, or postovulatory follicles, indicative of recent
spawning, were 285 and 297 mm FL respectively, and both were two years old.  Red snapper off
Alabama reached maturation at smaller sizes and younger ages than those sampled off Louisiana.
Growth rates did not differ between the two regions. Such differences in maturation schedules
may document an important stock response to reductions in populations size.
A comparison of maturity schedules indicated that red snapper captured off Alabama reached 50%    maturity before 275 mm FL and before they were 2.5 years old, and raw data showed 100% maturity by 575 mm FL (Jackson et al. 2007).  Females captured off Louisiana reached 50% maturity before 325 mm FL and before they were 2.5 years old, and raw data showed 100% maturity by 625 mm FL and 6.5 years old. Compared to Alabama, Louisiana female red snapper progressed more slowly to reach 100% maturity over size- and age-classes.
In the southeast Atlantic, White and Palmer (2004) noted that male red snapper reach maturity as early as age-1 or 200 mm TL, with all males mature by age-3 or 378 mm TL.  Females can be mature by age-2 or 287 mm TL, with all females mature after age-4 or 435 mm TL. The gonadosomatic index (GSI) of female red snapper peaked in June and remained high until September.
White et al. (2010) used data obtained from the NOAA/NMFS Marine Resources Monitoring, Assessment and Prediction (MARMAP) program to assess reproductive condition in red snapper in the southeastern Atlantic for the SEDAR24 stock assessment. The youngest sexually mature female red snapper was age-2 and the oldest was age-4. The smallest mature female was 265 mm TL, and the largest immature female was 435 mm TL.  Age at 50% maturity was 1.87 yr and length at 50% maturity was 370 mm.  Mature females were present in 0% of the age-1 class, 54% of age-2, 86% of age-3, 93% of age-4, and 100% of females age-5 or older.  Mature males were present in 50% of age-1 class, 93% of age-2, 97% of age-3, 100% of age-4, 97% of age-5, and 100% of males age-6 or older.  All male red snapper were mature at 451 mm TL and larger.
Fecundity:  Fecundity of fish sampled in northwest Florida ranged from 0.2 million  eggs for a female about 3 years old and 386 mm FL to 9.3 million for a fish about 12 years old and 754 mm FL (Collins et al. 1987).

Only limited fecundity information is available for red snapper along the Atlantic coast of the U.S. (SEDAR24 DW Report 2010). The relationship between batch fecundity (BF) and TL (BF = 9548*TL � 5,224,104; r2 = 0.67) was estimated for 12 specimens, 560-937 mm (Brown-Peterson et al. 2009). The small sample size and the lack of specimens < 560 mm made this equation of minimal use for the SEDAR24 assessment. An estimate of fecundity at age was available from the GOM, but was not as predictive as an estimate of fecundity at length (see Woods 2003; Fitzhugh et al. 2004) because batch fecundity reaches an asymptote at an age of approximately 10-12 yr.

Given the lack of a usable fecundity estimate from the Atlantic region, three proxies to estimate fecundity were considered: 1) gonad weight versus age, 2) gonad weight versus whole fish weight, and 3) gonad weight versus total length (SEDAR24 DW Report 2010).  The first proxy (gonad weight versus age; was not considered adequate because of a large gap in the age data, and, secondly, the linear nature of the relationship was inconsistent with the non-linear relationship evident between gonad weight and fish size (whole weight or TL) as fish grow. The second proxy is probably a better option, given the need to relate gonad weight to spawning biomass. The gonad weight (Wg) - whole fish weight (Wf) relationship is expressed as a power function:

Wg = 3.1416x10-5 Wf 1.743; SEa = 3.1836x10-5, SEb = 0.1107.

The gonad weight (Wg) - total length (Lt) relationship, third proxy, is expressed as a power function:

Wg = 1.207x10-11 Lt 4.524; SEa = 3.16x10-11, SEb = 0.3923.

The Life History Working Group for SEDAR24 recommended the use of the second proxy, gonad weight � fish weight, as an estimate of fecundity in the assessment (SEDAR24 2010). Recommendation was accepted at plenary session of Data Workshop.

sections.heading: Development
sections.content:
Egg/Parturition-In the laboratory, initial hatching began 20 h after fertilization (Minton et al. 1983), and about 50% of the eggs hatched within 25 h of fertilization (Rabalais et al. 1980).
Larva-	Newly hatched larvae in the laboratory averaged 2.2 mm SL (Rabalais et al. 1980). The larvae began actively feeding on a culture of algae and rotifers 3 days after hatching and were 2.5 mm SL 4 days after hatching.
                                                                                                                                                      Young of Year-                                                                                                                         Juvenile-                                                                                                                                        Adult-Porch et al. (2007a) modeled batch fecundity (BF) on size and age of red snapper for use in stock assessments in GOM waters. Batch fecundity is a principal determinant of the reproductive potential of indeterminate spawners.  BF appears to increase geometrically with length and asymptotically with age based upon combined data from reproductive sampling programs by NMFS in the GOM and MARFIN in the southeastern Atlantic. As the life history pattern of red snapper sets up a potential disconnection between size and age, Porsch et al. (2007a) modeled their interaction as explanatory variables of BF.  Visual analysis suggested a dome-shaped relationship between BF and age within a given size-class. To test this, a log-linear model and a new �standardized� age model (where the effect of age depends explicitly on the size of fish) were fitted to the data.  These analyses suggest that the effect of age, while statistically significant, was relatively small (the models with age and length terms explaining only slightly more of the variation in BF than a simple power function of length). The age effect seems to be most pronounced for fish that are exceptionally small or exceptionally large given their age, which constitute a small fraction of the sample and presumably also a small fraction of the population at large.  Hence, it seems unlikely that including this interaction would have any important ramifications for stock assessments of red snapper. Nevertheless, the effect of age on BF remains open to the degree that old fish (i.e., greater than age 13) were rare in the combined data set and tended to exhibit lower BF values than predicted. Age effects of other reproductive determinants remain to be evaluated but the authors found hydrated females to be of greater size-at-age than non-hydrated red snapper suggesting an age-length interaction on batch fecundity.

Mating/Spawning Duration: Only limited information is available for red snapper along the Atlantic coast of the U.S.   Brown-Peterson et al. (2009) reported that spawning occurs every 2.2 days based on a sample of 66 specimens collected during June through November. Estimates from the GOM revealed that spawning frequency increases until about Age 6; little information is available for older ages (Woods 2003, Fitzhugh et al. 2004).

Sex Ratio: Red snapper are gonochoristic with an equal sex ratio of 1:1 (Brown-Peterson et al. 2009, White et al. 2010)

sections.heading: Length Range
sections.content:
Egg/Parturition- Red snapper eggs averaged 0.82 mm in diameter (range: 0.77-0.85 mm) (Rabalais et al. 1980).

Larva- Newly hatched larvae in the laboratory averaged 2.2 mm SL (Rabalais et al. 1980). The larvae began actively feeding on a culture of algae and rotifers 3 days after hatching and were 2.5 mm SL 4 days after hatching.  A total of 96 hatchery-reared red snapper larvae ranged in body length (BL) from 1.9 to 26.1 mm BL, and a total of 118 wild caught-larvae ranged from 2.6 to 20 mm BL (Drass et al. 2000).  Body length (BL) is equivalent to notochord length or standard length (SL) depending on the stage of development of the larvae (Leis 1987).

Daily growth rates observed by Geary et al. (2007) of 1.09 mm per day at Freeport Rocks, 1.01 mm per day at Heald Bank, 1.01 mm per day at Sabine Bank) off Texas overlap the upper end of red snapper observed by Rooker at al. (2004) of 0.78-0.88 mm per day, and 0.54-0.86 mm per day found by Szedlemayer and Conti (1999).

Young of Year-The age-0 larvae undergo metamorphosis and settle to the bottom when they are 16-19 mm TL and 26 to 30 days of age in the GOM (Rabalais et al.1980, Szedlmayer and Conti 1999, Rooker et al. 2004, Gallaway et al. 2009).  Settlement was observed in July and the newly settled fish (most <40 mm TL) were found over open or low relief habitat off Alabama (Szedlemayr and Lee 2004). Age 0 red snapper enter the GOM penaeid shrimp trawl fishery at about 67 days of age and 50 mm TL (Galloway et al. 2009). Age-0 fish began moving onto reefs as they reached sizes approaching 100 mm TL and by December were found on the reefs from which age-1 fish had abruptly disappeared (Stedlmayer and Lee 2004).

Juvenile-Wells (2007), also working offshore Alabama, observed an increase in mean size of age-1 red snapper corresponding to a shift from sand (96.1 mm TL) to low-relief shell (127.0 mm TL) to high relief habitat (172.3 mm TL).

Nieland and Wilson (2003) analyzed size frequency distributions of red snapper killed by explosives at an oil and gas platform off Louisiana. A peak in the size frequency distribution indicated that age-2 red snapper ranged from 250-380 mm TL.  Because of the 15 inch minimum size limit imposed by the GMFMC age-2 red snapper were not observed in size frequencies representing catches of red snapper taken from either the commercial or recreational fisheries.

Adults-Nieland and Wilson (2003) found a second peak in the size frequency of red snapper killed by explosives at an oil and gas platform off Louisiana. Age-3 red snapper ranged in size from 381-480 mm TL.  Adult red snapper in the GOM range in length up to 104 cm TL (Scott-Denton et al. 2011).

Red snapper initially grow quickly and then growth slows steadily as larger size associated with long life span is reached (Bradley and Bryan 1975). In the GOM, under-yearling fish grew 25 mm/month in August and September according to Bradley and Bryan (1975).
Length Conversions: The relations of SL to FL and FL to TL (lengths in mm) and N (sample size) were reported by Futch and Bruger (1976) as follows:

FL = 1.1585 SL + 13.3 (N = 21)
TL = l.0678 FL + 3.5 (N = 100)

Nelson and Manooch  (1982) reported the following relation:
TL = 1.0712 FL + 1.7 (N = 180).
Additional length-length relations are given in Parrack (1986b). 	Length- length relations show a high linear correlation  (Parrack 1986b).


Weight-Length Conversions: Length-weight relations calculated for severa1    areas in the gulf were similar  Parrack 1986b). The length-weight  relation  changed  at 190-300 mm SL (Moseley 1966).

West Florida Both sexes Log10W = 2.966 log10 FL -4.7399  Nelson and Manooch
(1982).
Florida   Males        Log10W = 3.008 log 10 FL -4.8104
                   Females     Log10W =  3.028 log 10 FL -4.8618 Futch and Bruger (1976).
	Alabama  Both sexes   Log10W =  3.0092 log10TL -4.8539 Wade (1981).
	Texas       Both sexes   Log10W =  2.855  log10FL  -4.7921 Wakeman (1979).
	Campeche Both sexes  Log10W =   3.01   log10FL  -4.7921 Camber (1955).

sections.heading: Wet-Dry Weight Conversions
sections.content:
Length at Age:  Scale annulus formation off the U.S. gulf coast is complete by
early summer for fish ages 2 and older (Parrack 1986). Annual growth of fish
of age 1 to 4 or 5 in the GOM ranged from 60 to 75 mm (Bradley Bryan 1975) and 90
mm (Moseley 1966).

sections.heading: Female-
sections.content: Sexes Combined-Age-length keys for red snapper in the southeast Atlantic have been presented by Manooch et al. (1997, 1998), White and Palmer (2004), and McInerny (2007). Mean total lengths at age in the southeast Atlantic were presented by Manooch et al. (1997) and McInerny (2007).  McInerny presented a comparison of mean total lengths (TL) at age for the commercial fishery between 2003 and 2006 for Florida, and for North Carolina, South, Carolina, and Georgia combined (Table 5).  Table 6 presented a comparison of mean total lengths at age for the commercial fishery and for the recreational fishery off Florida between 2001 and 2006. In Table 7, McInerny (2007) presented a comparison of mean total lengths at age during the period of: a) no regulation, b) the fishery management plan (FMP), and c) after passage of Amendment 4.  Mean back-calculated total lengths at age for red snapper in the southeast Atlantic were presented  up to age-11 by Manooch et al. (1997), up to age-20 by McInerny (2007), and up to age 15 for various locations in the GOM (Louisiana, West Florida) and southeast Atlantic (Carolinas, East Florida) by Nelson and Manooch (1982). All of these studies cited presented mean lengths at age for the sexes combined.

sections.heading: Longevity
sections.content:
Egg/Parturition- The early life history includes a planktonic egg stage for 18-27 hours (Rabalais et al. 1980; Minton et al. 1983).
Larva- The larval stage has a duration of 25-47 days (Leis 1987).
Young-of-Year- A benthic young-of-year stage occurs after the larvae undergo metamorphosis and settle to the bottom (Szedlemayer and Conti 1999). Size at settlement is about 1.7 cm.
