Age-0 fish initially occur over sand, mud bottoms, then migrate to submerged banks of oyster shell (Lingo and Stedlmayer 2006, Piko and Stedlmayer 2007). Red snapper as small as 18 mm settled on relatively unstructured open shelf habitats in summer, but by the winter age-0 fish had recruited to artificial reefs that provided greater complexity and relief (Szedlemayer and Lee 2004).
Juvenile- A comparison of maturity schedules indicated that red snapper captured off Alabama reached 50% maturity before 275 mm FL and before they were 2.5 years old (Jackson et al. 2007).  Females captured off Louisiana reached 50% maturity before 325 mm FL and before they were 2.5 years old. Based on the age at which 50% of the fish are sexually mature, age-1 and age-2 red snapper can be classified as juveniles.
Adult- Maximum ages for red snapper derived from reading scales were age-4 in the northern GOM (Moseley 1966), age-13 off Louisiana (Nelson and Manooch 1982, age-9 off Alabama (Wade 1981), and age-11 off western Florida (Nelson and Manooch 1982). In the southeast Atlantic, Nelson and Manooch (1982) aged red snapper from east Florida and the Carolinas and found fish as old as 16 years using scales and otoliths.  Research by Beamish and McFarlane (1983) called into question the reliability of ages derived from scales and proposed the need for age validation studies.
Recent advances in otolith preparation methodology have allowed red snapper to be aged reliably in the GOM up to the following ages: 42 yr (Szedlemayer and Shipp 1994), 53 yr (Render 1995), 31 yr (Patterson 1999), 52 yr (Wilson and Nieland 1991), 47 yr (Allman et al. 2002), 53 yr (Mitchell et al. 2004), 55 yr (Baker and Wilson 2001), and 57 yr (Allman and Fitzhugh 2007).  Patterson et al. (2001b) found that the oldest female sampled was 34 years, and the oldest male was 33 years old.

Manooch and Potts (1997) aged red snapper from the southeast Atlantic up to 25 years old using sectioned otoliths. White and Palmer (2004) found that the age range determined from otoliths for fishery-independent samples in the southeast Atlantic was 1-22 years with a mean age of 3.1 years, and 1-45 years for fishery dependent samples with a mean age of 4.2 years.  The oldest red snapper aged using sectioned otoliths in the southeast Atlantic was 54 years old (McInerny 2007).

Potts et al. (2009) gathered otoliths to determine the age structure of red snapper collected from North Carolina to the east coast of Florida during the summer months of 2009.  All fish were collected with hook and line gear by recreational and commercial fishermen. The oldest red snapper caught off North Carolina was 12 yr, off South Carolina 20 yr, off Georgia 22 yr, and off northeast Florida 37 yr. Further studies are needed to determine whether older red snapper occur in deeper water offshore.
Aging Structures/Methods: Using scales to determine sizes at age, several studies found rapid growth in young fish. They grew from 137-177 mm TL at age 1 to 538-546 mm TL at age 5 and 784-794 mm TL at age 11 (Moseley 1966, Bradley and Bryan 1975, Nelson and Manooch 1982, Wade 1981).  They may reach 845 mm FL and 12 kg (Bradley and Bryan 1975) and an age of about 13 years (Nelson and Manooch 1982). Scale annulus formation off the U.S. GOM coast is complete by early summer for fish ages 2 and older (Parrack 1986).
A 35% decrease in the production in red snapper in the commercial GOM fishery from 1965 to 1975 prompted Futch and Bruger (1976) to further examine the age and growth of red snapper (Fisher 2007).  Among 240 red snapper taken off the west coast of Florida, they estimated red snapper ages of  1 to 5 yr from 200 readable whole otoliths; however, they postulated ages up to 20 yr for larger individuals whose otoliths were unreadable.
Bortone and Hollingsworth (1980) determined ages of red snapper using scale, otoliths, and vertebrae. They found that all three body parts had a statistically similar level of readability (between 75% and 80%). However, they only examined 46 red snapper.
Nelson and Manooch (1982) were used scales and also sectioned some otoliths to examine the age structure of red snapper in the northern GOM as well as the west-central Atlantic. They examined 2,151 scales (from both the GOM and SE Atlantic) and142 sectioned otoliths (Atlantic only) to examine the growth and mortality of red snapper along the southeastern U.S. and the northern GOM. They attempted to validate their ages using monthly mean marginal growth increments performed on scales (Fisher 2007).  This technique indicated that red snapper in the GOM form annuli during June and July. They were unable to perform marginal increment analyses on otoliths, because they did not have otoliths sampled throughout all 12 months of the year. However, 18 one-year-old red snapper sampled in the Carolinas during June all exhibited the beginning of new growth (translucence) at the otolith section edge, leading them to suggest that scale and otolith annuli form simultaneously.
A number of studies using sectioned otoliths have found greater longevity of red snapper than what was originally reported from age determinations using scales (Fisher 2007).  Szedlemayer and Shipp (1994) used counts of annuli on sectioned otoliths for 409 red snapper sampled with hook and line off Alabama. They reported a maximum age of 42 years, a substantial increase over the previously reported maximum age of 13 years determined from scales (Nelson and Manooch 1982).
Render (1995) estimated ages from sectioned otoliths for red snapper sampled from both the recreational and commercial fisheries off Louisiana. Render observed a maximum longevity of 53 years. He validated his age estimates through marginal increment analysis. The increased longevity estimates reported by Szedlemayer and Shipp (1994) and Render (1995) were available for the stock assessment conducted by Goodyear (1995).
A number of laboratories in the GOM region began routine annual aging programs of red snapper in an effort to track age structure trends over time for stock assessment purposes (Cowan et al. 1995, Wilson and Nieland 2001, Allman et al. 2002).  Wilson and Nieland (2001) tracked the age structure off Louisiana during eight years of variable collection effort from 1989 to 1998.  Allman et al. (2002) sampled commercial and recreational fisheries from Texas to the west coast of Florida in 1998 and 1999. A total of 8,169 otoliths were sectioned. Validation work was conducted using marginal increment analysis.
The consequences of incorrect age determination of red snapper was first pointed out by Rothschild et al. (1997) in their review of the red snapper GOM management plan. In particular some life history aspects of red snapper appeared to differ from typical long-lived marine species, such as their rapid growth and early maturity that were more consistent with short-lived species. Red snapper in the GOM mature as early as age two and show rapid growth within the first 10 years of life and fecundity increases with age (Szedlmayer and Shipp 1994, Collins et al. 2001, Woods et al. 2003). The inconsistency between red snapper life history and that of other long-lived species, and the lack of direct mark recapture studies, showed a need for further validation of annual increment formation in otoliths of red snapper, especially for older larger fish.
Szedlemayer (1998) studied the formation of daily otolith increments in age-0 red snapper after marking them with oxytetracycline dehydrate (OTC).   For wild red snapper, the mean otolith increment deposition rate was daily (0.97 increments per day) when growth rates were fast (0.63 mm FL, length of fish per day), but not daily (0.82 increments per day) when somatic growth was slow (0.2 mm length of fish per day). For reared larvae (N=8), increment deposition rates were daily (0.99 -1.03 increments per day), and growth rates ranged from 0.6 to 0.9 mm per day.  Growth rate affected increment deposition rate as a threshold function, i.e., when growth rate was <0.3 mm length of fish per day, deposition was less than daily, but above this level increment deposition did not exceed a daily rate. As growth rates increased increment widths increased.  Examination of a sub-sample (N=8) of the otoliths from the slowest growing wild fish by electron microscopy did not increase increment counts. Because red snapper are late spring-early summer spawners, young fish can expect maximum growth due to warm summer temperatures. Thus, daily ageing methods should be well suited for this species.
The use of bomb-radiocarbon was applied to validate otolith section ages in the GOM (Baker 1999, Baker and Wilson 2001).   Ages of red snapper ranged from 2 to 55 years with back-calculated years at birth ranging from 1943 to 1996.   Baker and Wilson (2001) stated that their radiocarbon chronologies based on accelerator mass spectrometry (AMS) provided evidence that otolith section-based age estimates for red snapper were valid.

A second age validation method applied to red snapper was radiometric testing, which measured the chemical disequilibria of 210 Pb (lead) to 226Ra (radium) (Wilson et al. 2001). Radiometric ageing of fish otoliths relies on the principal assumptions that (1) 226Ra is naturally incorporated into the otolith either at a constant rate or at a rate that is proportional to the mass increase of the otolith, (2) that the otolith remains a chemically closed system and there are no losses or gains of radionucleids (e.g., radon 222Rn), and (3) the initial activity ratio of 210Pb to 226Ra is close to zero.  Baker et al. (2001) showed that some of these assumptions were violated in red snapper otoliths.  In whole otoliths of both red snapper and red drum (Sciaenops ocellatus) 226Ra activity was inversely correlated with the otolith mass increase with age, validating the assumption that 226Ra accumulation in otoliths occurs at a rate proportional to that of calcium (Ca).  222Rn emanation from otoliths decreased as otolith mass increased.  222Rn loss occurred in all red snapper otolith samples (<=4.1%), and decreased with increasing size (age) of the otolith.
Although a validated aging method may have proved successful for a given study there is no guarantee that those structures will be interpreted the same by other readers (Campana 2001).  Allman et al. (2005) noted that while validation of aging methods is an important criterion in estimating growth and longevity, age interpretation remains largely subjective.  This subjectivity can pose a significant problem in aging red snapper otoliths due to challenges in interpreting the first annulus and in discerning annuli in older individual fish.
A measure of precision is a valuable means of assessing the reproducibility of age determinations beween individuals or laboratories (Campana 2001, Fisher 2007).  A number of the laboratories conducing red snapper age-growth studies have determined the average percent error (APE) to evaluate aging precision of red snapper (Render  1995, Patterson et al. 2001b, Wilson and Nieland 2001, Allman et al. 2002, Allman et al. 2005).
Wilson and Nieland (2001) noted that training and experience are critical to achieving accuracy and high between reader consensus on red snapper annulus counts due to the high level of difficulty of interpretation.
The Gulf States Marine Fisheries Commission (GSMFC) began to conduct yearly aging workshops in
2003 in an effort to bring together all aging laboratories in the GOM to discuss and standardize
processing and aging techniques (Mareska 2005, Fisher 2007).

Similar studies are being conducted in the Southeast Atlantic (White et al., 2010).  A red snapper aging
workshop was held during August 2009 in Charleston SC (Potts et al. 2009). Red snapper otoliths
(N=196) in a �reference� set from fishery-independent and fishery-dependent were aged during the inter-
laboratory workshop.  The average percent error (APE) for readers from South Carolina Department of
Natural Resources (SCDENR) was 9.13%.  Additonal red snapper otoliths (N=447) were aged with an
initial agreement of 67% and agreement within two annuli of 93% between two readers.  Ages
determined for red snapper otoliths ranged from 0 to 35 years.

The current ageing technique of counting annual growth increments on sectioned otoliths is often
difficult and subjective in young red snapper (Beyer and Szedlmayer 2010).  In particular, identification
of the first annulus is subject to reader identification and is a source of considerable error in aging young
fish (Holt and Arnold 1982, Wilson and Nieland 2001, Rooker et al. 2004,  Allman et al. 2005).

Interpretation of the putative first annulus in sectioned otoliths of red snapper has been a source of
debate among otolith readers throughout the GOM (Fisher at el. 2010).  The chemical marker alazarine
complexone was used to validate the periodicity of first  opaque annulus formation in red snapper otolith
sections.  Juvenile red snapper were immersed in 100 mg alizarin complexone per L seawater solution in
November 2005 and then reared in 6000 liter circular tanks until July 2006. Otoliths were then removed
from the fish and thin sectioned. All experimental otolith sections displayed a distinct fluorescent mark
ranging from 0.62 to 0.96 mm from the core when viewed under a microscope with a rhodamine filter.
The diffuse opaque annulus was located distally to the alizarine mark in all specimens (ranging from
0.88 to 1.51 mm).  The distal position of the presumptive first annulus relative to the alizarin mark in all
specimens indicates that this diffuse opaque annulus in red snapper sectioned otoliths forms during the
first winter after hatching. Translucent marginal edges of all otolith sections indicate that first annulus
formation is completed by mid-July.
A new method for determining the age of red snapper was developed involving shape analysis of otiliths (Beyer 2008, Beyer and Szedlemayer 2010).  Multidimensional scaling and non-parametric analysis showed significant shape differences of age-0, age-1, and age-2 fish.  Discriminant function analysis and cross-validation classification showed 65.6% correct age classification based on shape variables alone, and 86.7% correct age classifications with inclusion of otolith weight in the discriminant function.  Otolith shape can provide an objective method for ageing young red snapper.
The periodicity of otolith growth increments (opaque and translucent zones) from adult  red snapper was examined through a mark and recapture study conducted (2005-2010) and laboratory holding of hatchery-reared red snapper over a two year period (2002-2004) (Szedlmayer and Beyer 2011).  Wild red snapper (N=295) were caught on hook-and-line, marked with anchor tags, injected with oxytetracycline dihidrate (OTC), and released in the GOM off Alabama. Marked fish were recaptured up to 2.8 years after release (n=35) and sagittal otoliths were dissected, sectioned and examined under white and blue-violet light.  The number of opaque growth zones past the OTC mark was compared to time at liberty for each fish and supported an annual periodicity of growth increment formation. Also, most (87%) of the hatchery reared fish showed two opaque zones that supported an annual increment formation rate.  However, an unusual timing of opaque zone formation was shown for mark-recaptured fish.  Based on known timing of OTC marking, otoliths from mark-recapture fish showed opaque zone formation from late summer (August) to early winter (December). This fall formation of opaque zones is in contrast to previous studies and its timing may relate to the end of spawning for this species.

Research has been conducted to determine chemical signatures of red snapper otoliths associated with studies to determine differences in population demographics in the GOM (Patterson et al. 1998, 2001c, 2008; Gibson et al. 2010; Sluis  2011; Nowling et al.  2011). Some differences have been found indicating regional differences in age-0 red snapper between the eastern and western GOM (Patterson et al. 2008,  Sluis 2011).
Growth Equations: Ne1son and Manooch (1982) reported von Berta1anffy growth equations for fish from two areas in the GOM. They found that the von Bertalanffy growth curves for Louisiana, western Florida, eastern Florida, and the Carolinas differed statistically, as did the length-weight relations for fish from west Florida, east Florida, and the Carolina. However, the differences in growth curves were small and the differences in length-weight curves had little if any biological significance. Parrack (1986a) reported differences in growth curves between fish west of and fish east of the Mississippi Delta. This difference was inconclusive (Reef Fish Scientific Task Team and Special Scientific and Statistical Committee 1987).
A number of studies have developed von Bertalanffy growth equations for red snapper populations respectively in the GOM and southeast Atlantic (Collins et 1996, Nelson et al. 1985, Nelson and Manooch 1982, Manooch et al. 1998, Fisher et al. 2002, Szedlemayer and Shipp 1994, Wilson and Nieland 2001, Wilson et al. 2001, Patterson et al. 2001a, White and Palmer 2004, McInerny 2007, Saari 2011). Most of the studies fitted models for the sexes combined.  Wilson and Nieland (2001) and Fisher et al. (2002) developed separate models by sex of red snapper. Von Bertalanffy growth parameters for red snapper and other species of Lutjanidae were tabulated as part of a comparative study by Martinez-Andrade (2003).
Habitat varies greatly throughout the GOM and while numerous studies have aged red snapper, none have simultaneously compared the age and size structure and growth rates among standing and toppled oil and gas platforms with natural habitats (Saari 2011). The study examined the size and age structure and growth rates (using von Bertalanffy growth equations) of red snapper among three different habitats (shelf-edge banks, standing platforms, toppled platforms) and six recreational fishing regions of the GOM (South Texas, North Texas, Louisiana, Alabama, Northwest Florida, Central Florida). Across all of the habitats and regions, red snapper were small (mean TL = 526.84 mm, mean TW = 0.97 kg) and from younger age classes (mean age = 4.44 yr), representing the strong recruitments of 2004, 2005 and 2006, with few fish older than seven years (1.5%). Total length, weight, and age frequencies, and growth models differed significantly among the habitats. Red snapper from the banks were significantly smaller at age and slower growing than red snapper from the artificial habitats. Also, shelf-edge banks appeared to support a higher predominance of older red snapper compared to the artificial habitats. Demographic differences in red snapper size and age frequencies and growth parameters were found across the GOM. Small, fast-growing individuals dominated the recreational catches of South Texas, Northwest Florida, and Central Florida, whereas larger, slower-growing red snapper constituted the majority of the Alabama and Louisiana catches. Also, both of the Florida regions� catches were comprised of significantly younger red snapper than catches in the north-central and western regions. To prevent habitat- and region-specific overfishing and promote stock recovery, these differences should be weighed when evaluating future stock assessments and management decisions. It is also important for fisheries managers to note the absence of old red snapper in this study and its implications for the stock�s recovery status.

sections.heading: Commercial
sections.content:
Gulf of Mexico
The red snapper is the most important fish in the GOM commercial snapper-grouper fishery between  Cape San Blas, Florida, and the mouth of the Rio Grande (Allen and Tashiro 1976); 4.6 million lb were landed commercially at U.S. ports in the GOM in 1985 (National Marine Fisheries Service 1986, Moran  1988).
From the 1880s to the 1950s, the red snapper fishery primarily operated out of Pensacola Florida (Collins 1885, Bortone et al. 1997, Shipp and Bortone 2008).  Although the fishery began in the 1840s, red snapper  was established as a major commercial product in the 1870s when the railroad system permitted the shipment of fishes from Pensacola to northern and inland markets. As early as 1883, it was evident that the number of red snapper was decreasing on the existing fishing grounds off Pensacola.  Snapper fishermen had to go further east each year to obtain a profitable catch. Many smacks sailed over 200 miles to the Florida Middle Ground. This area was also soon overfished.  New red snapper grounds were discovered off the Dry Tortugas in 1885. From 1895 to 1929, the discovery of a large red snapper fishery on the Campeche Banks off Mexico brought the period of the highest production for Pensacola�s red snapper industry.
Snappers and groupers are often taken together in the snapper-grouper fishery. Various fishing methods for snappers and groupers have been used or tested over the years.  Most commercial fishing is done with baited hooks and li nes on e1ectric and hydraulic reels which were too expensive until recently (Moran 1988). These are all classified as handlines in National Marine Fisheries Service fishery statistics.  From 2 to 40 hooks may be used with one reel (Allen and Tashiro 1976).  Ladyfish and squid are the most effective bait (Carpenter 1965); red snapper select fish and squid equally often (Futch and Bruger 1976). The industry has experimented with other fishing methods, but many were deficient; an otter trawl adapted for rough bottoms was effective (Smith 1948; Captiva and Rivers 1960; Nelson and Carpenter 1968).  An extensive bottom longline fishery that may take red snapper developed in the Gulf of Mexico since about 1980.  The longline fishery in the eastern gulf has been directed primarily at yellowedge grouper (Epinephelus flavolimbatus) (Parrack and Mclellan 1986).
Commercial   fishing grounds for red snapper are well offshore in the Gulf of Mexico (Moran 1988). In 1955, the most important fishing grounds had 1ong been the Campeche Banks off the Yucatan Peninsula, Mexico, which were the principa1    grounds fished by the west Florida fleet (Camber 1955; Hildebrand 1955). Fishing there by American boats was curtailed, however, since the extension of Mexico's fishery conservation zone to the 200-mi limit. Red snapper 1andings from foreign waters have composed less than 13% of the total U.S. landings since 1973 (Gulf of Mexico Fishery Management Counci1   1981). Western Florida landings varied widely over the years (Camber 1955).  They increased progressively as the fishery developed from  1880  to  1902,  stabilized  as  the Campeche Banks were exploited during 1902-28, dropped with reduced effort during  the  Great  Depression  of 1929-35,  increased  again  as  the economy began to recover in 1936-39, declined markedly with reduced effort from 1939 to 1945 during World War II, and then began to recover again around 1946 (Camber 1955).

In the early 1960's, large numbers of commercia1    vesse1 s were bui1t to fish for   ssnappers and	groupers (Carpenter 1965). The average number of handline vessels in western Florida was 180 in 1957-60; increased to 290 in 1961-65; leveled off at 260 in 1966-70; and increased again to 320 in 1971-74.  The average total number of handline fishermen in western Florida was 780 in 1957-60; increased to 1200 in 1961-65; and stabilized at 1030-1100 in 1967-74 (Florida Sea Grant College 1980; Gulf of Mexico Fishery Management Council 1981).

Porsch et al. (2007) noted that statistics on commercial landings of red snapper have been recorded by the National Marine Fisheries Sevice (NMFS) and its predecessors as far back as 1880. However, there are many gaps in the historical records. Censuses were conducted sporadically prior to 1949 and the water body were the catch was obtained was not recorded until 1963. Landings data obtained from several state and private agencies were used to supplement NMFS landings statistics. The data suggest a substantial red snapper fishery existed as early as 1872. The reconstructed landings are consistent with major events in the history of the fishery, but considerable uncertaintly remains over uncanvassed years between 1890 and the 1920s.

Landings for western Florida declined greatly during 1982-85 to the second-lowest level ever recorded. In 1983-85 catch per unit of effort (catch rate) was relatively high, but declined 26% during that period in the gulf east of the Mississippi River Delta for fish 3 years old and older in the bottom longline and the rod-and-reel fisheries (Parrack and McClellan 1986). Also, in 1983-85, a stock assessment showed that initial biomass (without recruits) declined 17% and recruitment biomass declined 98% in this area (Parrack and McClellan 1986).

The principal commercial fishing grounds used by fishermen from Alabama, Mississippi, Louisiana, and Texas are on the reefs offshore from those States. The average number of handline vessels in these four states was 150 in 1957-60 and 180 in 1961-65; declined to 90 in 1966-70; and leveled off at 80 in 1971-74. The average size of the vessels increased from 30 gross tons in 1957 to 61 gross tons in 1974 (Florida Sea Grant College 1980; Gulf of Mexico Fishery Management Council 1981). Landings peaked in the early 1960�s in Alabama and Texas, and in 1968 in Mississippi. Landings in Alabama, Texas, and Mississippi declined 73%-93% after these peaks in the 1960s, but Louisiana landings increased to a record high in 1984.  A recent stock assessment showed that estimated initial biomass (without recruits) declined 45%, but estimated recruitment biomass increased 21%, for red snapper west of the Mississippi River Delta between 1980 and 1985 (Parrack and McLellan 1986).

An increase in the number of fishing boats and trips may cause competition among boats, because the number of boats that can make a good catch in the prime fishing areas is limited; competition among boats reduces the catch per unit of fishing effort. On the Campeche Banks, the catch rate declined from 1937 to 1940, when the number of fishing trips (and probably the competition) increased, and then greatly increased from 1941 to 1945 when competition probably declined because of reduced fishing effort during World War II. The catch rate declined from 1948 to 1951, but competition probably also declined (Camber 1966).

The commercial red snapper fishery in the GOM during the 1970s ranked eighth in total weight, seventh in total value, and sixth in price per pound (NMFS 1986b, Moran 1988). The only species regularly exploited by offshore fisheries in the mid-1970s in the western gulf was the red snapper and the gulf menhaden, Brevoortia patronus (Hildebrand 1954). The red snapper was the most important of about 17 species in the U.S. snapper fishery (Allen and Tashiro 1976). In the northern GOM, it made up about 86% of the total value of the catch by the large vessels (56-69 ft long) in the snapper-grouper fisher that could reach distant fishing grounds, and in the southeastern gulf, it made up about 37% of the total value of the catch of all vessels in the fishery (Cato and Prochaska 1976). At the time of their study, the Campeche Banks were not fished substantially by American boats for political reasons. Total profits were greater for the larger vessels in the northern gulf because the value per pound was higher for red snapper than for the other species that predominated in thethe southern gulf (Cato and Prochaska 1976).

sections.heading: South Atlantic
sections.content:
As early as 1886, red snapper were fished commercially on the east coast of Florida (Collins 1886).  Captain Latham fished on the east side of Florida, landing his catch
chiefly at Savannah, Georgia.  He generally fished for red snapper from off Cape
Canaveral southwards to the Indian River, in 12 to 15 fathoms (24-30 m) of water.
Comparatively few snapper were caught north of Cape Canaveral. The benthic habitat
fished was noted to differ from the west side of Florida. On the west coast, red snapper were generally caught in depressions of the sea bottom, commonly called �gullies�. On the east coast, the snapper were found most abundant on narrow coral ridges, which usually run parallel with the coast line, and are elevated 2 to 3 feet above the surrounding bottom. Some of these ridges were not more than 100 feet wide, while others may be 300 feet or more.  Red snappers were not so abundant on the east coast as they were on the west coast, but they averaged larger in size. A vessel carrying a crew of seven men made a trip of about two weeks, and an average fare (catch) was about 6,000 pounds (lbs.

A small commercial fishery for red snapper along the Atlantic coast has existed at least since
1902 when 155,000 pounds were landed, primarily in Georgia (SAFMC 2010).  The fishery continued at relatively low levels until after World War II. Landings jumped to approximately 250,000 pounds in 1945. By 1950, they had reached 363,000 pounds. Then, they fluctuated along a generally increasing trend through 1968, peaking at 974,000 pounds and declining to less than 100,000 pounds in 2006.  Commercial landings of red snapper in the south Atlantic increased from 1950 through the 1960s, reaching a peak in 1968 of 1,043,000 lbs (454 mt) (Manooch et al. 1998, White and Palmer 2004). From 1975 through 1998, annual landings fell from 721,100 to 60,949 lbs (White and Palmer 2004).  Eastern Florida landings dominated the catch through the middle 1970s after which a precipitous decline occurred.  During 1990-2001, 58% of the red snapper were landed in Florida (east coast), 6% in Georgia, 25% in South Carolina, and 11% in North Carolina.

sections.heading: Recreational
sections.content:
Gulf of Mexico
The red snapper is one of the most desired species of sport fish in the GOM. Sport fishing grounds overlap commercial grounds (Moran 1988).  In 1965 and 1970, the weight of the commercial catch was less than that of the sport fish catch (Nakamura 1976).  Sport-fishing boats range from small 12-ft private boats to 85-ft party boats (head boats). The number of boats increased from 1956 to 1976 and probably partly displaced the inshore commercial fishery (Allen and Tashiro 1976, St. Amant 1976).

Between 1982 and 1985, the GOM sport fishery catch of red snapper declined by about 60% in Florida and 78% in Louisiana (Moran 1988). In western Florida, the commercial catch also declined sharply between 1982 and 1985. In Louisiana, the commercial fishery may have supplanted the recreational fishery over this period.

The largest annual sport catch for Louisiana from 1979 (when accurate statistics became available) to 1985 was about 2.7 million fish-the highest recorded for any gulf state for the same time period (Moran 1988). For that period, Alabama�s sport catch fluctuated with high catches about every other year; in years between 1979 and 1985, when the sport catch was higher (1979, 1981, and 1983), the commercial catch was also generally higher-except that the commercial catch peaked in 1982. A trend in the Texas catch could not be determined because too few data were available.  Mississippi�s catch remained low, and the commercial catch in 1985 was the lowest in 17 years. Regulations in 1988 in the U.S. waters of the GOM allowed a maximum of 5 fish less than 12 inches in Florida per trip for headboats.

In summary, the sport catch and commercial catch were sometimes positively correlated�possibly because both declined after heavy fishing pressure or because of a natural 30�month cycle in abundance (Camber 1955) � and sometimes negatively correlated, possibly because one fishery replaced the other (Allen and Tashiro 1976).

The red snapper ranked 19th in number of fish caught among groups of sport fish for which statistics  were
recorded in the GOM in 1985; about 2 million red snapper were caught by sport fishermen in the
  GOM that         year (National Marine  Fisheries  Service 1986a).

sections.heading: South Atlantic
sections.content:
The South Atlantic recreational fishery is comprised of the private sector and for-hire sector (SAFMC  2010).  The private sector includes anglers fishing from shore (all land-based structures) and private/rental boats. The for-hire sector is composed of the charterboat and headboat (also called partyboat) sectors. Charterboats generally carry fewer passengers and charge a fee on an entire vessel basis, whereas headboats carry more passengers and payment is per person. The type of service, from a vessel- or passenger-size perspective, affects the flexibility to search different fishing locations during the course of a trip and target different species since larger concentrations of fish are required to satisfy larger groups of anglers.

In the U.S. south Atlantic, recreational landings peaked in 1985 at 619,000 lbs. In 2002, recreational fishermen
landed 390,908 lbs of red snapper (White and Palmer 2004).  Recreational snapper grouper harvest in the South Atlantic has been variable during the period 2003-2008, averaging slightly above 11 million pounds (SAFMC 2010). On average, the private/shore mode of fishing accounted for the largest harvests at around 7.62 million pounds (MP). Well below this harvest level are those of the charter mode at 1.92 MP and headboat at 1.63 MP. Harvests in each state  also fluctuated during the same period. On average, Florida accounted for most of the snapper grouper harvest in the South Atlantic at around 6.90 MP, followed by North Carolina at 2.21 MP, South Carolina at 1.51 MP, and lastly by Georgia at 0.62 MP.


Ecological Role:                                                                                                                        Species Stress: Based on 537 sectioned otoliths from red snapper collected in the southeast Atlantic from 1990-1996, Manooch and Potts (1997) found that red snapper length-at-age determinations were considerably smaller than the length-at-age estimates of red snapper determined from sectioned otoliths collected during 1974-1978 (Nelson and Manooch 1982).  The reduction in length-at-age found by Manooch and Potts (1997) may have been due to variation in sample sizes, differences in interpretation of the sectioned otoliths by investigators, or sustained heavy fishing pressure that may have selectively removed, over many generations, the faster growing individuals of the populations.
Nieland et al. (2007b) sampled 6,159 red snapper landed at a commercial dock in Cameron, Louisiana from October 1998 to May 2004 for morphometrics data and otoliths for age determination. The harvest was almost totally dominated by individuals of ages 2-6 years. Over the course of their sampling, they observed statistically significant decreases in mean total length (TL) of red snapper at ages 2-6 years.  The decline in mean sizes at age might be attributed to density-dependence wherein as the population increased in numbers there was a decrease in resources (food, habitat etc.) per individual fish, which might be manifested in a compensatory decrease in growth rate. Thus declines in red snapper mean TL age may be an expression of recovery from an overfished condition. Conversely, the heavy commercial and recreational harvest of young (juvenile and adult) red snapper in the northern GOM, many of them at the minimum TL required for retention, may have resulted in an inadvertent selection for the survival of slow-growing individuals.
Jackson et al. (2007) noted that red snapper in the GOM are managed as a unit stock and the fishery management plan is based on minimal data regarding reproductive output, and the size and age at sexual maturation is not certain. Differences in size and age at sexual maturity of red snapper between the northeast and north-central GOM were evaluated to test whether the population conforms to the unit stock hypothesis.  Red snapper were collected during the spawning season in 1999, 2000, and 2001 from the GOM off Alabama and Louisiana and were used to describe maturation schedules. Progression of oocyte maturation to vitellogenesis was used to define sexually mature females. Combined data showed the smallest mature red snapper was 267 mm FL and was two years old. The smallest with hydrated oocytes, indicative of imminent spawning, or postovulatory follicles, indicative of recent spawning, were 285 and 297 mm FL respectively, and both were two years old. Red snapper off Alabama reached maturation at smaller sizes and younger ages than those sampled off Louisiana.  Growth rates did not differ between the regions. Such differences in maturation schedules may document an important stock response by red snapper in the GOM to reductions in population size.  Jackson et al. (2007) stated that shifts in maturation schedules in red snapper may be attributable to genetic selection coincident with increased mortality.
Trippel (1995) reviewed fisheries literature worldwide and described situations where fish stock abundances have declined dramatically due to overfishing.  Evidence indicates that stocks comprised of a broad range of sizes and ages are able to spawn more eggs of a large range in size and that these eggs are spawned over a longer period of time than eggs produced by stocks comprised primarily of young fish.  He recommended that management should be pursued on the basis of reducing fishing pressure to levels that permit fish populations to reach older ages. The biological consequences of selective removal of large fish are now more clearly understood, and the excessive removal of fish can no longer be perceived as simply leading to a reduction in the number of eggs produced by the population. Important aspects of egg size and spawning time are also jeopardized by high levels of exploitation.
The truncated age structure and prevalence of faster growth rates of red snapper throughout the GOM are compensatory responses to overfishing that could severely hinder the population�s ability to recover (Saari 2011). Likewise, the temporal decrease in the length-at-age of red snapper and the precipitous decline in landings in the southeast Atlantic, and a low Spawning Potential Ratio (SPR) of 24-32% (SAFMC 2001) suggested that this species may have been overfished (SAFMC 2001, White and Potts 2004). Fisheries managers should consider these maladaptive responses in the stock when evaluating future assessments and management options, as well as the potential stock responses associated with future management options.

Size limits are commonly used to manage commercial and recreational fisheries (Stephen et al. 2010).  Minimum size limits, which are relatively easy to enforce, have been used to restrict total harvest, prevent growth overfishing, and allow individuals at least one spawning event before removal from the fishery. One widely acknowledged disadvantage of size limits is the mortality immediately at release for under-sized fish, but another emerging concern is that size-selective fisheries drive a phenotypic change in the life history traits of a population. Observed phenotypic changes can be driven by genetic and/or environmental influences. If the change is largely influenced by genetic changes, it may not be readily reversed.  Recent studies have shown that high levels of fishing pressure can change the size at age, age at maturation, and size at maturation of fish species. Vermilion snapper (Rhomboplites aurorubens) and red porgy (Pagrus pagrus) were recently shown to exhibit these traits due to differential mortality (Stephen et al. 2010). The study found that the hook-and-line fishery targeted young, but large fish with a fast-growing phenotype.  Their landed catch included many young, large fish, whereas discarded fish had a similar age range and mean ages, but smaller sizes at age than the landed fish. This indicated that the fisheries were altering the genetics of these species by selecting for the survival of slower-growing individuals. A similar shift to slower-growing red snapper populations has been documented in both the southeast Atlantic and the GOM (Manooch and Potts 1997, Nieland and Wilson 2007b). Stephen et al. (2010) concluded that managers need to consider the life history characteristics of each species in light of its susceptibility to phenotypic shifts due to minimum size limits. They suggested that managers should consider adopting an ecosystem-based management plan that includes a multispecies quota system.

Status: Recent stock assessments conducted in both the GOM (SEDAR7 2005, SEDAR7 Update 2009) and southeast Atlantic (SEDAR15 2007, SEDAR24 2010) indicate that red snapper have been subject to overfishing and are considered to be overfished.
Stock Status: Recent studies of red snapper population dynamics in the GOM are consistent with genetic studies	that indicated regional differences in population demographics. Patterson et al. (2001a) reported no significant difference existed in growth rates between red snapper sampled off Alabama and fish sampled off Louisiana west of the mouth of the Mississippi River. Fisher et al. (2004) reported that growth was not significantly different between Alabama and Louisiana samples, but fish sampled off Texas were significantly smaller at age than fish from the other two regions. Further evidence of significant regional differences in population demographics was reported by Woods et al. (2003). They reported fish off Alabama reached sexual maturity at smaller sizes and younger ages than in the western GOM, where size specific fecundity was greater.  The results reported by Woods et al. (2003), Fisher et al. (2004), and Jackson et al. (2007) indicate significant variability of GOM red snapper population dynamics and demographics exists among regions, despite the lack of genetic divergence in selectively neutral markers (Gold et al. 2001, Pruett  et al. 2005, Saillant and Gold 2006).  The main consequence of these studies demonstrating differences in age and growth and sexual maturity of red snapper populations between the eastern and western GOM, is that these differences have been incorporated into the catch-at-age model (CATCHEM); while still conducting the red snapper stock assessment Gulf-wide (SEDAR7 2005, SEDAR7 Update 2009).

Patterson et al. (2008) examined otolith microchemistry of age-0 red snapper in the northern GOM to determine if otolith elemental signatures could be employed as natural tags to estimate post-settlement connectivity.  Fish (n=755) belonging to five successive year classes (1996-2000) were sampled from three GOM regions.  Solution-based analysis of otolith chemistry was accomplished with sector field-induced coupled plasma-mass spectrometry (Ba, Mg, Mn, and Sr) and inductively coupled plasma-optical emissions spectrometry (Ca). Several regional trends observed for individual elements were consistent among year classes, yet elemental signatures were significantly different among years, as well as among regions (MANOVA, p<0.0001). Jackknifed classification accuracies from linear discriminant function analysis approached 80% (mean = 78.4%) in all years except 1998 (62.4%). Overall, these results indicate otolith elemental signatures may serve as effective region-specific natural tags of GOM red snapper.

Sluis (2011) investigated habitat-specific and region-specific otolith microchemistry of age-0 red snapper belonging to the 2005-2007 year classes.  Year class-specific quadratic discriminant function analyses (QDFAs) distinguished nursery areas with 71-84% accuracy.  Maximum likelihood analyses identified sources of sub-adult and adult red snapper sampled during the summer of 2006-2008 from the western Gulf and Mexico regions based on year-class specific otolith chemical core concentrations. Locally derived and Louisiana recruits were apparent among red snapper collected off Texas, but were inconclusive to estimate connectivity between the western Gulf and Mexico regions. Otoliths of red snapper collected from platforms and other habitats off Alabama, Louisiana, and Texas during the summer of 2007 and 2008 were analyzed to determine if platforms impart detectable signatures based on seventeen trace metals.  Mean jackknifed classification accuracies from QDFAs indicated higher success from discriminating among regions (86%) than habitats (79%).  Maximum likelihood estimate analyses estimated region and habitat origin of red snapper collected from natural habitats off Florida, Louisiana, and Texas during the summer of 2009.  Platform signatures were evident in otoliths from red snapper collected off Florida, a region devoid of platforms, possibly reflecting a western Gulf contribution to the western Gulf sub-stock. The microchemical otolith signatures of western Gulf red snapper demonstrated discrete regional populations with some interpopulation mixing, further supporting the metapopulation structure. Sluis (2011) suggested that further study may show that Gulf red snapper populations should be divided into four separate sub-stocks (TX, LA, AL/MS and FL), instead of the two-stock management approach currently established in the U.S. GOM.

No studies exist indicating differences in demographics between populations of red snapper in the southeastern Atlantic that would justify treating them as separate stocks or sub-stocks (SEDAR15 2005, SEDAR24 2010).

sections.heading: Commercial
sections.content:
The red snapper fishery in the GOM has been in existence since the mid-1800s (Hood et al. 2007).  Federal management of the fisheries in the GOM began in 1976 with the passage of the Magnusen-Stevens Fishery Conservation and Management Act and the establishment of the Gulf of Mexico Fishery Management Council (GMFMC).   One of the first fishery management plans (FMP) developed by the GMFMC was the Reef Fish FMP (GMFMC 1981). This FMP was implemented in November 1984 and established the first red snapper size and bag limits. In 1988, the stock was determined to be overfished . Since then, the fishery has been managed to stay within total allowable catch levelsin order to rebuild the stock. Management methods have included size limits, bag limits, seasonal closures, trip limits, and license limitation programs. The success of these methods has beem limited in part due to high levels of juvenile red snapper mortality associated with shrimp trawling, high rates of discard mortality from the directed fishery, and socioeconomic requirements of the directed fisheries to maintain some minimal level of harvest.

Strelcheck and Hood (2007) outlined strategies being undertaken to help rebuild the red snapper population in the GOM. Since the GOM population was declared overfished in the late 1980s, subsequent stock assessments (Schirripa and Legault 1999, NOAA Fisheries 2006, SEDAR7 2005, Porsch 2007) have concluded the population remains overfished and is undergoing overfishing. The first rebuilding plan was established in 1989, setting a target of rebuilding the red snapper population by 2000 (GMFMC 1989). Changes in scientific advice and new information on red snapper biology resulted in revisions to this plan. The most recent revision was approved in 2004 and set a goal of rebuilding red snapper to maximum sustainable yield by 2032 (GMFMC 2004). Despite the recent implementation of this plan, a 2005 red snapper population assessment indicated additional management restrictions were necessary for this plan to be successful (SEDAR7 2005). Managers are now confronted with several challenges to recover red snapper including addressing bycatch in the shrimp fishery and reducing discard and fishing mortality in the directed fishery. Social and economic considerations, competing conservation mandates, regulatory consistency, scientific uncertainty, political intentions, and the length of time allowed for recovery further complicate management and stock rebuilding. Managers will need to focus on short-term directions and periodically adjust management strategies to ensure adequate rebuilding progress is made. This will allow managers to incorporate new information and unanticipated developments when making adjustments to red snapper and shrimp regulations, should either insufficient progress or unexpected events occur.

Earlier in this review, huge bycatches of age-0 and age-1 red snapper were described associated with the shrimp trawl fisheries in the GOM (Branstetter 1997, Gallaway and Cole 1998, Gallaway et al. 1999).  There also are huge bycatches of undersized red snapper associated with the recreational headboat fishery and commercial hook-and-line fishery being discarded in both the GOM and the U.S. south Atlantic (Dorf 2003; Sauls and Wilson  2010; GSAFFI 2008, 2010; Diamond and Campbell 2009 ).  A broad-based public consensus has emerged that bycatch should be minimized to levels approaching insignificance (Crowder and Murawki 1998).  Bycatches in their various forms can have significant consequences for populations, food webs, and ecosystems.  The economic effects of bycatches can influence not only the levels of yields to fisheries, but also may have major effects on allocations among competing fisheries. The lack of comprehensive monitoring programs in most areas to assess bycatches and integrate them into population and multispecies models seriously impedes a full understanding of bycatch consequences and the efficacy of measures for their amelioration. Nevertheless, where evidence for significant bycatches exists, a risk-adverse and perhaps adaptive management philosophy is clearly warranted.  Establishing the benefits and costs associated with bycatch management is a priority as managers attempt to define the practicality of bycatches approaching zero given the institutional, scientific, and industry resources necessary to accomplish the job.

The most recent red snapper stock assessment for the GOM suggested that red snapper in the western GOM were beginning to recover from overfishing (SEDAR7 Update 2009), and it is expected that as the stock rebuilds, there will be a shift to an older age structure (SEDAR7 2005, Allman and Fitzhugh 2007). While an increase in red snapper biomass has been observed in the fisheries, an age shift is not readily apparent (Saari 2011), as well as in the stock assessments, and other recent studies (SEDAR7 2005, Allman and Fitzhugh 2007; Nieland et al. 2007a).  Identification and protection of the strong year-classes is necessary in order to 1) allow more red snapper to reach maximum spawning potential and ensure the success of future year-classes, and 2) repopulate the older age classes to eliminate the severely truncated age structure. It has been recommended that managers regularly review the red snapper rebuilding plan to include advances in scientific research and adapt the current policy in order to address the short-term directions while not losing site of the long-term goal (Strelcheck and Hood 2007, SEDAR7 Update

sections.heading: South Atlantic
sections.content:
The rapid decline of commercial and recreational landings of red snapper off the U.S. south Atlantic in the early 1980�s prompted the South Atlantic Fisheries Management Council to establish a minimum size of 12 inches and the bag limit of 10  red snapper per day in 1983 (SAFMC 1983).  In 1991, with landings of red snapper still declining, the SAFMC increased the minimum  size to 20 inches and the snapper bag limit was reduced from 10 fish to only two red snappers per day (SAFMC 1991).

The most recent stock assessments for red snapper in the South Atlantic (SEDAR15 2007, SEDAR24 2010) found that red snapper were seriously overfished.  The red snapper fishery in the south Atlantic was closed January 4, 2010. Members of the SAFMC, in a 9-4 vote, approved Amendment 17A to the Snapper Grouper Fishery Management Plan to end overfishing of red snapper and rebuild the South Atlantic stock during its June 2010 meeting in Orlando (SAFMC 2010). The amendment was designed to meet the Congressional mandates of the reauthorized Magnuson-Stevens Act.
Management measures that were considered by the SAFMC through Amendment 17A included:                                1) a continuation of the closure of the red snapper fishery; 2) a new area closure off of northeastern Florida and southern Georgia, where fishing for all snapper grouper species in water depths of 98 - 240 feet would be prohibited (with the exception of spearfishing and use of black sea bass pots); 3) a requirement for the use non-stainless steel circle hooks when fishing for snapper grouper species north of 28 degrees N. latitude; and 4) the development of a fishery-independent monitoring program to help track the rebuilding and recovery of red snapper (SAFMC 2010).
In addition to the red snapper closure, the area closure was considered to be necessary to reduce harvest of red snapper by 76%, including the estimated number of fish that die even when released (SAFMC 2010). The area closure was a highly controversial issue, and the Council discussed its size and configuration in an effort to meet the mandates of the Act and minimiz���e negative economic and social impacts. The Council reduced the size of the area, eliminating more than 1200 square miles off the coast of Georgia, after modifying the biological parameters and considering other variables such as enforcement compliance and effort shifts in the fishery. Eventually, the SAFMC decided to drop the area closure but decided to retain the closure of the red snapper fishery.
During a June 2012 meeting in Orlando, the SAFMC requested an emergency rule to provide recreational and commercial fishermen with the opportunity to harvest a limited number of red snapper during the fall of 2012 (SAFMC News Release June 18, 2012).  The Council determined that 13,067 red snapper could be harvested after reviewing the latest estimates of total removals of red snapper (dead discards).  The emergency rule recommended allows a total of 9,399 fish to be caught by recreational fishermen during three-day weekend openings, and 3,668 fish or 20,818 pounds (gutted weight) to be landed by the commercial fishery.  The commercial fishery would open in seven-day �mini-season� increments subject to the quota, with a limit of 50 pounds per trip and no size limits.  The current allocation for the red snapper fishery is 72% recreational and 28% commercial.

sections.heading: Commercial Fisheries Value
sections.content:
Commercial fishermen along the east coast of Florida dominated the commercial red snapper fishery until the mid-1970s (SAFMC 2010). By the late 1970s, the fishery had expanded into Georgia, South Carolina and North Carolina, and it declined in Florida. In 1993-2007, logbook-reported commercial landings of red snapper ranged from 202,000 pounds (whole weight) worth approximately $544,000 in current year dollars in 2001 to 81,000 pounds worth $263,000 in 2006. Dockside revenue and pounds landed fluctuate in the same direction, which suggests that ex-vessel demand is price elastic. The policy implication is that regulations that reduce industry landings in the short-term are expected to reduce dockside revenue in the short-term. Conversely, dockside revenue is expected to increase over time if regulations successfully increase biomass and landings. Average annual dockside prices for red snapper increased steadily in current year dollars. However, prices in 2007 dollars declined through 2002 before increasing in 2006 and 2007.

According to the NMFS logbook database, on average in 2003-2007, 1,385 trips a year landed
121,000 pounds of red snapper worth $388,000 in 2007 dollars, and 2.0 million pounds of other
species worth $4.5 million on trips with at least one pound of red snapper (SAFMC 2010). Clearly, red snapper was not the primary revenue species on most of these trips. Boat revenue for all species
and trips came to $9.8 million, with 4% for red snapper. Among the 220 boats that landed at
least one pound of red snapper, 102 boats landed less than 100 pounds of red snapper per year,
84 boats landed 101-1000 pounds, and 34 boats landed more than 1000 pounds.

Red snapper was the primary source of trip revenue on an average of 163 trips per year, 12% of
the trips on which it was landed (SAFMC 2010). These trips accounted for approximately 31% of
the total commercial harvest, with an annual average of 38,000 pounds of red snapper worth
$125,000 in 2007 dollars, and 49,000 pounds of other species worth $103,000. On the 1,222 trips wherein red snapper was a lesser source of trip revenue, it accounted for an annual average of 82,000 pounds of red snapper ($263,000 in 2007 dollars) and 1.9 million pounds of other species ($4.4 million in 2007 dollars). Red snapper is part of the mid-shelf snapper grouper complex that includes scamp, gag, vermilion snapper, red porgy, gray triggerfish, and red grouper, among other species. Red snapper is most commonly caught on trips with vermilion snapper, gag or scamp as the primary revenue species on the trip. Red snapper is landed mostly in South Carolina, Georgia and northeast Florida, and central-southeast Florida and it is caught mostly with vertical lines.

sections.heading: Recreational Value
sections.content:
Gillig et al. (2000) stated they had estimated the recreational value of red snapper fishing in the Gulf of Mexico. The paper discusses the statistical approaches taken, but no quantitative estimates for the fishery were presented.

Estimates of the economic value of a day of saltwater recreational fishing in the South Atlantic
indicate that the mean value of access per marine recreational fishing trip is $109.31 for the
South Atlantic (Haab et al. 2001). While this estimate is not specific to snapper grouper fishing
trips, it may shed light on the magnitude of an angler�s willingness to pay for this type of
recreational experience.

Willingness to pay for an incremental increase in catch and keep rates per trip was also estimated
to be $3.01 for bottom fish species by Haab et al. (2001). Whitehead et al. (2001) estimated the
marginal willingness to pay to avoid a one fish red snapper bag limit decrease to be $1.06 to
$2.20.  Finally, Haab et al. (2001) provided a compensating variation (the amount of money a
person would have to receive to be no worse off after a reduction of the bag limit) estimate of
$2.49 per fish when calculated across all private boat anglers that targeted snapper grouper
species in the South Atlantic.

In their study of the North Carolina for-hire fishery, Dumas et al. (2009) estimated several
measures of consumer surplus (CS) for anglers fishing through the for-hire mode. Anglers were
distinguished as to whether fishing was their primary or secondary purpose for taking the trip to
the coasts. An additional snapper-grouper caught and kept would generate consumer surplus of
$93.51 per trip, for primary purpose anglers, and $60.79 per trip for secondary purpose anglers.
Consumer surplus per site per trip for primary purpose anglers ranged from $4.88 to $27.03 in
charter trips taken in Federal waters, or from $0.35 to $9.55 in charter trips taken in state waters.
The corresponding range of values for secondary purpose anglers were $0.24 to $16.62 for
charter trips in Federal waters, or $0.12 to $16.54 for charter trips in state waters. On headboat
trips in both state and Federal waters, consumer surplus per site per trip ranged from $0.59 to
$4.12 for primary purpose anglers, and from $0.48 to $4.76 for secondary purpose anglers.
Consumer surplus trip for the opportunity to take a for-hire fishing trip was estimated at $624.02
per angler per trip on charterboats and $101.64 per anger per trip on headboats.

In addition to the above economic values, there are estimates of the economic value of a red
snapper and a red snapper trip in the GOM provided by NMFS (2008). Although these values are derived for the Gulf of Mexico recreational fishery, they can be used as proxy values for the South Atlantic fishery. It is noted, however, that red snapper is a significantly more important recreational
target fishery in the Gulf of Mexico than in the South Atlantic. As a result, the estimates of
economic value may overstate the true values for the South Atlantic. The estimated CS to a
recreational angler of one red snapper is $6.04, while the estimated CS of a red snapper fishing
trip is $53.53. These values were used to estimate the impacts of the red snapper interim rule in
the South Atlantic (SAFMC 2010).  Extrapolations were made to estimate the respective values of the various recreational fisheries from North Carolina to Florida. While the total value for the snapper-grouper fisheries is in the millions of dollars, the value of the recreational fisheries for red snapper was not presented; since it was not separated from the other species of reef fish

sections.heading: STOCK ENHANCEMENT
sections.content:
Induced Breeding: Red snapper were spawned in captivity when held at temperatures and photoperiods which approximated conditions in the Texas Gulf of Mexico region (Arnold et al. 1978).  Multiple spawns were observed in May and June 1978.  Minton et al (1983) induced red snapper to ovulate following injections of human chorionic gonadotropin (HCG).  Females were injected initially with 1.1 IU/g body weight. When subsequent injections were necessary, 0.55 IU/g of body weight was used. Ovulation occurred between 42 and 56 h following injection. Eggs were wet stripped and fertilized simultaneously with sperm from two males. Initial mitosis was detected 30 min post fertilization.  Hatching occurred in 20 h at 27oC.  Further details concerning induced spawning are given by Collins et al. (1996) and Bourque (2007).
Phelps et al. (2009) provides a good review and new information concerning spawning of red snapper in response to hormonal induction in a hatchery setting.  When, female red snapper collected from off Alabama in the GOM were injected with HCG, 56% of the females ovulated. Fecundity (ovulated floating eggs) was noted to vary; for 60 spawns it averaged 197,212 eggs/kg female. Percentage hatch averaged 42.1%.  Wild-caught and adult red snapper can be held in confinement and natural spawning obtained when temperature and photoperiod are controlled. Adult red snapper held in tanks (8-10 fish per tank), where temperature and photoperiod were adjusted, spawned naturally 63 times over a 105-day period, with a mean egg production per tank of 4.2 million eggs. Mean fertilization rate, hatch rate, and survival at 36-40 hours post-hatching were 90.5%, 83%, and 49%. Natural spawns produce better quality seed, but the occurrence of fertilized spawns was unpredictable.  Hormone-induced spawns are easier to schedule but egg quality can be variable. Further information on induced spawning of red snapper can be found in theses by Bootes (1998), Bourque (2001), Bueno (2002), and Papanikos (2004), and from meeting abstracts (Phelps et al. 1996,  Bourque et al. 2000, Laidley and Ostrowski 2001, Phelps 2003).
Rearing: The diet of juvenile red snapper in the wild has been fairly well documented (Camber 1955, Bradley and Bryan 1976, Futch and Bruger 1976, Moran 1988, Lee 1998) and consists of prey items with high levels of protein and moderate levels of lipids. Nutritional data regarding levels of crude protein and lipid necessary to promote growth in Lutjanidae are sparse (Miller et al. 2005).   Some information exists for red snapper with the publications by Wakeman et al. (1979) and Marnell (1999).
Many marine fish can be held in captivity and will spawn naturally when given a proper environment and an appropriate diet. Papanikos et al. (2003) compared egg and larval quality of red snapper from natural spawns of domesticated brooders with hormone-induced spawns of wild fish.  Eggs and larvae from natural spawns were more viable in terms of fertilization, hatching, and survival rate. Also, eggs from natural spawns were larger, and eggs and recently hatched larvae had large oil-globules. The findings indicated that natural spawning of red snapper can be a sustainable and reliable source of good quality eggs.

Papanikos et al. (2008) conducted two experiments to evaluate the spontaneous spawning of red snapper under controlled temperature and photoperiods in association with broodstock diets supplemented with oils rich in polyunsaturated fatty acids.  In experiment 1, broodstock were fed a standard diet (ST1) and one enriched with menhaden oil (ER1) over a 355-d period.  ER1-influenced egg fatty acid profile, however, it did not positively influence egg production. Both diets produced highly viable eggs and larvae but results varied with treatments. In Experiment 2, broodfish were fed either with a standard diet (ST2) or one supplemented with oils (ER 2) rich in docosahexaenoic and arachidonic acid using a 203-d cycle. Both treatments produced eggs but fertilization rates ranged from 0-10%.  There was no clear influence of the diets on egg fatty acid profiles.  These results indicate that red snapper can spawn spontaneously in tanks under controlled environmental conditions and produce viable eggs and larvae when fed diets based on squid, shrimp, and fish. The fatty acid composition of the diets was reflected in the eggs to some degree, but the oil enrichments did not further enhance the reproductive performance of egg quality under the conditions of this study.
The challenge with red snapper aquaculture has centered around meeting the food
requirements for larvae at the time of exogenous feeding (English 2008). Snapper larvae demand sufficient quantities of small prey organisms at the onset of first-feeding (Lan 2001, Ogle and Lotz 2000, Lemus et al. 2004, Rhodes and Phelps 2008). Copepod nauplii have proved to be an appropriate prey for red snapper larvae (Ogle et al. 2002, Lemus et al. 2002, Ogle et al. 2005).

Chigbu et al. (2002) evaluated the relationship between copepod nauplii available per fish on the day of first feeding and survival of larval red snapper. Additionally, they assessed the suitability of various types of containers, from 10 L black plastic containers through 20 L polycarbonate containers filled with 100 L of seawater, for rearing red snapper larvae. There was a significant positive correlation between prey number per fish on the day of first feeding and survival of red snapper Similarly, larval survival was positively correlated with the number of copepod nauplii.

Rearing studies using 10 L and 20 L black plastic containers resulted in 100% mortality of larvae by day 7 post-hatch (Chigbu et al. 2002).  Experiments carried out using polycarbonate containers and 200 L black tubs containing 50 L or 100 L of brown seawater resulted in 0 to 34% larval survival. The number of larvae that survived was significantly higher in polycarbonate containers than in black tubes with 50 or 100 L of water.  Differences in larval survival in the culture containers probably resulted from interactions between the amount of light present in the containers and container color that, presumably, affected prey visibility to, and therefore consumption by larval snapper.

 In 2004 experiments were conducted to formulate red snapper culture methods using marine primary nursery ponds (English 2008). Twenty 0.1 ha ponds were prepared with either 250 or 500 kg/ha rice bran organic fertilizer. Two day-old red snapper larvae were stocked in ponds at either 5, 7, or 10 days post-filling (dpf). At the end of 30 d the ponds were harvested. Zooplankton results showed high densities of copepod nauplii (averaging 774.65 � 962.9 org/L) during the first 5 days following larval stocking in ponds receiving the 250 kg/ha fertilizer rate. These low rate ponds experienced significantly higher densities of nauplii than the 500 kg/ha ponds (p=0.021). A high degree of variation in nauplii abundance was observed between and within ponds during the study period. Average red snapper survival also varied greatly between treatments, ranging from nearly 0% survival in treatment 2 (250 kg/ha and stocked 7 dpf) to 1.07 % in treatment 5 (500 kg/ha, stocked 10 dpf, and continuous aeration). The treatment receiving 250 kg/ha of rice bran and stocked 10 days post-filling resulted in higher snapper survival when compared to the remaining low fertilizer treatments. Following these results recommendations for future research might suggest incorporating continuous aeration with the low rate fertilizer treatment and stocking larvae at 10 dpf. In addition to the pond study a computer model was constructed to predict the best day to stock red snapper determined by copepod nauplii density. The model used a forecasting method incorporating 29 pond parameters and resulted in an adjusted R� of 0.6954. The model was inconsistent at predicting nauplii abundance for 3 out-of-sample pond nauplii counts and therefore was not recommended as an appropriate management design. Alternatively, an empirical approach was evaluated to determine the number of ponds that would be needed to satisfy stocking requirements under conditions of uncertainty. This approach yielded more manageable results.

Williams, et al. (2004) described the development of yolk-sac larvae of red snapper from endogenous utilization of nutrient sources to the development of feeding ability.  Larvae from several spawns were reared at a salinity of 31 g/L and a temperature of 28oC.  Yolk utilization rate, changes in body parameters and the development of morphological characters were observed. Maximum standard length (SL) and body depth were observed concurrently with yolk-sac exhaustion at 56 hours post-fertilization (hpf).  A decrease in SL, body width and body depth was observed following yolk-sac exhaustion. Orbit pigmentation, followed by jaw articulation, were observed at 65 hpf. Substantial cranial and body cavity development occurred in the absence of visibly yolk-sac material and less than 2% of the oil globule volume at hatching were observed at the time of development of feeding ability. This indicates an absence of a transitional feeding period and the critical nature of first-feeding in this species within controlled environments.

Ogle and Lotz (2006) developed an experimental-scale rearing system for larval red snapper that combined extensive outdoor production of live-feed zooplankton with intensive larval fish rearing. The salient features of the system are (1) use of size graded copepods as life feed; (2) culture in clear water; (3) three-phase water management consisting of an initial static water phase followed by a volume doubling phase in which water is gradually added and, finally, a recirculation-biofiltration phase; (4) a lowered salinity of 25 g/L water; and (5) an indoor location at constant temperature under artificial light.  A total of 19,835 juvenile red snapper were produced from 12 larval rearing tanks in three separate batches with an overall survival of 16.5%.  Survival varied from 1% to 31% in individual larval rearing tanks.  Water quality variables (oxygen, temperature, salinity, total and un-ionized ammonia, nitrite, nitrate, pH, and alkalinity) were not significantly correlated with larval fish survival. A mean number of 5.36 copepods/mL was added daily to larval tanks during the culture period, with a range of 0.57-23.48 copepods/mL. There was no correlation between mean feed rates and survival in individual tanks. The mean residual copepods per milliliter averaged 2.24, with a range of from 0 to 15.86.  There was a significant negative correlation between residual copepod density and survival.

Larval mortality at first feeding remains a fundamental challenge for the culture and artificial propagation of red snapper (Williams et al. 2004). Red snapper show evidence of starvation within hours of the appearance of functional mouth parts. The observed reductions in larval body parameters may be symptomatic of tissue reabsorption, and suggest that red snapper larvae may be more sensitive to starvation than commonly cultured fish species. Further advances in larval rearing protocols are likely to come from an improved understanding of the reproductive life history and the energetic dynamics of the prefeeding stages.

Feeding: Miller et al. (2005) formulated twelve diets to contain varying levels of protein and lipid to evaluate their effects on growth and body condition of juvenile and sub-adult red snapper. In trial 1, juvenile red snapper (initial weight 5.9 g) were offered diets with graded levels of dietary protein (32%, 36%, 40%, and 46%) and practical protein to energy ratios. In trial 2, juvenile red snapper (initial weight 8.64 g) were offered isonitrogenous diets (44% protein) containing graded levels of dietary lipid (8%, 10%, 12%, 14%). Sub-adult fish (initial mean weight 151.5 g) were used in trial 3 and maintained on diets similar to trail 1 (32-44% protein). Sub-adult fish (initial mean weight 178.3 g) in trial 4 were offered isonitrogenous diets containing 32% dietary protein and graded levels of dietary lipid (6%, 8%, 10%, 12%).  There were no significant differences in growth, feed conversion ratio (FER), or survival of juvenile fish. Juvenile fish offered 32% dietary protein exhibited a significantly greater (P=0.0497) protein conversion efficiency (PCE) than fish offered a diet of 44% dietary protein.  Juvenile fish in trial 2 also had significantly higher (P=0.005) intraperitoneal fat ratios (IPFRs) at 14% dietary lipid than fish offered diets containing 8-10 % lipid, and displayed trends towards greater protein as a percent of whole-body composition at 8-10% dietary lipid.  Sub-adult snapper in trials 3 and 4 showed no significant differences in growth, FER or survival.  However, in trial 4 there was a general trend towards increasing % weight gain (P=0.0615), FER (P=0.0601) andfinal mean weight (P = 0.0596) with increasing dietary levels of lipid.  Fish in trial 4 offered 6% dietary lipid also had significantly lower (P= 0.03439) IPFR and PCE (P= 0.0188) than fish offered 12% dietary lipid. Based on data obtained in these trials, inclusion of dietary protein at levels of 32-36% appears sufficient to support growth. For this level of protein, dietary lipid should be ~ 10% in order to meet the energetic demands of the fish and to spare dietary protein growth.
Stocking: Pruder et al. (1999) described the U.S. Gulf of Mexico Stock Enhancement five-year program: 1999-2004.  They noted that many fisheries in the United States are under stress from overexploitation and/or habitat degradation.  In response, Congress mandated the restoration of depleted fisheries, within a given time period.  Preliminary estimates indicate that conventional restrictive management protocols alone cannot satisfy these congressional mandates. The tools and options of fishery management need to be expanded to include proactive actions and activities. One such potentially proactive option is stock enhancement. A decision was made to fund a research stock enhancement program to better evaluate its potential value. The U.S. Gulf of Mexico Marine Stock Enhancement Program (USGMSEP) is a multi-institutional, multi-year and multi-million dollar integrated science effort to develop and demonstrate sound and broad-based stock enhancement methods to augment conventional management strategies. The authors identified and characterized the critical components of an integrated, scientifically sound investigation of a highly complex stock enhancement system. It initiates use of a computerized management approach which enhances planning, review, and evaluation of efforts by identifying and tracking critical activities, institutional assignments and responsibilities, developing time line and completion projections, and managing resource allocation.
Blaylock et al. (2000) described the components of the USGMSEP.  The program investigated the use of aquaculture technology as an additional tool for the restoration of marine stocks, particularly the red snapper. Molecular genetics, feed production technology, and larval production technology were used to address three critical stock enhancement issues: 1) understanding the nature of the system to be enhanced, 2) producing robust, compatible individuals for release, and 3) critically evaluating the effects of releases. The program developed: 1) microsatellite and mitochondrial DNA markers that allow population analysis, broodstock analysis, and offspring analysis; 2) a method of copepod culture that allows mass production of red snapper; and 3) a manageable repeatable procedure for larval rearing of large numbers of red snapper, a species which heretofore could not be cultured in large numbers.
Stock enhancement has been proposed to facilitate stock recovery for GOM red snapper (Gibson et al. 2010).  While recent advances in red snapper culture have made stock enhancement more feasible (Williams et al. 2004, Ogle and Lotz  2006, Rhodes and Phelps 2008, Phelps et al. 2009), there are other concerns that need to be addressed. Among these are the potential effect of stocking on genetic diversity of red snapper populations, some of which already may be showing signs of being genetically compromised due to overfishing (Saillant and Gold 2006, Gold and Saillant 2007). Another concern is whether large-scale stocking efforts are likely to have a measurable positive effect on red snapper Spawning Stock Biomass (SSB) (Maloney et al. 2003). Clearly, if stock enhancement is pursued further for GOM red snapper, then development of a method to estimate the effect of stocking on red snapper population size will be essential.
Gibson et al. (2010) evaluated otolith chemical signatures as natural tags to distinguish wild from hatchery-produced juvenile red snapper. Otoliths were sampled from 59 hatchery-reared fish and 146 wild fish collected over the continental shelf from northwest Florida to Texas. One sagitta from each fish was cleaned, dissolved in ultrapure nitric acid, and analyzed with a sector field inductively coupled plasma mass spectrometry to test for differences in otolith element: Ca ratios (Ba:Ca, Li:Ca, Mg:Ca, Mn:Ca, and Sr:Ca) between wild and hatchery fish. The second sagitta was cleaned, ground to fine powder, and analyzed with stable isotope ratio mass spectrometry to test for differences in delta (?) values of the stable isotopes 13C and 18O.  Significant differences were found in otolith chemical signatures between hatchery and wild juveniles. Jackknifed classification accuracies from linear discriminant function analysis indicated that hatchery fish could be distinguished from wild fish with 100% accuracy based on otolith chemical signatures. Overall results suggest that otolith chemical signatures may be employed as effective natural tags for mass marking of future stockings of red snapper or other marine fishes to estimate the hatchery contribution to wild populations.
A critical component to any stock enhancement program is assessing the effect of stocking on spawning stock biomass (SSB) or fisheries yield. Gibson et al. (2010) concluded that a relatively simple approach to marking hatchery-reared fish could be manipulation of hatchery water chemistry or feeds such that unique chemical signatures are imparted onto otoliths of hatchery-reared fish. In the case of ?13C values, this could be accomplished simply by including terrestrial plant material, with its lower ?13C values, in hatchery feeds.

sections.content:
Stock Assessments:The red snapper fishery in the GOM has been in existence since the mid-1800s (Hood et al. 2007).  Federal management of the fisheries in the GOM began in 1976 with the passage of the Magnusen-Stevens Fishery Conservation and Management Act and the establishment of the Gulf of Mexico Fishery Management Council (GMFMC).

sections.heading: ECOLOGICAL INTERACTIONS
sections.content:
Competition-The grey snapper (Lutjanus griseus) probably competitively excludes juvenile red snapper from inshore waters in some localities (Smith 1976).
Predation-Sharks sometimes strike at fish being brought up by hook and line (Bradley and Bryan 1976).
Parasites/Diseases-Parasitic leeches have been found attached to the gills of red snapper (Williams 1979).

sections.heading: HUMAN IMPACTS
sections.content:
Oil Spills:Red snapper in an offshore oilfield were not contaminated with petroleum hydrocarbons, although 13 other species of fish were contaminated (Middleditch et al. 1979). No evidence of toxic effects was found in testes of five red snapper from oilfields in the gulf (Scott et al. 1980).
Contaminants:Concentrations of chlorinated hydrocarbons were lower in flesh samples of red snapper than in samples of species with a natural oil content (3% of oil), though contaminant levels in this group were low (Stout 1980). Wet snapper fillets had an average of 0.039 ppm of DDT and metabolites; the U.S. legal maximum is 5 ppm (Stout 1980). The same fillets had 0.121 ppm of PCB�s; the U.S. legal limit is 3 ppm. Only one of nine samples of red snapper had detectable levels of the pesticides dieldrinand endrin.
